# GTNW leaders & cabinets dataset

Coverage 1789-2030, data current to 2026-10. 33 named nations, 12967 office-holder records. Tier-3 nations use generic titles (generic_roles.json).

Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, official government/parliament histories where cited, rulers.org and worldstatesmen.org (Ben Cahoon) as cross-checks, Wikipedia only as a cross-check. Holders flagged `uncertain` have conflicting or unverified dates.

## Austria (Habsburg Monarchy / Austria-Hungary / Republic) (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1804-08 | Habsburg Monarchy (Archduchy of Austria; Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire) | absolute_monarchy | Vienna | death_in_office, foreign_occupation, revolution |
| 1804-08 | 1848-03 | Austrian Empire (Metternich system) | absolute_monarchy | Vienna | death_in_office, royal_dismissal, revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1848-03 | 1860-10 | Austrian Empire (revolution and neo-absolutism) | absolute_monarchy | Vienna (court at Olmütz Oct 1848-1849) | royal_dismissal, abdication, revolution |
| 1860-10 | 1867-12 | Austrian Empire (constitutional experiments) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Vienna | royal_dismissal, foreign_occupation |
| 1867-12 | 1918-11 | Austria-Hungary (Dual Monarchy) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Vienna (Budapest for the Kingdom of Hungary) | royal_dismissal, abdication, revolution, assassination |
| 1918-11 | 1933-03 | Republic of (German-)Austria (First Republic) | parliamentary_republic | Vienna | no_confidence, general_election, coup |
| 1933-03 | 1938-03 | Federal State of Austria (Austrofascism / Ständestaat) | one_party_state | Vienna | coup, assassination, foreign_occupation |
| 1938-03 | 1945-04 | Annexed to Germany (Ostmark / Alpine and Danube Reichsgaue) | colonial_or_occupied | Vienna (Berlin as Reich capital) | foreign_occupation |
| 1945-04 | 1955-07 | Second Republic under Allied occupation | parliamentary_republic | Vienna (four-power occupied) | no_confidence, general_election, foreign_occupation |
| 1955-07 | present | Second Republic (sovereign, neutral; EU member from 1995) | parliamentary_republic | Vienna | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, presidential_dismissal, impeachment |

- **Habsburg Monarchy (Archduchy of Austria; Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire) (1789–1804-08)**: Hereditary Habsburg-Lorraine succession (Pragmatic Sanction). The State Chancellor/foreign minister acts as leading minister.
- **Austrian Empire (Metternich system) (1804-08–1848-03)**: Francis II proclaimed himself Emperor of Austria (Aug 1804) and dissolved the HRE (Aug 1806). Vienna occupied by Napoleon 1805 and 1809. Under the incapacitated Ferdinand I (1835-48) a State Conference (Archduke Ludwig, Metternich, Kolowrat) ruled.
- **Austrian Empire (revolution and neo-absolutism) (1848-03–1860-10)**: Revolution forces Metternich out (Mar 1848); Ferdinand abdicates for Franz Joseph (2 Dec 1848). Constitutions of 1848/49 revoked by the Sylvester Patent (Dec 1851).
- **Austrian Empire (constitutional experiments) (1860-10–1867-12)**: October Diploma (1860) and February Patent (1861) create an Imperial Council; ministers remain responsible to the emperor. Defeat by Prussia (1866) leads to the Compromise with Hungary.
- **Austria-Hungary (Dual Monarchy) (1867-12–1918-11)**: Emperor of Austria is also King of Hungary. Two governments (Cisleithania/Austria and Hungary), each with a Minister-President; three common ('k.u.k.') ministries for Foreign Affairs, War and Finance answer to the monarch. Minister-Presidents served at the emperor's pleasure; Reichsrat obstruction often led to rule by Emergency Decree (§14). Game: the Austrian Minister-President is head of government; the common Foreign, War and Finance Ministers are the cabinet. Hungarian Minister-Presidents (e.g. Andrássy 1867-71, Kálmán Tisza 1875-90, István Tisza 1903-05, 1913-17) are a separate, powerful actor.
- **Republic of (German-)Austria (First Republic) (1918-11–1933-03)**: Chancellor elected by the National Council (to 1929), then appointed by the President after the 1929 constitutional amendment; responsible to parliament. President elected by the Federal Assembly (direct election introduced 1929 but not held).
- **Federal State of Austria (Austrofascism / Ständestaat) (1933-03–1938-03)**: Dollfuss suspended parliament (Mar 1933); Fatherland Front sole party; civil war Feb 1934; May 1934 corporatist constitution. Dollfuss murdered in the Nazi July Putsch (1934). Ended by German annexation (Anschluss, 13 Mar 1938).
- **Annexed to Germany (Ostmark / Alpine and Danube Reichsgaue) (1938-03–1945-04)**: Part of Nazi Germany; see DEU. Seyss-Inquart Reichsstatthalter 1938-39, then Gauleiters (Bürckel, Schirach).
- **Second Republic under Allied occupation (1945-04–1955-07)**: Renner provisional government (Apr 1945) recognized by the Allies; Allied Council could veto legislation. State Treaty (15 May 1955) restored full sovereignty; permanent neutrality declared Oct 1955.
- **Second Republic (sovereign, neutral; EU member from 1995) (1955-07–present)**: Federal President directly elected (6-year term, max two); appoints and may dismiss the Chancellor and government. National Council can force out the government by a (non-constructive) no-confidence vote - first successful use 27 May 2019 against Kurz. Coalition governments are the norm. Since 2025: ÖVP-SPÖ-NEOS coalition under Stocker.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: 1789-1848: no formal prime minister - the State Chancellor / foreign minister (Kaunitz, Thugut, Stadion, Metternich) acted as leading minister. 1852-61 the emperor presided over the government himself (neo-absolutism) with a chairman of the ministers' conference. 1867-1918 the list is the Austrian (Cisleithanian) Minister-President; Hungary had its own Minister-President. 1938-45 no Austrian government (part of Germany).
- **Foreign affairs**: 1867-1918 the common (k.u.k.) Foreign Minister also chaired the joint Council of Ministers - in game, treat him as the senior advisor. 1920-36 chancellors frequently held foreign affairs themselves; that span is flagged uncertain. No foreign minister 1938-45.
- **Defence / war**: Before 1848 military administration lay with the Court War Council (Hofkriegsrat), whose presidents are not listed. Separate Landwehr/Honvéd ministries existed in each half of the Dual Monarchy. No army 1945-55; ministry created 1956. Austria is permanently neutral since 1955 (game should restrict alliances).
- **Finance / treasury**: 1867-1918 the common Finance Minister handled only joint expenditure (and Bosnia); each half also had its own finance minister. 1919-38 coverage partial.
- **Interior / home**: Cisleithanian interior ministers 1867-1918 (except Taaffe) and First Republic 1918-38 interior/security ministers not listed - game should fall back to the generic title 'Minister of the Interior'. Security under Austrofascism was run by Vice-Chancellor/Security Minister Emil Fey (1933-35).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No public civilian intelligence chief before the Second Republic. Staatspolizei (1945-2002) heads not listed. Use the generic title where no holder exists.
- **Military chief**: Second Republic chiefs before 2008 not listed; use the generic 'Chief of the General Staff' title.

### Foreign affairs

## Brazil (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1808-01 | State of Brazil (Portuguese colony, Viceroyalty) | colonial_or_occupied | Rio de Janeiro | royal_dismissal, revolution |
| 1808-01 | 1815-12 | Seat of the Portuguese monarchy (court in Rio de Janeiro) | absolute_monarchy | Rio de Janeiro | death_in_office, revolution |
| 1815-12 | 1822-09 | Kingdom of Brazil (United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves) | absolute_monarchy | Rio de Janeiro | revolution, abdication, death_in_office |
| 1822-09 | 1831-04 | Empire of Brazil - First Reign (Pedro I) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Rio de Janeiro | abdication, revolution, royal_dismissal |
| 1831-04 | 1840-07 | Empire of Brazil - Regency | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Rio de Janeiro | general_election, revolution, coup |
| 1840-07 | 1847-07 | Empire of Brazil - Second Reign (before the Council presidency) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Rio de Janeiro | royal_dismissal, general_election |
| 1847-07 | 1889-11 | Empire of Brazil - Second Reign (parliamentary cabinets) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Rio de Janeiro | royal_dismissal, no_confidence, general_election |
| 1889-11 | 1891-02 | Provisional Government of the Republic | military_junta | Rio de Janeiro | coup |
| 1891-02 | 1930-10 | First Republic ('Old Republic') | presidential_republic | Rio de Janeiro | term_limit, general_election, coup, revolution |
| 1930-10 | 1937-11 | Vargas Era: Provisional and Constitutional Government | presidential_republic | Rio de Janeiro | coup, revolution, general_election |
| 1937-11 | 1945-10 | Estado Novo | personalist_dictatorship | Rio de Janeiro | coup |
| 1945-10 | 1961-09 | Fourth (Populist) Republic | presidential_republic | Rio de Janeiro (to 21 Apr 1960), then Brasília | general_election, term_limit, coup, impeachment |
| 1961-09 | 1963-01 | Parliamentary Republic (Additional Act) | parliamentary_republic | Brasília | no_confidence, presidential_dismissal |
| 1963-01 | 1964-04 | Presidential Republic restored (Goulart) | presidential_republic | Brasília | coup, impeachment, general_election |
| 1964-04 | 1985-03 | Military Regime | military_junta | Brasília | coup, junta_decision |
| 1985-03 | present | New Republic (Constitution of 1988) | presidential_republic | Brasília | general_election, term_limit, impeachment |

- **State of Brazil (Portuguese colony, Viceroyalty) (1789–1808-01)**: Viceroys appointed by the Portuguese Crown (Queen Maria I; Prince João regent from 1792/1799). Not a sovereign actor. Inconfidência Mineira conspiracy crushed 1789-92.
- **Seat of the Portuguese monarchy (court in Rio de Janeiro) (1808-01–1815-12)**: Hereditary Braganza monarchy; Prince Regent João governed for the incapacitated Maria I. The court fled Napoleon's invasion of Portugal (arrived Jan/Mar 1808). Brazil's ports opened to friendly nations (1808). Portugal's government sat in Rio; game may treat Brazil as the Portuguese empire's capital.
- **Kingdom of Brazil (United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves) (1815-12–1822-09)**: Hereditary. João VI returned to Lisbon Apr 1821 after the Porto liberal revolution, leaving Prince Pedro as regent of Brazil. Pernambuco revolt 1817 suppressed. Independence proclaimed by Pedro at Ipiranga 7 Sep 1822.
- **Empire of Brazil - First Reign (Pedro I) (1822-09–1831-04)**: Hereditary constitutional monarchy (1824 Constitution) with a Moderating Power held by the emperor, who freely appointed and dismissed ministers and could dissolve the Chamber. Cisplatine War with Argentina 1825-28 (loss of Uruguay). Pedro I abdicated 7 Apr 1831 in favour of his 5-year-old son.
- **Empire of Brazil - Regency (1831-04–1840-07)**: Regents elected by the General Assembly (trina 1831-35), then by national vote (single regent 1835-40). Ended by the 'Majority Coup' declaring Pedro II of age at 14 (23 Jul 1840). Many provincial revolts (Cabanagem, Sabinada, Balaiada, Ragamuffin War 1835-45).
- **Empire of Brazil - Second Reign (before the Council presidency) (1840-07–1847-07)**: Emperor appointed and dismissed cabinets through the Moderating Power.
- **Empire of Brazil - Second Reign (parliamentary cabinets) (1847-07–1889-11)**: From 20 Jul 1847 a President of the Council of Ministers led the cabinet. Pedro II alternated Liberal and Conservative cabinets, dissolving the Chamber so the government could win elections ('parlamentarismo às avessas'). The emperor himself was removable only by revolution/coup. Paraguayan War 1864-70 (with Argentina and Uruguay). Abolition of slavery 13 May 1888 (Lei Áurea). Military coup of 15 Nov 1889 deposed Pedro II; the imperial family was exiled.
- **Provisional Government of the Republic (1889-11–1891-02)**: Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca as head of the provisional government. Republic proclaimed 15 Nov 1889; Constitution of 24 Feb 1891.
- **First Republic ('Old Republic') (1891-02–1930-10)**: Direct (restricted, literate-male) election every 4 years, no immediate re-election; 'café com leite' alternation of São Paulo and Minas Gerais oligarchies. Vice-president succeeds. Deodoro forced out Nov 1891; Naval Revolts 1891/1893-94; tenentista revolts 1922, 1924. Ended by the Revolution of 1930.
- **Vargas Era: Provisional and Constitutional Government (1930-10–1937-11)**: Vargas head of a provisional government 1930-34; elected by the Constituent Assembly under the 1934 Constitution. Constitutionalist Revolution of São Paulo 1932; Communist uprising 1935; Integralist movement.
- **Estado Novo (1937-11–1945-10)**: Vargas ruled by decree under the 1937 Constitution; Congress closed; parties banned. Brazil declared war on the Axis Aug 1942; Brazilian Expeditionary Force fought in Italy 1944-45. Vargas deposed by the army 29 Oct 1945.
- **Fourth (Populist) Republic (1945-10–1961-09)**: Direct election every 5 years, no immediate re-election; vice-president elected separately. Vargas (elected 1950) committed suicide 24 Aug 1954 under military pressure. Lott's 'preventive coup' of 11 Nov 1955 secured Kubitschek's inauguration; Congress declared Café Filho and Carlos Luz 'impeded'. Quadros resigned 25 Aug 1961.
- **Parliamentary Republic (Additional Act) (1961-09–1963-01)**: Compromise to let Vice-President Goulart take office with reduced powers: a Prime Minister responsible to Congress. Presidentialism restored by referendum 6 Jan 1963 (effective 23 Jan 1963).
- **Presidential Republic restored (Goulart) (1963-01–1964-04)**: As 1946 Constitution. Overthrown by the military coup of 31 Mar - 1 Apr 1964; Congress declared the presidency vacant 2 Apr 1964.
- **Military Regime (1964-04–1985-03)**: General-presidents chosen by the Army High Command, then ratified by an indirectly elected Congress/Electoral College (ARENA majority). Institutional Acts (AI-5, Dec 1968) suspended civil rights. 1969: a junta of the three service ministers barred the civilian vice-president from succeeding. Game: 'junta_decision' here stands for the military high-command succession process. Gradual 'abertura' from 1974; amnesty 1979; multiparty system 1979; Electoral College elected civilian Tancredo Neves (Jan 1985), who died before inauguration.
- **New Republic (Constitution of 1988) (1985-03–present)**: Direct two-round election; 4-year term (5 years until 1994); one consecutive re-election allowed since 1997 amendment. Vice-president succeeds; impeachment requires 2/3 of the Chamber to open and 2/3 of the Senate to convict. Impeachments: Collor (opened Sep 1992, resigned 29 Dec 1992 as the Senate convicted), Rousseff (suspended 12 May 2016, removed 31 Aug 2016). 8 Jan 2023 attack on the Three Powers; Bolsonaro convicted in 2025 of attempting a coup.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Colonial era: the Portuguese monarch. Regents of the Empire (1831-40) and Princess Isabel (regent during Pedro II's travels 1871-72, 1876-77, 1887-88) are listed as acting. Republic: the President is head of state and of government.
- **Head of government**: 1789-1808: Viceroys of Brazil. 1808-1847: no formal premier - rulers.org lists the Minister of the Kingdom (Reino; from 1822 of the Empire, Império) as principal minister. 1847-1889: President of the Council of Ministers (Presidente do Conselho de Ministros). 1889-1961 and 1963-present: presidential system, the President is head of government. Sep 1961 - Jan 1963: Prime Ministers under the parliamentary Additional Act.
- **Foreign affairs**: Ministro dos Negócios Estrangeiros (Empire), Ministro das Relações Exteriores (Itamaraty) from 1889. Pre-independence (1808-1821) foreign affairs were handled by Portuguese crown ministers in Rio and are not listed.
- **Defence / war**: Minister of War (Ministro da Guerra) 1822-1967; Minister of the Army (Ministro do Exército) Mar 1967 - Jun 1999 (Navy and, from 1941, Air Force had separate ministries); Minister of Defence (Ministro da Defesa, civilian) from 10 Jun 1999. Pre-1822 Portuguese war ministers in Rio are omitted.
- **Finance / treasury**: Ministro da Fazenda (Finance/Treasury) 1822-1990 and 1992-2019 and again from 2023; Ministro da Economia, Fazenda e Planejamento 1990-92 and Ministro da Economia 2019-2022 (super-ministry).
- **Interior / home**: Empire: Minister of the Empire (Negócios do Império, the home/interior ministry, 1822-1889). Republic: Minister of Justice and Internal Affairs (Justiça e Negócios Interiores, 1891-1967), then Minister of Justice (Justiça; Justiça e Segurança Pública 2018-19 and from 2023), which controls the Federal Police. The separate 'Ministério do Interior' of 1967-1990 was a regional-development ministry and is not mapped here.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Serviço Nacional de Informações (SNI) 1964-1990 - its chief had cabinet rank and two chiefs (Médici, Figueiredo) became president. 1990-1999 intelligence was a secretariat of the presidency (SAE) with no prominent public chief; Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (ABIN) from Dec 1999, director-general under the Institutional Security Cabinet (GSI).
- **Military chief**: Chief of the Armed Forces General Staff (EMFA, minister-rank, 1946-1999) and Chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces (EMCFA, from 2010). No joint chief existed before 1946 (the Army chief of staff was subordinate to the War Minister) or between 1999 and 2010 (the service commanders reported to the Defence Minister). Game: for those gaps, use the War/Army minister (defense list) as the military chief.

- Minister lists before Apr 1964 (War, Finance, Empire, Justice, Foreign) and EMFA/EMCFA are transcribed from pt.wikipedia tables (which cite the ministries' official galleries); from Apr 1964 Foreign, War/Army/Defence, Finance and Justice come from rulers.org's Brazilian ministries page. Short interim stand-ins nested inside a minister's term were dropped.
- Brief acting stand-ins (<45 days) between two terms of the same minister were folded into that minister's tenure.
- 2026 changes (Finance: Fernando Haddad -> Dario Durigan, Mar 2026; Justice: Ricardo Lewandowski -> Wellington César Lima e Silva, Jan 2026) agree between rulers.org and pt.wikipedia but were not checked against gov.br.
- ABIN director-general dates after 2008 are approximate (prose source); intelligence 1990-1999 (SAE) not listed.
- No joint military chief 1889-1946 and 1999-2010 (see role note).

## Canada (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1867-07 | 1931-12 | Dominion of Canada | dominion | Ottawa | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |
| 1931-12 | 1982-04 | Canada (autonomous dominion / Commonwealth realm) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Ottawa | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |
| 1982-04 | present | Canada | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Ottawa | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |

- **Dominion of Canada (1867-07–1931-12)**: Westminster system under the British Crown, represented by a Governor General appointed on the British government's advice. PM is the leader commanding a House of Commons majority. Foreign policy and declarations of war controlled by London until the 1920s (Canada entered WWI automatically in 1914). The 1926 King-Byng affair shows the Governor General's reserve power to refuse dissolution. Game: Canada cannot conduct independent diplomacy before ~1923 (Halibut Treaty) and becomes fully autonomous with the Statute of Westminster (Dec 1931).
- **Canada (autonomous dominion / Commonwealth realm) (1931-12–1982-04)**: Separate declaration of war in Sep 1939 (one week after the UK). Governor General Canadian-born from 1952. Constitution still amended by the UK Parliament until patriation. Minority governments common and fragile (1957, 1962-68, 1972-74, 1979).
- **Canada (1982-04–present)**: Constitution Act 1982 patriated the constitution and added the Charter of Rights. Fixed election dates (2007 law) but a minority government may still fall on confidence. Party leaders chosen by membership vote; a new party leader becomes PM without an election (Turner 1984, Campbell 1993, Martin 2003, Carney 2025). Game: remove a Canadian player via a Commons no-confidence vote (last successful 2011), an election defeat, or a party/caucus revolt forcing resignation (Trudeau 2025). No coups.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: The monarch is represented in Canada by the Governor General (not listed). The game may show the GG as the in-country head-of-state figure.
- **Foreign affairs**: No Canadian foreign minister 1867-1909; external relations were conducted by the British Foreign Office (game: London decides for Canada). 1912-1946 the post was held by the PM.
- **Interior / home**: Canada has no interior ministry in the European sense. The 1873-1936 'Minister of the Interior' handled western lands and settlement, not security, and is not used. Policing/security: Minister of Justice (RCMP/NWMP, 1867-1966; not listed), Solicitor General (1966-2003), Minister of Public Safety (2003-). Game: for 1867-1965 use the Minister of Justice as a generic advisor.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No separate public intelligence chief before CSIS (Jul 1984); domestic security intelligence was the RCMP Security Service (1950s-1984). Canada has no foreign HUMINT service; the Communications Security Establishment (SIGINT) chief is not listed.
- **Military chief**: 1867-1904 the militia was commanded by a British General Officer Commanding; 1904-1964 the Chief of the General Staff (army), Chief of the Naval Staff and Chief of the Air Staff were coequal (not listed). From 1951 the Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee coordinated them; from Aug 1964 the Chief of the Defence Staff. For the game, 1867-1950 the senior officer is unlisted - use a generic 'Chief of the General Staff'.

## China (Qing Empire / Republic of China / People's Republic of China) (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1912-02 | Great Qing Empire | absolute_monarchy | Beijing | death_in_office, abdication, revolution, coup, family_council |
| 1912-01 | 1928-06 | Republic of China: Beiyang (Beijing) government | presidential_republic | Beijing (Nanjing provisional government 1912-01 to 1912-04) | coup, presidential_dismissal, no_confidence, revolution |
| 1928-06 | 1949-12 | Republic of China: Nationalist (Kuomintang) Government | one_party_state | Nanjing (wartime capital Chongqing 1937-11 to 1946-05) | coup, revolution, foreign_occupation, party_congress |
| 1949-10 | 1966-05 | People's Republic of China (early Mao era) | one_party_communist_state | Beijing | party_congress, death_in_office, coup |
| 1966-05 | 1976-10 | PRC: Cultural Revolution | one_party_communist_state | Beijing | party_congress, death_in_office, coup |
| 1976-10 | present | PRC: Reform era (post-Mao) | one_party_communist_state | Beijing | party_congress, death_in_office, coup, revolution |

- **Great Qing Empire (1789–1912-02)**: Hereditary; the emperor secretly designated an heir (from Yongzheng's time). Minor emperors ruled through regents (Cixi). The Grand Council (軍機處) and Six Boards formed the inner government; no prime minister until the 1911 cabinet. Opium Wars (1839-42, 1856-60), Taiping Rebellion (1850-64), Self-Strengthening, Sino-Japanese War (1894-95), Boxer Uprising (1900), late-Qing constitutional reforms (1906-11). Ended by the Xinhai Revolution. Game: removal of the player = revolution or palace coup (1861 Xinyou, 1898 Wuxu).
- **Republic of China: Beiyang (Beijing) government (1912-01–1928-06)**: Presidents elected by the National Assembly (often coerced or bribed); premiers needed parliamentary approval but changed with warlord fortunes. Real power with Beiyang warlord cliques (Anhui, Zhili, Fengtian) from 1916. Warlord era; frequent coups. Rival southern (Guangzhou) governments under Sun Yat-sen 1917-25. Game: treat as fragmented; coups common.
- **Republic of China: Nationalist (Kuomintang) Government (1928-06–1949-12)**: KMT 'political tutelage': the party Central Executive Committee appointed the National Government. 1947 Constitution introduced an elected president (by the National Assembly) from 1948. Japanese invasion 1937-45; Civil War with the CCP 1945-49. Xi'an Incident 1936 (Chiang kidnapped). Japanese puppet regimes (Manchukuo 1932-45, Wang Jingwei 1940-45) not modeled. Government retreated to Taipei 1949-12 (see TWN).
- **People's Republic of China (early Mao era) (1949-10–1966-05)**: CCP Chairman (Mao) supreme; state posts filled by the National People's Congress on party nomination. Korean War, First Five-Year Plan, Great Leap Forward (1958-62).
- **PRC: Cultural Revolution (1966-05–1976-10)**: Mao's personal authority; designated successors purged (Liu Shaoqi 1968, Lin Biao 1971). State presidency vacant from 1968 and abolished 1975. Ended with Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four (1976-10, effectively a palace coup).
- **PRC: Reform era (post-Mao) (1976-10–present)**: General Secretary chosen by the Central Committee at party congresses (every 5 years) after Politburo Standing Committee consensus; state president and premier elected by the NPC. Term limits (1982) removed for the presidency in 2018. Game: the player is the General Secretary; removal = Politburo/Central Committee vote (Hu Yaobang 1987, Zhao Ziyang 1989) or mass unrest. No no-confidence vote.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: Qing (to 1911): no head of government in the modern sense. The emperor ruled through the Grand Council (軍機處); its leading Grand Councillor is the closest analogue (e.g. Heshen under Qianlong, Prince Gong 1861-84, Prince Li/Shiduo 1884-1898, Ronglu 1898-1903) but the list is not modeled. Powerful regional viceroys such as Li Hongzhang (Zhili, 1870-95, 1900-01) and Zeng Guofan effectively ran diplomacy and military modernization. PRC: Premier of the State Council (government), under the party General Secretary (see paramount_leader).
- **Paramount leader (party)**: Use paramount_leader as the player's office for Qing regencies (Cixi), the KMT era (Chiang Kai-shek) and the PRC (CCP Chairman/General Secretary, plus Deng Xiaoping 1978-89 who held no top formal post).
- **Foreign affairs**: Qing: before 1861 diplomacy was handled by the Board of Rites, the Lifanyuan (Court of Colonial Affairs) and Canton officials; Zongli Yamen 1861-1901, Waiwubu 1901-11. Beiyang foreign ministers changed very frequently; list is partial.
- **Defence / war**: Qing Board of War (兵部) presidents and the 1906 Ministry of the Army not modeled. Beiyang Ministers of War not modeled (power lay with warlords). PRC: the Minister of National Defense is largely a diplomatic/administrative post; real command lies with the CCP Central Military Commission Chairman (Mao, Hua, Deng, Jiang, Hu, Xi).
- **Finance / treasury**: Qing Board of Revenue (戶部) presidents and Beiyang finance ministers not modeled (gap).
- **Interior / home**: Qing Board of Civil Appointments / 1906 Ministry of Civil Affairs, Beiyang and Nationalist Ministers of the Interior not modeled (gap). PRC: Minister of Public Security used as interior/police chief (the Ministry of Civil Affairs is a minor welfare portfolio).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Nationalist era: two services, Juntong (military, Dai Li) and Zhongtong (party, CC Clique/Xu Enzeng); only Juntong listed. PRC before 1983: Central Investigation Department (foreign) and Kang Sheng's security apparatus; Minister of State Security from 1983.
- **Military chief**: Qing: no general staff until the 1906-1911 reforms; armies commanded by viceroys (Hunan/Huai/Beiyang armies). PRC: Chief of the General Staff (to 2016) / Joint Staff Department (from 2016); real authority is the CMC Chairman and Vice-Chairmen.

### Paramount leader (party)

- 1776 → 1799-02: **Heshen**, Regent / de facto ruler — Grand Councillor and favourite of Qianlong; de facto chief minister, arrested and forced to suicide by Jiaqing 1799 ⚠ uncertain
- 1861-11 → 1873-02: **Empress Dowagers Cixi and Ci'an (co-regents)**, Regent / de facto ruler — 'Listening to politics behind the curtain' after the Xinyou Coup; Prince Gong as Prince-Counsellor
- 1875-02 → 1881-04: **Empress Dowagers Cixi and Ci'an (co-regents)**, Regent / de facto ruler — Second regency for the Guangxu Emperor; Ci'an died 1881-04
- 1881-04 → 1889-03: **Empress Dowager Cixi**, Regent / de facto ruler — Sole regent; Guangxu took personal rule 1889-03 but Cixi remained the real power
- 1898-09 → 1908-11: **Empress Dowager Cixi**, Regent / de facto ruler — Resumed rule after the Wuxu coup against the Hundred Days' Reform; died 1908-11-15
- 1908-12 → 1911-12: **Zaifeng, Prince Chun**, Regent / de facto ruler — Prince Regent for Puyi; resigned 1911-12-06
- 1926-07 → 1949-01: **Chiang Kai-shek**, Paramount leader (Kuomintang) — Commander-in-Chief of the National Revolutionary Army 1926; Director-General (Zongcai) of the KMT from 1938-03; real power regardless of state title
- 1949-10 → 1976-09: **Mao Zedong**, Paramount leader / Chairman or General Secretary of the CCP Central Committee — *中国共产党中央委员会主席 / 总书记* — CCP Chairman (from 1943/1945) until death 1976-09-09; CMC Chairman
- 1976-10 → 1981-06: **Hua Guofeng**, Paramount leader / Chairman or General Secretary of the CCP Central Committee — *中国共产党中央委员会主席 / 总书记* — CCP Chairman; arrested the Gang of Four 1976-10; sidelined by Deng from 1978-12
- 1978-12 → 1989-11: **Deng Xiaoping**, Paramount leader / Chairman or General Secretary of the CCP Central Committee — *中国共产党中央委员会主席 / 总书记* — Paramount leader without the top party/state post (Vice-Premier; CMC Chairman 1981-06 to 1989-11); influence until death 1997

## East Germany (German Democratic Republic) (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1949-10 | 1989-11 | German Democratic Republic (SED rule) | one_party_communist_state | East Berlin | party_congress, death_in_office, revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1989-11 | 1990-10 | GDR transition (Peaceful Revolution to reunification) | parliamentary_republic | East Berlin | no_confidence, general_election, revolution |

- **German Democratic Republic (SED rule) (1949-10–1989-11)**: Real power with the SED First/General Secretary and Politburo; state posts (President/Council of State, Council of Ministers) filled by party decision and rubber-stamped by the Volkskammer. Leaders change by Central Committee/Politburo vote, often with Moscow's backing: Ulbricht forced out 1971, Honecker ousted by Politburo 17-18 Oct 1989. Soviet forces stationed throughout; 17 June 1953 uprising crushed by Soviet troops.
- **GDR transition (Peaceful Revolution to reunification) (1989-11–1990-10)**: Berlin Wall opened 9 Nov 1989; SED's leading role struck from the constitution 1 Dec 1989; free Volkskammer election 18 Mar 1990; de Maizière government negotiated accession to the FRG (3 Oct 1990).

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Paramount leader (party)**: The SED First/General Secretary is the real ruler; the game should make this the player's office, with Council of State / Council of Ministers posts as advisors. Removal by Politburo/Central Committee vote (Ulbricht 1971, Honecker 1989).
- **Defence / war**: No defence ministry 1949-56 (armed police under the Interior Ministry). Treat the Interior Minister as defence advisor 1949-56.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: MfS (Stasi) was briefly downgraded to a State Secretariat under the Interior Ministry (Jul 1953-Nov 1955).
- **Military chief**: Soviet Group of Forces in Germany held real military power. NVA chiefs of the Main Staff: dates for 1958-1979 approximate.

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |

| 1871-02 | 1940-07 | Third Republic | parliamentary_republic | Paris (Assembly and government sat at Bordeaux Feb-Mar 1871 and at Versailles 1871-1879; government at Bordeaux Sep-Dec 1914; Tours/Bordeaux Jun 1940) | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |
| 1940-07 | 1944-08 | French State (Vichy regime) | personalist_dictatorship | Vichy | foreign_occupation, coup |

| 1946-10 | 1958-10 | Fourth Republic | parliamentary_republic | Paris | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, coup |
| 1958-10 | present | Fifth Republic | semi_presidential_republic | Paris | general_election, term_limit, impeachment, no_confidence, presidential_dismissal |

- **Kingdom of France (last months of the Ancien Régime; Estates-General / National Constituent Assembly from May-Jul 1789) (1789-01–1789-10)**: Hereditary (Salic law, male primogeniture). Ministers serve at the king's pleasure; there is no prime minister by law, though a 'principal minister' (Necker) dominated. The Estates-General opened 5 May 1789, declared itself the National Assembly 17 Jun 1789; Bastille 14 Jul 1789. The court was forced from Versailles to Paris 5-6 Oct 1789.
- **Kingdom of France - constitutional monarchy (Constitution of 1791; Legislative Assembly from Oct 1791) (1789-10–1792-08)**: Hereditary 'King of the French'. Ministers appointed by the king but answerable to the Assembly, which could impeach (décret d'accusation) them; the king had a suspensive veto. Monarchy suspended by insurrection of 10 Aug 1792. For the game: insurrection/revolution removes the king; the Assembly can force out ministers (Girondin ministry dismissed Jun 1792).
- **First Republic - Provisional Executive Council and National Convention (Committee of Public Safety from Apr 1793) (1792-08–1795-11)**: No individual head of state. The Convention (elected Sep 1792) was sovereign; its president rotated every two weeks. Executive power lay with the Provisional Executive Council of ministers (Aug 1792-Apr 1794) and, in practice, the Committee of Public Safety, whose members the Convention re-elected monthly. Game handling: treat the player as the leading member of the Committee of Public Safety; removal = Convention vote / purge (e.g. 9 Thermidor, 27 Jul 1794: Robespierre arrested by Convention vote and executed). Ministries were abolished 20 Apr 1794 and replaced by 12 executive commissions until Nov 1795.
- **First Republic - Directory (Constitution of Year III) (1795-11–1799-11)**: Collective executive of five Directors chosen by the Council of Ancients from a list drawn up by the Council of Five Hundred; one Director replaced each year (chosen by lot to leave). Two-chamber legislature elected annually by thirds. Repeated coups: 18 Fructidor V (4 Sep 1797), 22 Floréal VI (11 May 1798), 30 Prairial VII (18 Jun 1799), and 18-19 Brumaire VIII (9-10 Nov 1799) which ended the Directory. No prime minister.
- **Consulate (1799-11–1804-05)**: Three consuls under the Constitution of Year VIII; First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte held real power (Consul for life from Aug 1802, confirmed by plebiscite). No prime minister; ministers report individually to the First Consul. Plebiscitary legitimacy. Removal only by coup/assassination (e.g. rue Saint-Nicaise bomb plot, Dec 1800) or military defeat.
- **First French Empire (1804-05–1814-04)**: Hereditary in Napoleon's line (Constitution of Year XII). No prime minister; the Arch-Chancellor (Cambacérès) presided over the Senate and Council of State in the Emperor's absence. Ended with Allied capture of Paris (31 Mar 1814), Senate deposition (3 Apr) and abdication (6 Apr, Treaty of Fontainebleau 11 Apr 1814).
- **First Bourbon Restoration (Charter of 1814) (1814-04–1815-03)**: Hereditary (Louis XVIII). Ministers responsible to the king; bicameral parliament (Chamber of Peers, Chamber of Deputies elected on high property franchise). Interrupted by Napoleon's return (Hundred Days).
- **Hundred Days (restored Empire) (1815-03–1815-07)**: Napoleon I restored; after Waterloo (18 Jun 1815) abdicated 22 Jun 1815 in favour of Napoleon II; a Provisional Government Commission under Fouché governed until the Bourbon return (7-8 Jul 1815). Louis XVIII's court sat at Ghent during this period.
- **Second Bourbon Restoration (1815-07–1830-08)**: Hereditary (Louis XVIII, then Charles X). The king chooses the President of the Council; in practice a ministry needed a workable Chamber majority (Villèle fell after the 1827 election). July Revolution (27-29 Jul 1830) forced Charles X to abdicate (2 Aug 1830).
- **July Monarchy (Charter of 1830) (1830-08–1848-02)**: Hereditary 'King of the French' (Louis-Philippe, House of Orléans). Ministries depended on both the king's confidence and a Chamber majority (semi-parliamentary 'dual confidence'). February Revolution 1848: Louis-Philippe abdicated 24 Feb 1848 and the Republic was proclaimed.
- **Second Republic - Provisional Government, Executive Commission and Cavaignac (1848-02–1848-12)**: Provisional Government (24 Feb), then Executive Commission elected by the Constituent Assembly (10 May), then General Cavaignac as Chief of the Executive Power appointed by the Assembly (28 Jun 1848). Constituent Assembly could remove the executive by vote.
- **Second Republic - presidential regime (Constitution of 1848) (1848-12–1851-12)**: President elected by universal male suffrage for a single four-year term with no immediate re-election; unicameral Legislative Assembly. Ministers appointed by the president. Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte's self-coup of 2 Dec 1851 overthrew the constitution.
- **Second Republic - Prince-President's dictatorship (Constitution of Jan 1852) (1851-12–1852-12)**: President for ten years, confirmed by plebiscite; Empire restored by plebiscite Nov 1852.
- **Second French Empire (1852-12–1870-09)**: Hereditary (Napoleon III). Until 1869 ministers answered only to the Emperor (no prime minister; the Minister of State was the government's spokesman). The 'Liberal Empire' (1869-70) introduced ministerial responsibility to the Corps législatif (Ollivier cabinet, Jan 1870; Ollivier fell to a Chamber vote 9 Aug 1870). Collapsed after Sedan (2 Sep 1870); Republic proclaimed 4 Sep 1870.
- **Government of National Defence (1870-09–1871-02)**: Self-constituted provisional government of Paris deputies under General Trochu. Paris besieged Sep 1870-Jan 1871; armistice 28 Jan 1871; National Assembly elected 8 Feb 1871 met at Bordeaux.
- **Third Republic (1871-02–1940-07)**: President of the Republic elected for seven years by the National Assembly (both chambers in joint session at Versailles). The President of the Council (prime minister; formally 'Vice-President of the Council' 1871-1876) needed the confidence of the Chamber of Deputies and, in practice, the Senate. Extremely unstable cabinets (over 100 governments). Presidents could be forced out by parliament (MacMahon 1879, Grévy 1887, Millerand 1924). The Paris Commune (Mar-May 1871) was a rival revolutionary authority in Paris. Ended when the National Assembly voted full powers to Pétain (10 Jul 1940).
- **French State (Vichy regime) (1940-07–1944-08)**: Marshal Pétain as Head of the French State with full executive and legislative powers; designated successors (Laval, then Darlan, then Laval). No parliament. Germany occupied the north from Jun 1940 and the whole country from Nov 1942; German pressure imposed Laval's return as Head of Government (Apr 1942). After the Liberation the remnant was moved to Sigmaringen, Germany (Sep 1944-Apr 1945).
- **Free France / French National Committee / CFLN (parallel claimant) (1940-06–1944-06)**: Led by General de Gaulle (Free French leader from 18 Jun 1940; French National Committee from Sep 1941; French Committee of National Liberation, CFLN, from 3 Jun 1943, co-chaired with Giraud until Nov 1943). Parallel government to Vichy. Game: playable as a government-in-exile; the CFLN could reorganise its leadership (Giraud was eased out Nov 1943 - Apr 1944).
- **Provisional Government of the French Republic (GPRF) (1944-06–1946-10)**: Chairman of the Provisional Government elected by the Constituent Assembly (from Nov 1945); de Gaulle resigned 20 Jan 1946. Acted as both head of state and head of government.
- **Fourth Republic (1946-10–1958-10)**: President elected for seven years by Parliament. President of the Council invested by the National Assembly; governments fell to censure/confidence votes or coalition break-ups. Ended by the May 1958 Algiers crisis (military putsch threat) and de Gaulle's investiture (1 Jun 1958).
- **Fifth Republic (1958-10–present)**: President elected by direct universal suffrage (from 1965; seven-year term until 2002, five-year since; at most two consecutive terms since 2008). The President appoints the Prime Minister; the National Assembly can bring down the government by a censure motion (Art. 49: Pompidou 1962, Barnier Dec 2024, Bayrou lost a confidence vote Sep 2025). The President can be removed only by Parliament sitting as the High Court (Art. 68) for breach of duty. Cohabitation possible when the President's opponents hold the Assembly (1986-88, 1993-95, 1997-2002). Game: president removed by election/term limit/High Court; PM by censure motion or presidential request.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Collective or vacant headship: Provisional Executive Council (10 Aug-21 Sep 1792), National Convention (Sep 1792-Oct 1795, presidency rotated fortnightly), Executive Directory (five Directors, Nov 1795-Nov 1799; all 13 Directors listed with overlapping tenures). Free France (1940-44) is a parallel claimant to Vichy. Game: during collective periods let the player be the most powerful member (Committee of Public Safety leader, then Barras) and use coups/purges as removal.
- **Head of government**: No prime minister existed 1792-1815 (Convention, Directory, Consulate, Empire) or 1849-1870 (Louis-Napoléon governed directly; Ministers of State were spokesmen). The Committee of Public Safety entries (Danton, Robespierre) are de facto leaders of a collective body, listed for game use. During the Directory there is no head of government at all: the Directors collectively directed the ministers. Title changes: Président du Conseil des ministres (1815-30, 1947-59), Président du Conseil (1830-49, 1876-1942), Vice-Président du Conseil (1871-76), Chef du Gouvernement (Vichy 1942-44), Premier ministre (since Jan 1959).
- **Foreign affairs**: Complete 1789-2026 from rulers.org. Ministries were abolished 20 Apr 1794 - 3 Nov 1795 and replaced by a Commission for External Relations (commissioners listed). Free French national commissioners (1941-44) overlap Vichy ministers.
- **Defence / war**: Minister of War 1789-1947 (with a coordinating Minister of National Defence above War/Navy/Air in 1932-1940 and 1946-1948, so overlapping holders with different titles are correct), then National Defence / Armed Forces / Defence / Armies. During 1803-1814 a separate Minister of War Administration (Dejean, Lacuée, Daru) handled supply and is not listed. No minister Apr 1794 - Nov 1795 (Commission of Land Armies). Separate navy ministers are listed under navy_minister; air ministers (1928-1947) are not listed.
- **Finance / treasury**: Controllers-General / Director-General of Finances to 1791, then Minister of Public Contributions (1791-94), Finance (from 1795). Napoleon also had a separate Minister of the Public Treasury (Barbé-Marbois 1801-06, Mollien 1806-14/1815) not listed here. Post-1958 portfolio names vary (Economy and Finance, etc.).
- **Interior / home**: Complete 1790-2026 (the Ministry of the Interior was created Aug 1790; before that internal administration belonged to the Secretary of State of the King's Household). Gap Apr 1794 - Nov 1795 (executive commission).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Ministers of General Police (1796-1802, 1804-1818; Fouché, Savary) are the closest public security/intelligence chiefs of the Revolutionary-Napoleonic era, plus Maupas (Minister of Police 1852-53). From 1818 to 1940 there was no publicly named national intelligence chief: military intelligence (Deuxième Bureau of the General Staff) and the Sûreté générale (Interior Ministry) were run by officials not generally public; the game should model this as an interior-ministry/war-ministry function. Free French BCRA (Passy) 1940-44; DGER/SDECE (1945-1982) and DGSE (1982-) directors are public. The domestic service (DST 1944-2008, DCRI 2008-14, DGSI since 2014) is not listed.
- **Military chief**: No permanent general staff before 1871: Napoleon was his own commander-in-chief with Berthier as chief of staff; 1815-1870 the Minister of War was the senior military authority. Chief of the General Staff of the Army 1871-1940 (wartime commanders-in-chief Joffre, Nivelle, Pétain, Foch listed); Vichy's Armistice Army chiefs 1940-42 are NOT covered; armed-forces chief (CEMGDN/CEMA) from Nov 1943. 1948-1951 gap: armed-forces chief post effectively vacant/handled by committee.
- **navy_minister**: Ministers of the Navy (and Colonies to 1894) 1789-1947 from rulers.org; merged into Armed Forces/National Defence from 1947.

### Head of state

- 1774-05 → 1792-08: **Louis XVI**, King of France and of Navarre (King of the French from Oct 1789) — *Roi de France et de Navarre / Roi des Français* — Suspended by the Legislative Assembly 10 Aug 1792; monarchy abolished 21 Sep 1792; executed 21 Jan 1793
- 1792-08 → 1792-09: **Provisional Executive Council (collective)**, Collective executive — *Conseil exécutif provisoire* — No individual head of state; see role_notes
- 1792-09 → 1795-10: **National Convention (collective; presidency rotated fortnightly)**, Sovereign assembly (no individual head of state) — *Convention nationale* — Game: use the Committee of Public Safety's leading member as player (see head_of_government)

- 1795-11 → 1799-05: **Jean-François Reubell**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur*
- 1795-11 → 1799-11: **Paul Barras**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur* — Only Director to serve the whole Directory; most influential member
- 1797-05 → 1797-09: **François-Marie, marquis de Barthélemy**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur* — Purged in the coup of 18 Fructidor
- 1797-09 → 1798-05: **François de Neufchâteau**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur* — rulers.org gives 4 Sep 1797 - 15 May 1799 for his directorship; most references give May 1798 (he then returned as Interior minister Jun 1798) ⚠ uncertain
- 1797-09 → 1799-06: **Philippe-Antoine Merlin de Douai**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur*
- 1798-05 → 1799-06: **Jean-Baptiste Treilhard**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur* — rulers.org gives 15 May 1799 as start; he succeeded François de Neufchâteau in May 1798 ⚠ uncertain
- 1799-05 → 1799-11: **Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur*
- 1799-06 → 1799-11: **Louis-Jérôme Gohier**, Member of the Executive Directory (president at the time of Brumaire) — *Directeur*
- 1799-06 → 1799-11: **Roger Ducos**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur*
- 1799-06 → 1799-11: **Jean-François-Auguste Moulin**, Member of the Executive Directory — *Directeur*
- 1799-11 → 1804-05: **Napoléon Bonaparte**, First Consul (Provisional Consul from 10 Nov 1799; Consul for life from 2 Aug 1802) — *Premier Consul*
- 1804-05 → 1814-04: **Napoléon I**, Emperor of the French — *Empereur des Français* — Abdicated 6 Apr 1814
- 1814-04 → 1815-03: **Louis XVIII**, King of France and of Navarre — *Roi de France et de Navarre* — Recalled by the Senate 6 Apr 1814; entered Paris 3 May 1814; fled to Ghent 20 Mar 1815
- 1815-03 → 1815-06: **Napoléon I**, Emperor of the French (Hundred Days) — *Empereur des Français* — Abdicated 22 Jun 1815
- 1815-06 → 1815-07: **Napoléon II (proclaimed; never reigned)**, Emperor of the French (nominal) — Proclaimed by the Chambers after his father's abdication; a Provisional Government Commission (Fouché) actually governed
- 1815-07 → 1824-09: **Louis XVIII**, King of France and of Navarre — *Roi de France et de Navarre* — Died 16 Sep 1824
- 1824-09 → 1830-08: **Charles X**, King of France and of Navarre — *Roi de France et de Navarre* — Abdicated 2 Aug 1830 after the July Revolution
- 1830-08 → 1848-02: **Louis-Philippe I**, King of the French — *Roi des Français* — Lieutenant-General of the Kingdom 31 Jul - 9 Aug 1830; king from 9 Aug 1830; abdicated 24 Feb 1848
- 1848-02 → 1848-05: **Jacques-Charles Dupont de l'Eure**, President of the Provisional Government — *Président du Gouvernement provisoire*
- 1848-05 → 1848-06: **François Arago**, President of the Executive Commission — *Président de la Commission exécutive* — Five-member commission (Arago, Garnier-Pagès, Marie, Lamartine, Ledru-Rollin)

- 1871-02 → 1873-05: **Adolphe Thiers**, Chief of the Executive Power, then President of the Republic (from 31 Aug 1871) — *Chef du pouvoir exécutif / Président de la République* — Resigned after losing an Assembly vote, 24 May 1873
- 1873-05 → 1879-01: **Patrice de MacMahon**, President of the Republic — *Président de la République* — Resigned 30 Jan 1879 after republicans won both chambers

- 1969-06 → 1974-04: **Georges Pompidou**, President of the Republic — *Président de la République* — Died in office 2 Apr 1974
- 1974-04 → 1974-05: **Alain Poher** (acting), Acting President of the Republic (President of the Senate) — *Président de la République par intérim*
- 1974-05 → 1981-05: **Valéry Giscard d'Estaing**, President of the Republic — *Président de la République*

## Germany (Prussia / German Reich / Federal Republic) (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 1806-08 | 1815-06 | Kingdom of Prussia (Napoleonic era & wars of liberation) | absolute_monarchy | Berlin (court at Königsberg/Memel 1806-1809) | death_in_office, royal_dismissal, foreign_occupation |

| 1848-03 | 1850-01 | Kingdom of Prussia (Revolution of 1848) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Berlin | royal_dismissal, revolution |

| 1990-10 | present | Federal Republic of Germany (reunified) | parliamentary_republic | Berlin (Bonn remained seat of government until 1999) | constructive_no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, impeachment |

- **Kingdom of Prussia (Holy Roman Empire member) (1789–1806-08)**: Hereditary Hohenzollern male primogeniture. Ministers (Kabinettsminister) serve at the king's pleasure. King governs through a cabinet of ministers; foreign affairs led by 'Kabinettsminister' who doubled as leading minister.
- **Kingdom of Prussia (Napoleonic era & wars of liberation) (1806-08–1815-06)**: Hereditary. Stein-Hardenberg reforms create modern ministries (1808) and the office of State Chancellor (1810). Defeated at Jena-Auerstedt (1806); Treaty of Tilsit (1807) halves Prussia. Napoleon forced Stein's dismissal (1808).
- **Kingdom of Prussia (German Confederation) (1815-06–1848-03)**: Hereditary. Promised constitution not granted until 1848/1850.
- **Kingdom of Prussia (Revolution of 1848) (1848-03–1850-01)**: March ministries appointed under revolutionary pressure; king dissolved the Prussian National Assembly (Dec 1848) and imposed a constitution.
- **Kingdom of Prussia (constitutional monarchy, 1850 constitution) (1850-01–1867-07)**: Ministers responsible to the king, not the Landtag (three-class franchise). The Landtag could refuse budgets (constitutional conflict 1862-66) but could not remove ministers.
- **North German Confederation (Prussian presidency) (1867-07–1871-01)**: King of Prussia holds the Bundespräsidium; Bismarck is Bundeskanzler and Prussian Minister-President.
- **German Empire (Kaiserreich) (1871-01–1918-11)**: King of Prussia is German Emperor (hereditary). Reichskanzler appointed/dismissed by the Kaiser alone; the Reichstag votes budgets and laws but cannot force out the chancellor (until the October 1918 reforms made the chancellor dependent on Reichstag confidence). Reich ministries were 'Reichsämter' headed by State Secretaries subordinate to the chancellor, not a collegial cabinet. War ministry remained Prussian (plus Bavarian/Saxon/Württemberg ministries).
- **Revolutionary period (Council of People's Deputies) (1918-11–1919-02)**: Kaiser abdicates 9 Nov 1918; power held by the six-member Rat der Volksbeauftragten (SPD/USPD) until the National Assembly convenes.
- **Weimar Republic (parliamentary) (1919-02–1930-03)**: Reichspräsident directly elected for 7 years; appoints/dismisses the Reichskanzler, who also needs Reichstag confidence (Art. 54: simple no-confidence vote, non-constructive). Coup attempts: Kapp Putsch (1920), Beer Hall Putsch (1923). Art. 48 gives the president emergency decree powers; Art. 25 allows dissolution of the Reichstag.
- **Weimar Republic (presidential cabinets) (1930-03–1933-01)**: Brüning, Papen, Schleicher govern by Art. 48 emergency decree with the president's confidence rather than a Reichstag majority; the president's withdrawal of support is the real removal mechanism.
- **Nazi Germany (Third Reich) (1933-01–1945-05)**: Enabling Act (Mar 1933) ends parliamentary control; NSDAP the sole party (Jul 1933). On Hindenburg's death (Aug 1934) Hitler merges presidency and chancellorship as 'Führer und Reichskanzler'. No legal removal mechanism; only coup/assassination (20 July 1944 plot failed) or defeat. Hitler's testament named Dönitz Reichspräsident. Ministers rarely met as a cabinet after 1938; power lay with Hitler and party/SS offices.
- **Allied occupation (1945-05–1949-09)**: Supreme authority held by the Allied Control Council (US, UK, France, USSR) from 5 Jun 1945; no German national government.
- **Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) (1949-09–1990-10)**: Bundeskanzler elected by the Bundestag; removable only by a constructive vote of no confidence (Art. 67 GG), used successfully once (Kohl replaced Schmidt, Oct 1982). Bundespräsident elected by the Federal Convention for 5 years (max two terms); impeachable before the Constitutional Court (Art. 61).
- **Federal Republic of Germany (reunified) (1990-10–present)**: As FRG. Chancellors may also call a confidence vote (Art. 68) to trigger early elections (Schröder 2005, Scholz Dec 2024).

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Prussian kings 1789-1871; from 18 Jan 1871 the King of Prussia is also German Emperor. 1945-49: Allied Control Council (no German head of state). GDR heads of state are in the DDR nation.
- **Head of government**: Before 1848 Prussia had no formal prime minister except Hardenberg as State Chancellor (1810-22); the 'leading minister' list is the de facto chief minister. Prussian Minister-Presidents after 1871 are omitted except where they were also Reich Chancellor (Roon 1873 and Botho zu Eulenburg 1892-94 were separate). 1945-49: no German government.
- **Foreign affairs**: Prussian foreign ministers to 1871, then State Secretaries of the Auswärtiges Amt (subordinate to the chancellor) until Feb 1919, then Reich Foreign Ministers. No German foreign minister May 1945-Mar 1951.
- **Defence / war**: Prussian War Ministers act for the whole Reich 1871-1919 (Bavaria, Saxony and Württemberg kept their own). After Blomberg (Feb 1938) the post was abolished and Hitler commanded through the OKW (Keitel) - in game, treat the OKW chief as the defence advisor 1938-45. No German armed forces/defence ministry 1945-55. Navy: State Secretary of the Reichsmarineamt (Tirpitz 1897-1916) was a separate office.
- **Finance / treasury**: Prussian finance holders before 1825 omitted (split departments). 1871-79 Reich finance was handled by the Prussian finance minister and the Reichskanzleramt; Reich Treasury (Reichsschatzamt) from 1879.
- **Interior / home**: Prussian interior ministers to 1878 (Prussia kept its own interior ministry after 1871 - Prussian holders after 1878 are omitted); Reich domestic affairs under the Reichskanzleramt (1867-79) then the Reichsamt des Innern. Nazi era: the interior ministry lost control of the police to Himmler (1936).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No public intelligence chief before 1913 (Section IIIb of the General Staff existed from 1889). 1933-45: Abwehr (military) and Gestapo/SD/RSHA (party-state security) coexisted - Abwehr chiefs and Gestapo/RSHA chiefs both listed; game may treat RSHA chief as the security advisor. FRG: two parallel lists - BND (foreign intelligence, primary advisor) and BfV (domestic security); both listed with distinguishing titles. 1945-56: Organisation Gehlen under US control.
- **Military chief**: Prussian/German Chief of the (Great) General Staff to 1919; Chef der Heeresleitung 1919-35; Commander-in-Chief of the Army 1935-38; OKW chief 1938-45 (Hitler as supreme commander). No German military 1945-55. Generalinspekteur der Bundeswehr from 1957.

## India (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1858-11 | British East India Company rule | colonial_or_occupied | Calcutta | foreign_occupation, revolution |
| 1858-11 | 1947-08 | British Raj | colonial_or_occupied | Calcutta (to Dec 1911), Delhi / New Delhi (from 1911; New Delhi inaugurated Feb 1931); summer capital Simla | foreign_occupation, revolution |
| 1947-08 | 1950-01 | Dominion of India | dominion | New Delhi | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |
| 1950-01 | 1975-06 | Republic of India | parliamentary_republic | New Delhi | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, death_in_office |
| 1975-06 | 1977-03 | Republic of India (The Emergency) | parliamentary_republic | New Delhi | general_election, revolution |
| 1977-03 | present | Republic of India | parliamentary_republic | New Delhi | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |

- **British East India Company rule (1789–1858-11)**: Governor-General appointed by the Company's Court of Directors under the Board of Control (London). Princely states (Mysore to 1799, Maratha Confederacy to 1818, Sikh Empire to 1849, Mughal emperor at Delhi nominally to 1857) were separate actors. Not a sovereign playable India; the game could treat the Marathas, Mysore, the Sikh Empire or Hyderabad as tier-3 states. Ended by the 1857 rebellion and the Government of India Act 1858.
- **British Raj (1858-11–1947-08)**: Viceroy and Governor-General appointed by the Crown on the advice of the British Cabinet (Secretary of State for India). Viceroy's Executive Council functioned as a cabinet; Indian members from 1909. Interim Government (Nehru as Vice-President of the Executive Council) from 2 Sep 1946. Independence and Partition 15 Aug 1947 (Indian Independence Act 1947).
- **Dominion of India (1947-08–1950-01)**: Governor-General represents George VI; Prime Minister responsible to the Constituent Assembly (acting as legislature). Partition war with Pakistan over Kashmir 1947-48; princely states integrated by Patel.
- **Republic of India (1950-01–1975-06)**: President elected for 5 years by an electoral college of MPs and state MLAs; President appoints as PM the leader commanding a Lok Sabha majority. PM and Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Vice-President acts if the presidency falls vacant; the senior-most minister is sworn in as interim PM if a PM dies (Nanda 1964, 1966). Congress Party dominance; wars with China 1962 and Pakistan 1965, 1971.
- **Republic of India (The Emergency) (1975-06–1977-03)**: Indira Gandhi ruled by decree under Art. 352 emergency powers; elections postponed, civil liberties suspended, opposition jailed. Ended when Gandhi called elections (Mar 1977) and lost to the Janata Party. Game: an incumbent can suspend no-confidence/elections at a legitimacy cost.
- **Republic of India (1977-03–present)**: As 1950-75. No-confidence has actually removed PMs: Morarji Desai resigned ahead of one (1979), V.P. Singh lost a confidence vote (Nov 1990), Deve Gowda (Apr 1997) and Vajpayee (Apr 1999, by one vote) lost confidence votes. Coalition-era governments 1989-2014. BJP-led NDA since 2014. President Murmu's term runs to Jul 2027; next general election due 2029.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Ceremonial President; acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers. Can impose President's Rule in states (Art. 356) and proclaim a national emergency (Art. 352) on cabinet advice.
- **Head of government**: Pre-1947 entries are British Governors-General/Viceroys (not sovereign Indian government). Real executive since 1947 is the PM.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Intelligence Bureau (domestic, 1887-) was the only service until R&AW (external) split off in Sep 1968; listed here are IB directors to 1968 and R&AW secretaries after. Current IB Director Tapan Deka (2022-). National Security Advisor (Brajesh Mishra 1998-2004, J.N. Dixit 2004-05, M.K. Narayanan 2005-10, Shivshankar Menon 2010-14, Ajit Doval 2014-) is the PM's top security adviser and a good game 'intelligence advisor' alternative. R&AW tenures before 2000 are year-only in public sources.
- **Military chief**: Listed: army chief (C-in-C to 1955, COAS after). The President is supreme commander. Chief of Defence Staff created Jan 2020: Bipin Rawat (Jan 2020-Dec 2021, killed in helicopter crash), vacant to Sep 2022, Anil Chauhan (Sep 2022-May 2026), N. S. Raja Subramani (May 2026-). Game may prefer CDS as tri-service chief from 2020.
- **Foreign affairs**: PM often held External Affairs (Nehru for all 17 years).

- **Qajar-Zand civil war (1789–1796-03)**: Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar held the north from Tehran; the Zand dynasty (Jafar Khan d. Jan 1789, Sayyed Morad Khan Jan-May 1789, Lotf Ali Khan May 1789-1794) held Fars. Lotf Ali Khan was captured at Kerman in 1794. Agha Mohammad was formally crowned Shah in March 1796. Game: start 1789 Iran as Qajar under Agha Mohammad Khan; a Zand rump state can be a tier-3 rival until 1794.
- **Qajar Persia (absolute monarchy) (1796-03–1906-08)**: Hereditary in the Qajar line; the designated crown prince (vali-ahd) traditionally governed Tabriz/Azerbaijan. Grand Viziers served at the Shah's pleasure and were often executed (Qa'em-Maqam 1835, Amir Kabir 1852). Russo-Persian wars 1804-13 and 1826-28 (Treaties of Gulistan and Turkmenchay); Anglo-Persian War 1856-57; Naser al-Din Shah assassinated 1896. No regular cabinet until the 1850s-70s; foreign ministry from 1821.
- **Qajar constitutional monarchy (First Majlis) (1906-08–1908-06)**: Constitution of Aug/Dec 1906 created the Majlis; ministers responsible to it under the 1907 Supplementary Fundamental Law. PM (ra'is al-vozara) appointed by the Shah. 1907 Anglo-Russian Convention split Persia into spheres of influence.
- **Lesser Autocracy (Estebdad-e Saghir) (1908-06–1909-07)**: Mohammad Ali Shah shelled the Majlis (23 Jun 1908) with the Russian-officered Cossack Brigade and ruled by decree until constitutionalist forces took Tehran and deposed him (16 Jul 1909).
- **Qajar constitutional monarchy (Ahmad Shah) (1909-07–1925-10)**: Ahmad Shah succeeded as a boy under regents (Azod al-Molk 1909-10, Naser ol-Molk 1910-14). Cabinets fell every few months. 1911 Russian ultimatum closed the Second Majlis; WWI occupation by Russian, British and Ottoman forces despite neutrality; 21 Feb 1921 coup by Reza Khan and Zia'eddin Tabatabaee. Majlis deposed the dynasty on 31 Oct 1925. Ahmad Shah largely absent in Europe after 1923.
- **Pahlavi Iran under Reza Shah (1925-10–1941-09)**: Constituent Assembly made Reza Khan Shah (12 Dec 1925); hereditary in the Pahlavi line. Majlis was a rubber stamp; ministers dismissed (and some, like Teymourtash 1933, killed) at the Shah's will. Country renamed Iran internationally in 1935. Anglo-Soviet invasion (25 Aug 1941) forced Reza Shah's abdication in favour of his son (16 Sep 1941).
- **Mohammad Reza Shah - parliamentary interlude (1941-09–1953-08)**: Majlis vote of inclination (tamayol) nominated PMs, the Shah issued the farman. Allied occupation to 1946 (Azerbaijan crisis). PMs Hazhir (1949) and Razmara (1951) assassinated. Mosaddegh nationalised oil (1951); the 30 Tir uprising (Jul 1952) restored him after the Shah replaced him with Qavam. Ended by the Anglo-American-backed coup of 19 Aug 1953 (28 Mordad) that installed Gen. Fazlollah Zahedi.
- **Pahlavi royal autocracy (1953-08–1979-02)**: Shah appointed and dismissed PMs; Majlis managed through official parties (Iran Novin, then the single Rastakhiz Party from 1975). SAVAK from 1957. White Revolution 1963. Revolution of 1978-79: Shah left Iran 16 Jan 1979 leaving a Regency Council and PM Bakhtiar; the army declared neutrality 11 Feb 1979.
- **Provisional revolutionary government (1979-02–1979-12)**: Khomeini as Leader of the Revolution appointed Bazargan's Provisional Government (named 4-5 Feb 1979) alongside the clerical Council of the Islamic Revolution. Bazargan resigned after the US embassy seizure (6 Nov 1979); the Revolutionary Council governed until 1980. Islamic Republic proclaimed 1 Apr 1979 after referendum; constitution ratified Dec 1979.
- **Islamic Republic (with prime minister) (1979-12–1989-08)**: Supreme Leader (Vali-ye Faqih) holds ultimate authority; directly elected president plus a PM confirmed by the Majlis. Majlis declared President Banisadr politically incompetent (21 Jun 1981) and Khomeini dismissed him. President Rajai and PM Bahonar killed by a bomb (30 Aug 1981). Iran-Iraq War 1980-88. 1989 constitutional revision abolished the PM post.
- **Islamic Republic (presidential executive) (1989-08–present)**: Assembly of Experts elects and may in theory dismiss the Supreme Leader (lifetime office). President directly elected (two consecutive 4-year terms) after Guardian Council vetting; Majlis can impeach ministers (used often: Nouri 1998, Kordan 2008, Karbasian 2018, Hemmati 2025) and declare the president incompetent, with the Leader's approval to dismiss. If the president dies, the first vice-president acts and an election follows within 50 days (2024). Ali Khamenei killed in a US-Israeli strike 28 Feb 2026; an interim Leadership Council (President, Chief Justice, a Guardian Council faqih) served 1-9 Mar 2026 until the Assembly of Experts chose Mojtaba Khamenei. Game: Supreme Leader is the player's office; IRGC loyalty is the key coup/revolution variable.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Qajar/Pahlavi Shah, then the Supreme Leader (Vali-ye Faqih), who commands the armed forces, appoints the judiciary chief, half the Guardian Council and the heads of state media, and can dismiss the president. Game: in 1979+ the player is the Supreme Leader; the president is a powerful advisor/rival.
- **Head of government**: Pre-1906: Grand Viziers (Sadr-e A'zam) — there was no cabinet as such; long vacancies (1858-71) when the Shah ruled through a council. 1906-1989: Prime Minister. 1980-89 the President coexisted with the PM (listed here with notes; game should treat the PM as head of government in that window). From Aug 1989 the President is head of government.
- **Foreign affairs**: Foreign ministry founded 1821; Qajar-era holders are year-only and partly unverified. Pahlavi 1925-38 is not reliably covered (see uncertainty).
- **Defence / war**: Before 1858 there was no Minister of War: the Shah, crown prince (Abbas Mirza, 1799-1833) or a royal prince commanded. 1982-1989 a separate Ministry of the IRGC existed (Mohsen Rafiqdoost 1982-88, Ali Shamkhani 1988-89) — not listed as main holders. Since 1989 the MODAFL minister is a procurement/logistics role; operational command runs Supreme Leader -> General Staff.
- **Finance / treasury**: Pre-1906: finances run by the Mostowfi al-Mamalek (chief accountant) and the Shah's treasury; foreign advisers (Shuster 1911, Millspaugh 1922-27, 1943-45) held real fiscal power. Pahlavi-era finance holders 1924-1979 are year-only in available sources and flagged uncertain.
- **Interior / home**: Qajar interior ministers (post-1906) are not covered; Pahlavi and Islamic Republic lists complete per Wikipedia cross-check. 1979-80 gap covered by acting ministers (Rafsanjani, others).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No modern intelligence chief before SAVAK (1957); 1979-84 intelligence was split among IRGC intelligence, revolutionary committees and the PM's office; Ministry of Intelligence (VAJA/MOIS) from 1984. IRGC Intelligence Organization is a parallel, often more powerful service. After Khatib's death (Mar 2026) the ministry was run by an acting minister whose name was not confirmed in sources checked.
- **Military chief**: IRGC commanders-in-chief (separate force, politically decisive): Javad Mansouri 1979, Abbas Agha-Zamani 1979-80, Morteza Rezaee 1980-81, Mohsen Rezaee 1981-97, Yahya Rahim Safavi 1997-2007, Mohammad Ali Jafari 2007-19, Hossein Salami 2019-Jun 2025 (killed), Mohammad Pakpour Jun 2025-Feb 2026 (killed), Ahmad Vahidi Mar 2026- (confirmed 10 Aug 2026). Artesh commanders-in-chief since 1998: Ali Shahbazi, Mohammad Salimi, Ataollah Salehi, Abdolrahim Mousavi (2017-25), Amir Hatami (Jun 2025-). Qajar era had no general staff; Persian Cossack Brigade (Russian-officered, 1879-1921) was the main modern unit.

## Israel (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1948-05 | 1949-02 | Provisional Government of Israel | revolutionary_government | Tel Aviv | general_election, no_confidence |
| 1949-02 | 1996-06 | State of Israel (parliamentary) | parliamentary_republic | Jerusalem (declared capital Jan 1950; Knesset moved Dec 1949). Most foreign embassies stayed in Tel Aviv. | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |
| 1996-06 | 2001-03 | State of Israel (directly elected PM) | parliamentary_republic | Jerusalem | no_confidence, general_election |
| 2001-03 | present | State of Israel (parliamentary, constructive no-confidence) | parliamentary_republic | Jerusalem | constructive_no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |

- **Provisional Government of Israel (1948-05–1949-02)**: Provisional State Council (Moetzet HaMedina HaZmanit) and Provisional Government governed until the first Knesset convened (14 Feb 1949). War of Independence 1948-49. Weizmann was President of the Provisional State Council.
- **State of Israel (parliamentary) (1949-02–1996-06)**: President (elected by the Knesset) asks the MK most likely to form a coalition; government needs Knesset confidence. PM resignation brings down the whole government. Coalition collapse typically leads to Knesset self-dissolution and early elections. Unicameral 120-seat Knesset, pure national-list proportional representation; every government has been a coalition.
- **State of Israel (directly elected PM) (1996-06–2001-03)**: PM directly elected (1996, 1999, special PM-only election Feb 2001). A Knesset no-confidence vote (61 MKs) removed the PM but forced new elections for both PM and Knesset. Direct election repealed in 2001 (Basic Law: The Government 2001).
- **State of Israel (parliamentary, constructive no-confidence) (2001-03–present)**: Constructive no-confidence: the Knesset must approve an alternative government (since 2014 amendment) to topple the incumbent. Failure to pass a budget triggers automatic dissolution and elections. Rotation agreements (2020 Netanyahu-Gantz, 2021 Bennett-Lapid) can hand office over without a vote; 'alternate prime minister' post created 2020. Election for the 26th Knesset scheduled for 27 Oct 2026 (Knesset dissolved July 2026); Netanyahu heads the 37th government at the data cut-off.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Ceremonial President elected by the Knesset (7-year single term since 2000; previously 5-year renewable). Pardon power and the mandate to form a government are its main game levers.
- **Head of government**: Real executive. 'Alternate Prime Minister' (2020-) is a designated successor under rotation deals: Gantz 2020-21, Lapid 2021-22, Bennett 2022.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Three agencies: Mossad (foreign intelligence, listed here), Shin Bet/Shabak (internal security; directors: Isser Harel 1948-52, Izi Dorot 1952-53, Amos Manor 1953-63, Yosef Harmelin 1964-74, Avraham Ahituv 1974-80, Avraham Shalom 1981-86, Yosef Harmelin 1986-88, Yaakov Peri 1988-95, Carmi Gillon 1995-96, Ami Ayalon 1996-2000, Avi Dichter 2000-05, Yuval Diskin 2005-11, Yoram Cohen 2011-16, Nadav Argaman 2016-21, Ronen Bar Oct 2021-Jun 2025 (dismissal contested in court; resigned), acting deputy 'Sh.' Jun-Oct 2025, David Zini Oct 2025-), and Aman (military intelligence directorate). Mossad and Shin Bet report directly to the PM. Mossad directors' exact month boundaries 1949-1968 are approximate.
- **Defence / war**: PM frequently holds Defence concurrently (Ben-Gurion, Eshkol, Begin, Rabin, Peres, Barak, Netanyahu).
- **Military chief**: Ramatkal is the only lieutenant-general; appointed by the cabinet on the defence minister's recommendation, normally 3-4 year terms.

## Italy (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1861-03-17 | Pre-unification (no Italian state) | colonial_or_occupied | — |  |
| 1861-03-17 | 1922-10-30 | Kingdom of Italy (liberal monarchy) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Turin (1861-1865); Florence (1865-1871); Rome (from Jul 1871) | no_confidence, royal_dismissal, general_election, assassination |
| 1922-10-30 | 1943-07-25 | Fascist Italy | one_party_state | Rome | royal_dismissal, coup |
| 1943-07-25 | 1946-06-02 | Badoglio/Bonomi royal governments; co-belligerent Kingdom of the South | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Rome; Brindisi (Sep 1943-Feb 1944); Salerno (Feb-Jul 1944); Rome from Jul 1944 | royal_dismissal, revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1946-06-02 | present | Italian Republic | parliamentary_republic | Rome | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, impeachment |

- **Pre-unification (no Italian state) (1789–1861-03-17)**: No unified Italy. The peninsula was divided (Kingdom of Sardinia, Papal States, Two Sicilies, Austrian Lombardy-Venetia, Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy 1805-1814 under Napoleon with Eugène de Beauharnais as viceroy). Game: Italy should not be playable before 17 Mar 1861; the Kingdom of Sardinia (capital Turin; Cavour PM 1852-1859, 1860-61) is its predecessor if the game models it.
- **Kingdom of Italy (liberal monarchy) (1861-03-17–1922-10-30)**: Hereditary Savoy monarchy (Salic law). The Statuto Albertino (1848) made ministers formally responsible to the King, but by convention governments needed the confidence of the Chamber of Deputies; cabinets usually fell to parliamentary crises rather than formal votes. King Umberto I assassinated 1900. Senate appointed by the King; Chamber elected on a narrow franchise until 1912 (near-universal male suffrage 1912/1918).
- **Fascist Italy (1922-10-30–1943-07-25)**: Mussolini appointed after the March on Rome; from 1925-26 'Capo del Governo' answerable only to the King; single-party state from 1926/1928. The Grand Council of Fascism could advise on succession. Removed 25 Jul 1943 when the Grand Council passed the Grandi motion and Victor Emmanuel III dismissed and arrested him. Game: no-confidence impossible; removal only by royal dismissal backed by a Grand Council revolt (palace coup).
- **Badoglio/Bonomi royal governments; co-belligerent Kingdom of the South (1943-07-25–1946-06-02)**: Royal government without an elected parliament; from Jun 1944 cabinets formed by the CLN parties under Allied supervision; Umberto Lieutenant General of the Realm from 5 Jun 1944. Parallel German puppet state, the Italian Social Republic (RSI, 23 Sep 1943-25 Apr 1945), seat at Salò/Gargnano on Lake Garda: Mussolini head of state and government and his own foreign minister; Rodolfo Graziani minister of defence; Domenico Pellegrini Giampietro finance; Guido Buffarini Guidi then Paolo Zerbino interior. Mussolini executed by partisans 28 Apr 1945.
- **Italian Republic (1946-06-02–present)**: President elected for 7 years by Parliament in joint session plus regional delegates. Government needs the confidence of BOTH chambers (Art. 94); a government that loses confidence (or whose coalition breaks) resigns and the President consults to form a new one or dissolves Parliament. President removable only for high treason/attack on the Constitution (impeachment by Parliament, trial by Constitutional Court). Constitution in force 1 Jan 1948. Extremely frequent cabinet changes (68 governments 1946-2022). Monarchy abolished by the 2 Jun 1946 referendum.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: Before 1926 the PM was formally President of the Council of Ministers; Mussolini held the distinct office of Capo del Governo 1926-1943. PMs frequently held the Interior and/or Foreign portfolio concurrently.
- **Defence / war**: 1861-1947: Minister of War (army only; separate Ministers of the Navy and, from 1925, of the Air Force - not listed). Ministry of Defence from 4 Feb 1947.
- **Finance / treasury**: Kingdom: Minister of Finance (Finanze) listed; a separate Treasury (Tesoro) existed 1877-1922 and 1944-1946. Republic 1946-2001: Minister of the Treasury (the senior economic post; a separate Finance ministry handled taxation). From 2001: Minister of Economy and Finance.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No national intelligence chief before 1925 (army 'Ufficio Informazioni'). 1925-1945 SIM (military); the Fascist political police OVRA was run by the Chief of Police (Bocchini, Senise). 1949-1977 SIFAR then SID (military). 1977-2007 SISMI (military/foreign) and SISDE (civil/domestic, not listed). From 2007 AISE (external) and AISI (internal, not listed). SID/SISMI months are approximate.
- **Military chief**: 1882-1925: Chief of Staff of the Army (no joint chief before). 1925-1945: Chief of the General Staff (Capo di Stato Maggiore Generale, Comando Supremo from 1941). Republic: Chief of the Defence Staff (formally so-titled from 1948/1950). The King was nominal commander-in-chief; in 1940 Mussolini took operational command as First Marshal of the Empire.

### Head of state

- 1861-03-17 → 1878-01-09: **Victor Emmanuel II**, King of Italy — *Re d'Italia* — King of Sardinia from 1849; proclaimed King of Italy 17 Mar 1861
- 1878-01-09 → 1900-07-29: **Umberto I**, King of Italy — *Re d'Italia* — Assassinated at Monza
- 1900-07-29 → 1946-05-09: **Victor Emmanuel III**, King of Italy — *Re d'Italia* — Also Emperor of Ethiopia 1936-1941 and King of Albania 1939-1943; transferred powers to Umberto as Lieutenant General of the Realm 5 Jun 1944; abdicated 9 May 1946
- 1944-06-05 → 1946-05-09: **Umberto, Prince of Piedmont**, Lieutenant General of the Realm (regent) — *Luogotenente Generale del Regno* — Exercised royal prerogatives while Victor Emmanuel III remained nominal king
- 1946-05-09 → 1946-06-18: **Umberto II**, King of Italy — *Re d'Italia* — "King of May"; left Italy 13 Jun 1946 after the 2 Jun 1946 referendum
- 1946-06-13 → 1946-07-01: **Alcide De Gasperi** (acting), Provisional Head of State — *Capo provvisorio dello Stato (funzioni)*
