## Japan (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1868-01 | Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo bakufu) | absolute_monarchy | Edo (shogun's seat; Emperor resided in Kyoto) | death_in_office, abdication, assassination, revolution, coup |
| 1868-01 | 1885-12 | Meiji Restoration: Daijōkan (Council of State) government | absolute_monarchy | Kyoto, then Tokyo (from 1868-69) | royal_dismissal, assassination, revolution, coup |
| 1885-12 | 1918-09 | Empire of Japan: Meiji constitutional order (oligarchic/genrō cabinets) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Tokyo | royal_dismissal, loss_of_party_leadership, no_confidence, assassination |
| 1918-09 | 1932-05 | Empire of Japan: 'Taishō democracy' party cabinets | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Tokyo | general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, royal_dismissal, assassination |
| 1932-05 | 1945-09 | Empire of Japan: militarist 'national unity' cabinets | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Tokyo | royal_dismissal, coup, assassination, foreign_occupation |
| 1945-09 | 1952-04 | Allied (U.S.) Occupation | colonial_or_occupied | Tokyo | no_confidence, general_election, foreign_occupation |
| 1952-04 | present | Japan (post-war constitutional monarchy) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Tokyo | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |

- **Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo bakufu) (1789–1868-01)**: Hereditary shogunate within the Tokugawa house, chosen from the main line or the Gosanke/Gosankyō branch houses; the Emperor is a sacral figure without executive power. Senior councillors (rōjū) run day-to-day government and are dismissed by the shogun. Feudal military government (bakufu) under a nominal Emperor; seclusion policy (sakoku) until 1854. Ended by the Boshin War/Meiji Restoration. Game: treat shogun as the ruler; 'removal' = palace intrigue (rōjū dismissal) or revolution.
- **Meiji Restoration: Daijōkan (Council of State) government (1868-01–1885-12)**: Imperial rule in name; policy made by an oligarchy of Satsuma-Chōshū leaders (genrō-to-be). Ministers (kyō) appointed by the throne. Satsuma Rebellion 1877; ministers held -kyō titles until the cabinet system of 1885-12.
- **Empire of Japan: Meiji constitutional order (oligarchic/genrō cabinets) (1885-12–1918-09)**: PM nominated to the Emperor by the genrō (elder statesmen, e.g. Itō, Yamagata, Matsukata, later Saionji). Meiji Constitution 1889 (Diet from 1890-11): cabinet responsible to the Emperor, not the Diet, but needed Diet consent for budgets. Army/Navy ministers had to be serving officers (1900-1913, again 1936-45), giving the services a veto over cabinets. Game: no formal no-confidence; a hostile Diet can block budgets, and military resignation can topple cabinets ('cabinet collapse' event).
- **Empire of Japan: 'Taishō democracy' party cabinets (1918-09–1932-05)**: Convention ('normal course of constitutional government') that the leader of the majority party in the House of Representatives is nominated by the last genrō Saionji. Universal male suffrage 1925. PMs Hara (1921) and Hamaguchi (shot 1930) assassinated; ended by the May 15 Incident 1932.
- **Empire of Japan: militarist 'national unity' cabinets (1932-05–1945-09)**: PM chosen by the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal and senior statesmen (jūshin), effectively requiring Army acceptance. Political parties dissolved into the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (1940). February 26 Incident 1936 (failed army coup). Imperial General Headquarters from 1937. Game: Army can veto/topple cabinets by withholding a War Minister.
- **Allied (U.S.) Occupation (1945-09–1952-04)**: Japanese cabinet governed under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (MacArthur, then Ridgway). New Constitution in force 1947-05-03: PM elected by the Diet. Military and Home Ministry abolished; Article 9 renounces war. Sovereignty restored by the San Francisco Treaty (in force 1952-04-28).
- **Japan (post-war constitutional monarchy) (1952-04–present)**: PM designated by the National Diet (House of Representatives prevails). A no-confidence resolution forces resignation or dissolution within 10 days. In practice the LDP presidential election chooses the PM (LDP in power 1955-93, 1994-2009, 2012-present). Emperor is 'symbol of the State'. Self-Defense Forces from 1954. Game: removal mainly by losing the LDP leadership or an election; no-confidence has succeeded in 1948, 1953, 1980, 1993.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: The Emperor reigned but before 1868 had no executive power; 1868-1945 sovereign in law but acted on advice; since 1947 purely symbolic.
- **Paramount leader (party)**: 1789-1868 only: the Tokugawa shogun was the de facto ruler; the game should make the shogun the player's office for this era.
- **Head of government**: 1789-1868: rōjū shuseki / tairō act as chief minister (list here is partial: only major figures). 1871-1885 Daijō-daijin (Sanjō) was nominal; real power with Ōkubo then Itō. Cabinet PM from 1885-12-22.
- **Foreign affairs**: Before 1869 foreign affairs were handled by bakufu Gaikoku-bugyō (commissioners); not modeled. PMs frequently held the portfolio concurrently for days/weeks; only notable acting stints listed.
- **Defence / war**: Pre-1945 the Army Minister is listed as defence and the Navy Minister separately (navy_minister). 1945-1952 no military ministry (Article 9). Defense Agency Director-Generals 1954-2007 (about 60 holders) are only partially listed here — known gap. Minister of Defense from 2007-01-09.
- **Interior / home**: Home Ministry abolished 1947-12. 1948-2001 functions split among Ministry of Home Affairs (Jichishō), National Public Safety Commission and others; those ministers are a known gap. Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications from 2001-01.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No unified intelligence chief before 1945: Army Kempeitai (military police, also political policing in occupied areas) and the Home Ministry Special Higher Police (Tokkō) were the security apparatus; commanders not modeled. Post-war: Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office (Naichō); Director of Cabinet Intelligence from 2001. Only Kitamura Shigeru listed (gap). Public Security Intelligence Agency (PSIA, Ministry of Justice) is a secondary option.
- **Military chief**: Pre-1945: Chief of the Army General Staff (the Navy General Staff had its own chief, not listed). Supreme command was independent of the cabinet (tōsuiken). Post-war: Chairman of the Joint Staff Council 1954-2006 (gap), Chief of Staff, Joint Staff from 2006-03.

## Mexico (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1821-09 | Viceroyalty of New Spain | colonial_or_occupied | Mexico City | royal_dismissal, revolution |
| 1821-09 | 1823-03 | First Mexican Empire (Regency, then Agustín I) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Mexico City | coup, abdication, revolution |
| 1823-03 | 1824-10 | Supreme Executive Power (provisional triumvirate) | revolutionary_government | Mexico City | coup, revolution |
| 1824-10 | 1835-10 | First Federal Republic | presidential_republic | Mexico City | general_election, coup, revolution, term_limit |
| 1835-10 | 1846-08 | Centralist Republic (Siete Leyes 1836; Bases Orgánicas 1843) | presidential_republic | Mexico City | coup, revolution, general_election |
| 1846-08 | 1853-04 | Second Federal Republic (restored 1824 Constitution, Acta de Reformas 1847) | presidential_republic | Mexico City | coup, revolution, general_election, foreign_occupation |
| 1853-04 | 1855-08 | Dictatorship of Santa Anna ('His Most Serene Highness') | personalist_dictatorship | Mexico City | revolution, coup |
| 1855-08 | 1858-01 | Liberal Reform (Ayutla governments; Constitution of 1857) | presidential_republic | Mexico City | coup, revolution, general_election |
| 1858-01 | 1861-01 | Reform War (rival Liberal and Conservative governments) | revolutionary_government | Mexico City (Conservative) / Veracruz (Liberal, Juárez) | coup, revolution |
| 1861-01 | 1863-06 | Restored Constitutional Government (Juárez) and French Intervention | presidential_republic | Mexico City | general_election, foreign_occupation, revolution |
| 1863-06 | 1867-06 | Second Mexican Empire (Maximilian I) vs. itinerant Republic | absolute_monarchy | Mexico City (Empire) / San Luis Potosí, Chihuahua, Paso del Norte (Republic) | foreign_occupation, revolution, assassination |
| 1867-06 | 1876-11 | Restored Republic | presidential_republic | Mexico City | general_election, revolution, coup |
| 1876-11 | 1911-05 | Porfiriato | personalist_dictatorship | Mexico City | revolution, death_in_office |
| 1911-05 | 1913-02 | Maderista Republic | presidential_republic | Mexico City | coup, revolution, general_election |
| 1913-02 | 1914-07 | Huerta dictatorship | personalist_dictatorship | Mexico City | revolution, foreign_occupation, coup |
| 1914-07 | 1917-05 | Revolutionary civil war (Constitutionalists vs. Conventionists) | revolutionary_government | Mexico City (contested; Carranza at Veracruz Nov 1914 - Oct 1915) | revolution, coup |
| 1917-05 | 1929-03 | Post-revolutionary republic (Sonoran dynasty / early Maximato) | presidential_republic | Mexico City | revolution, coup, assassination, term_limit |
| 1929-03 | 2000-12 | PNR/PRM/PRI hegemonic-party era | one_party_state | Mexico City | term_limit, party_congress |
| 2000-12 | present | Multi-party democracy | presidential_republic | Mexico City | term_limit, general_election, impeachment |

- **Viceroyalty of New Spain (1789–1821-09)**: Viceroys appointed and recalled by the Spanish Crown (Charles IV to 1808, then Ferdinand VII; Cortes of Cádiz/Regency 1808-14). Not a sovereign actor before independence. War of Independence 16 Sep 1810 (Grito de Dolores) - 27 Sep 1821. Foreign/defence policy run from Madrid.
- **First Mexican Empire (Regency, then Agustín I) (1821-09–1823-03)**: Plan of Iguala / Treaty of Córdoba: Regency under Iturbide; Congress proclaimed Iturbide Emperor 19-21 May 1822. Iturbide dissolved Congress Oct 1822; Plan of Casa Mata revolt (Santa Anna, Feb 1823) forced abdication 19 Mar 1823.
- **Supreme Executive Power (provisional triumvirate) (1823-03–1824-10)**: Three-member executive (members rotated the presidency monthly) appointed by the Constituent Congress. Ended by the 1824 Federal Constitution.
- **First Federal Republic (1824-10–1835-10)**: President elected by state legislatures for 4 years, no immediate re-election. In practice military pronunciamientos (Plan de la Acordada 1828, Plan de Jalapa 1829) decided power. Spanish reconquest attempt defeated 1829.
- **Centralist Republic (Siete Leyes 1836; Bases Orgánicas 1843) (1835-10–1846-08)**: President chosen indirectly for 8-year (1836) then 5-year (1843) terms; Supreme Conservative Power could declare the president incapacitated (1836-41). Texas secession 1836; Pastry War with France 1838-39; Yucatán secession 1841-48. Santa Anna repeatedly in and out of power via pronunciamientos.
- **Second Federal Republic (restored 1824 Constitution, Acta de Reformas 1847) (1846-08–1853-04)**: As 1824 constitution. Mexican-American War 1846-48; U.S. Army occupied Mexico City 14 Sep 1847 - 12 Jun 1848 (government at Toluca/Querétaro). Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ceded ~55% of territory.
- **Dictatorship of Santa Anna ('His Most Serene Highness') (1853-04–1855-08)**: Santa Anna recalled by conservatives as dictator; made dictatorship perpetual Dec 1853. Gadsden Purchase 1853/54. Overthrown by the Revolution of Ayutla (1854-55).
- **Liberal Reform (Ayutla governments; Constitution of 1857) (1855-08–1858-01)**: 1857 Constitution: president elected indirectly for 4 years; the President of the Supreme Court is constitutional successor. Comonfort's self-coup (Plan of Tacubaya, Dec 1857) triggered the Reform War.
- **Reform War (rival Liberal and Conservative governments) (1858-01–1861-01)**: Liberals recognised Supreme Court president Benito Juárez as constitutional president; Conservatives installed Zuloaga then Miramón in Mexico City. Game: model as civil war with two claimant governments. The U.S. recognised Juárez in 1859.
- **Restored Constitutional Government (Juárez) and French Intervention (1861-01–1863-06)**: Juárez elected 1861. Debt moratorium (Jul 1861) led to British-Spanish-French intervention (Dec 1861); French victory at Puebla 1863 and occupation of Mexico City (Jun 1863).
- **Second Mexican Empire (Maximilian I) vs. itinerant Republic (1863-06–1867-06)**: Assembly of Notables offered the crown to Maximilian of Habsburg (accepted 10 Apr 1864, Miramar). Republican government under Juárez continued (term extended by decree 1865). French-backed monarchy ruled by imperial decree (Provisional Statute 1865, no constitution). French troops withdrew 1866-67; Maximilian captured at Querétaro and executed 19 Jun 1867.
- **Restored Republic (1867-06–1876-11)**: 1857 Constitution; Juárez re-elected 1867 and 1871 (died 1872); Lerdo succeeded as Supreme Court president. Ended by Díaz's Plan of Tuxtepec revolt (1876).
- **Porfiriato (1876-11–1911-05)**: Nominal elections every 4 (from 1904: 6) years; Díaz re-elected 1884-1910 after amending the no-re-election clause. Vice-presidency restored 1904 (Ramón Corral). Stable authoritarian modernisation; cabinet of 'científicos'. Revolution began 20 Nov 1910 (Plan of San Luis); Díaz resigned 25 May 1911 (Treaty of Ciudad Juárez).
- **Maderista Republic (1911-05–1913-02)**: Interim León de la Barra; Madero elected Oct 1911. Ended by the Decena Trágica coup (9-19 Feb 1913); Madero and VP Pino Suárez murdered 22 Feb 1913.
- **Huerta dictatorship (1913-02–1914-07)**: Huerta became president via Foreign Secretary Lascuráin's 45-minute presidency (constitutional line of succession manipulated). Constitutionalist revolt (Carranza, Villa, Zapata, Obregón); U.S. occupation of Veracruz Apr-Nov 1914. Huerta resigned 15 Jul 1914.
- **Revolutionary civil war (Constitutionalists vs. Conventionists) (1914-07–1917-05)**: Carranza as First Chief of the Constitutionalist Army held executive power; the Convention of Aguascalientes named rival presidents (Gutiérrez, González Garza, Lagos Cházaro). Game: two claimant governments until Carranza's de facto recognition by the U.S. (Oct 1915). Constitution of 1917 promulgated 5 Feb 1917.
- **Post-revolutionary republic (Sonoran dynasty / early Maximato) (1917-05–1929-03)**: 1917 Constitution: direct election, 4-year term (6 years from 1928), no re-election (briefly relaxed 1927-28 for Obregón). Carranza killed 1920 after Agua Prieta revolt; Obregón assassinated as president-elect July 1928; Calles as 'Jefe Máximo' dominated 1928-1935 (Maximato). Cristero War 1926-29.
- **PNR/PRM/PRI hegemonic-party era (1929-03–2000-12)**: Single six-year term (sexenio) without re-election; the outgoing president personally chose the PRI candidate ('el dedazo'), who then won non-competitive elections. Interim/substitute presidents are chosen by Congress (Art. 84-85). Formally a presidential republic with elections, but in practice a dominant-party regime until the 1990s reforms (IFE 1990/1996); PRI lost the lower house in 1997. Game: no coups after 1929 (last major military revolt: Escobar 1929, Cedillo 1938); presidential removal effectively impossible, power ends at the sexenio.
- **Multi-party democracy (2000-12–present)**: Direct election, single 6-year term, no re-election ever. Vacancy filled by Congress (Secretary of the Interior acts provisionally since 2012 reform). Since 2019 a presidential recall referendum (revocación de mandato) can remove the president (first held 2022, not binding for lack of turnout). Impeachment (juicio político) of a sitting president is limited to treason and serious common crimes (Art. 108); since 2021 the president can be tried for corruption. Game: treat recall referendum as a 'no_confidence'-like popular trigger mid-term.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: 1789-1821 the head of state is the King of Spain (Charles IV 1788-1808, Ferdinand VII 1808-1833 with the Joseph Bonaparte/Regency interlude); viceroys are listed under head_of_government as the local executive. From 1824 the President is both head of state and head of government; 'interim', 'substitute' and 'provisional' presidents are distinct constitutional categories and are marked acting=True with the category in the note.
- **Head of government**: Presidential system: the President of Mexico is head of government (see head_of_state). Only the colonial viceroys (1789-1821) and the Second Empire's Presidents of the Council of Ministers (1864-67) are listed here.
- **Foreign affairs**: 1821-1843 the ministry was 'Relaciones Exteriores e Interiores' (foreign + interior combined), so the same person appears under interior for those years. From 1858-67 rulers.org lists the Liberal (Juárez) government's ministers by default; Conservative/Imperial ministers are flagged in the note. 19th-century tenures are to the year only (rulers.org); exact dates in the SRE official list where noted.
- **Defence / war**: Secretaría de Guerra y Marina 1821-1937; Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional (SEDENA) from 1 Jan 1937. The navy became a separate ministry (Marina Nacional, SEMAR) on 31 Dec 1940 - see navy_minister. SEDENA secretaries are always serving army generals and are the senior officer of the Army and Air Force.
- **Military chief**: Mexico has no joint chief of staff: the Secretary of National Defence (an active-duty general) commands the Army and Air Force and the Secretary of the Navy (an active-duty admiral) commands the Navy. Game: map the military chief advisor to the SEDENA secretary (defense list). Pre-1876 armies were led by whichever caudillo held the presidency or field command.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Public chiefs only: Dirección Federal de Seguridad (DFS, 1947-1985, political police under Gobernación); DISEN (1985-89); CISEN (1989-2018); Centro Nacional de Inteligencia (CNI, Dec 2018-). Before 1947 no national intelligence chief existed (intelligence was a Gobernación/army function).
- **Interior / home**: 1821-1843 the interior portfolio was combined with foreign affairs ('Relaciones Exteriores e Interiores'), then 'Relaciones Exteriores, Gobernación y Policía' 1842-53; Gobernación separate from 1853. Since 2012 reform the Secretary of the Interior (Gobernación) is first in the line of provisional presidential succession. Public security was split off to SSP (2000-2013) and SSPC (2018-).
- **Finance / treasury**: Secretaría de Hacienda (y Crédito Público from 1891). Officials marked acting were 'encargados del despacho' (oficial mayor / undersecretary in charge).

### Uncertainties

- 19th-century foreign ministers (1821-1919) are dated to the year only (rulers.org); exact day-level dates exist in the SRE's official list but were not transcribed.
- Defence, Navy, Finance and Interior holders come from the INAP cabinet compendium (Quijano Torres 2012) as tabulated on Spanish Wikipedia; brief acting stand-ins (<45 days) that interrupt the same minister were folded into the minister's tenure.
- Reform War (1858-61) and Second Empire (1863-67): two rival governments existed; holders of the Conservative/Imperial side are flagged in notes. Defence/finance/interior lists may mix both sides for those years.
- DISEN period (Aug 1985 - Feb 1989) intelligence directors not listed (not reliably public).
- 2026 change of Foreign Secretary (Juan Ramón de la Fuente -> Roberto Velasco Álvarez) taken from rulers.org/es.wikipedia; not verified against an official SRE announcement.
- Intelligence / security chief: Gilberto Suárez Torres (1958–1959)
- Intelligence / security chief: Alejandro Poiré Romero (2011–2011) — short tenure; month dates not confirmed
- Intelligence / security chief: Francisco Almazán Barocio (2024-10–) — appointment reported Oct 2024; not cross-checked against an official gob.mx roster

| 1983-12-13 | 2018-07-09 | Republic of Turkey (1982 constitution, parliamentary) | parliamentary_republic | Ankara | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, coup |

- **Ottoman Empire (classical/early reform era) (1789–1839-11-03)**: Sultan chosen from the House of Osman (seniority/agnatic, not primogeniture); deposition by Janissary revolt or palace coup was common (Selim III 1807, Mustafa IV 1808). Grand Viziers served at the Sultan's pleasure and were dismissed, exiled or executed at will. No cabinet: the Imperial Council (Divan-ı Hümayun) under the Grand Vizier; foreign affairs handled by the Reis ül-Küttab (chief scribe) until the Foreign Ministry was created in 1836; the Janissary Agha and later the Serasker (1826) led the army.
- **Ottoman Empire (Tanzimat) (1839-11-03–1876-12-23)**: As above. The Sultan remained absolute but a Council of Ministers (Meclis-i Vükelâ) with Western-style ministries (Foreign 1836, Interior 1836/37, Finance 1838) emerged; the Grand Vizier led it. Abdülaziz was deposed by his ministers in 1876. Game: removal of the player-sultan only by palace coup/deposition (fetva of the Şeyhülislam) or death; ministers by royal dismissal.
- **Ottoman Empire (First Constitutional Era) (1876-12-23–1878-02-14)**: Constitution of 1876 created an elected Chamber of Deputies, but ministers answered to the Sultan, who could exile anyone deemed dangerous (Art. 113 used against Midhat Pasha). Abdülhamid II prorogued parliament 14 Feb 1878.
- **Ottoman Empire (Hamidian autocracy) (1878-02-14–1908-07-23)**: Personal rule of Abdülhamid II from Yıldız Palace; extensive informer network (jurnal system) rather than a formal intelligence agency. Ended by the Young Turk Revolution (CUP), which forced restoration of the constitution.
- **Ottoman Empire (Second Constitutional Era) (1908-07-23–1913-01-23)**: 1909 amendments made the cabinet responsible to the Chamber of Deputies; Abdülhamid II deposed after the 31 March Incident (Apr 1909). Military factions (CUP, Savior Officers 1912) repeatedly forced cabinets out.
- **Ottoman Empire under CUP (Three Pashas) (1913-01-23–1918-11-01)**: Raid on the Sublime Porte (23 Jan 1913) brought the Committee of Union and Progress to power; from mid-1913 effective rule by Talat (Interior), Enver (War) and Cemal (Navy) Pashas; Sultan a figurehead. Game: removal only by coup, military defeat or collapse (the triumvirs fled 2 Nov 1918).
- **Ottoman Empire under Allied occupation (Istanbul government) (1918-11-01–1922-11-01)**: Sultan Mehmed VI governed through grand viziers acceptable to the Allies; parliament dissolved Apr 1920. Overlaps with the rival Ankara government from Apr 1920. Sultanate abolished 1 Nov 1922 by the Ankara Grand National Assembly; the last grand vizier resigned 4 Nov 1922.
- **Government of the Grand National Assembly (Ankara) (1920-04-23–1923-10-29)**: Assembly government: the GNA elected each Commissar (Vekil) individually and the Speaker (Mustafa Kemal) chaired the Council of Executive Commissars; commissars could be voted out by the Assembly. Game: a rival state to the Istanbul sultanate during the War of Independence (1919-1922); Treaty of Lausanne 24 Jul 1923.
- **Republic of Turkey (single-party CHP era) (1923-10-29–1946-07-21)**: President elected by the GNA for the Assembly's term (no limit in practice); PM appointed by the President. Only the Republican People's Party (CHP) was permitted (brief opposition experiments 1924-25 and 1930).
- **Republic of Turkey (multi-party democracy) (1946-07-21–1960-05-27)**: President elected by the GNA; government responsible to the GNA. Democrat Party governments 1950-1960. Ended by the 27 May 1960 military coup.
- **National Unity Committee (military junta) (1960-05-27–1961-11-20)**: Junta of 38 officers under Gen. Cemal Gürsel; new constitution 1961; PM Menderes, FM Zorlu and Finance Minister Polatkan executed.
- **Second Republic (1961 constitution) (1961-11-20–1980-09-12)**: Bicameral GNA; President elected by GNA for 7 years. National Security Council gave the military a formal voice. 12 March 1971 'coup by memorandum' forced Demirel out and installed technocratic cabinets until 1973. Game: elected government removable by no-confidence or by a military ultimatum (memorandum).
- **National Security Council (military junta) (1980-09-12–1983-12-13)**: Gen. Kenan Evren and the service chiefs ruled as the NSC; 1982 constitution approved by referendum, Evren became president.
- **Republic of Turkey (1982 constitution, parliamentary) (1983-12-13–2018-07-09)**: Unicameral GNA; PM and Council of Ministers responsible to the GNA. President elected by GNA (7 years) until 2014, then by popular vote (5 years). 28 February 1997 memorandum forced Erbakan out; 15 July 2016 coup attempt failed.
- **Republic of Turkey (executive presidency) (2018-07-09–present)**: 2017 referendum abolished the office of Prime Minister; the popularly elected President is head of state and government and appoints ministers (not MPs) without parliamentary confirmation. Two-term limit (a third if parliament calls an early election). Impeachment requires a 2/3 majority to send to the Constitutional Court. Vice President: Cevdet Yılmaz (from 2023).

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: 1789-1922 Grand Vizier (Sadrazam), dismissed at the Sultan's will. 1920-23 the Ankara government had a Chairman of the Council of Executive Commissars (overlapping the Istanbul grand viziers). 1923-2018 Prime Minister (Başbakan). From 9 Jul 2018 the President heads the government.
- **Foreign affairs**: Before 1836 foreign affairs were run by the Reis ül-Küttab (Chief Scribe of the Imperial Council) - not listed; game should treat the Grand Vizier/Sultan as foreign-policy maker. Ottoman Foreign Ministers 1836-1922 are year-level (all flagged uncertain); short gaps exist. 1920-1923 Ankara foreign commissars listed.
- **Defence / war**: No war ministry before 1826: the Grand Vizier commanded field armies and the Janissary Agha led the standing infantry - model as the Grand Vizier. 1826-1908 the Serasker (commander-in-chief/war minister); names are listed only from 1876 (1826-1876 seraskers not covered). 1908-1922 Minister of War (Harbiye Nazırı). Ankara/Republic: Minister of National Defence. Navy Ministry (Bahriye Nezareti) not listed.
- **Finance / treasury**: Ottoman finance ministers 1838-1922 are INCOMPLETE (only those with dates in available lists; large gaps 1855-1860, 1863-1880, 1891-1908) - all flagged uncertain. Republic list complete.
- **Interior / home**: Ottoman interior ministry existed 1836-1839 and again from 1869 (in between the functions sat with the Grand Vizier's deputy, Sadaret Kethüdası). Ottoman list is year-level and flagged uncertain.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No formal service before 1913 (Abdülhamid II used a palace informer network). 1913-1918 Teşkilât-ı Mahsusa (CUP special organisation). 1918-1926 Karakol/ad-hoc nationalist networks (not listed). 1926-1965 MAH; from 1965 MİT (Undersecretary, retitled President in 2017/18).
- **Military chief**: Ottoman Chief of the General Staff from 1908 (the Serasker served as the de facto army chief before). Republic: Chief of the General Staff (Genelkurmay Başkanı); answerable to the PM until 2018, to the Ministry of National Defence/President since.

## Russia (Russian Empire / USSR / Russian Federation) (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1905-10 | Russian Empire (autocracy) | absolute_monarchy | St Petersburg | death_in_office, coup, assassination, royal_dismissal |
| 1905-10 | 1917-03 | Russian Empire (Duma monarchy) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | St Petersburg (renamed Petrograd Sep 1914) | royal_dismissal, abdication, revolution, assassination |
| 1917-03 | 1917-11 | Russian Provisional Government (Russian Republic from Sep 1917) | revolutionary_government | Petrograd | revolution, coup |
| 1917-11 | 1922-12 | Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (civil war) | one_party_communist_state | Petrograd; Moscow from Mar 1918 | party_congress, coup, revolution, death_in_office |
| 1922-12 | 1991-12 | Union of Soviet Socialist Republics | one_party_communist_state | Moscow | party_congress, death_in_office, coup, revolution |
| 1991-12 | 1993-12 | Russian Federation (transitional, 1978 RSFSR constitution as amended) | semi_presidential_republic | Moscow | impeachment, general_election, no_confidence, coup |
| 1993-12 | present | Russian Federation (1993 constitution) | semi_presidential_republic | Moscow | general_election, impeachment, term_limit, presidential_dismissal, no_confidence |

- **Russian Empire (autocracy) (1789–1905-10)**: Hereditary autocracy. From Paul I's Pauline Laws (Apr 1797) succession is by male primogeniture within the Romanov (Holstein-Gottorp) house. Emperors were removed only by death or palace coup (Paul I murdered by officers, Mar 1801) or assassination (Alexander II, Mar 1881). Ministers served and were dismissed at the emperor's pleasure; there was no parliament. Ministries created by Alexander I's manifesto of Sep 1802 (replacing Peter the Great's colleges). The Committee of Ministers (from 1802) and State Council (1810) were advisory; there was no prime minister in the Western sense before Oct 1905. Coronations took place in Moscow, the 'second capital'.
- **Russian Empire (Duma monarchy) (1905-10–1917-03)**: October Manifesto (Oct 1905) and Fundamental Laws (May 1906) created an elected State Duma and a Council of Ministers under a chairman. Ministers remained responsible to the emperor, not the Duma; the Duma could not pass no-confidence votes (the emperor could dissolve it, as in 1906 and 1907). Nicholas II abdicated on 15 Mar 1917 (NS) during the February Revolution; his brother Michael declined the throne the next day. Stolypin (PM) assassinated Sep 1911. Game: the Duma can only obstruct (budget, scandal); removal of the player is by revolution or forced abdication.
- **Russian Provisional Government (Russian Republic from Sep 1917) (1917-03–1917-11)**: Self-appointed cabinet drawn from the Duma's Provisional Committee, sharing power with the Petrograd Soviet ('dual power'). No head of state; the minister-chairman acted for one. Overthrown by the Bolshevik October Revolution (7-8 Nov 1917 NS). Kornilov affair (Sep 1917) = attempted military coup.
- **Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (civil war) (1917-11–1922-12)**: Power held by the Bolshevik (RCP(b)) leadership through the Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom); the Constituent Assembly was dispersed in Jan 1918. Left SRs left the coalition in Mar 1918, after which the state was effectively one-party. Rival White governments existed 1918-20 (Kolchak, Denikin, Wrangel). Lenin was leader by authority, not by a party office; the post of General Secretary was created Apr 1922 (Stalin).
- **Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (1922-12–1991-12)**: Real power lay with the General (First) Secretary of the CPSU Central Committee and the Politburo. Leaders left office by death (Lenin, Stalin, Brezhnev, Andropov, Chernenko) or were removed by the Central Committee/Presidium (Khrushchev, Oct 1964; the 'Anti-Party Group' attempt failed in Jun 1957). State offices (Premier, Chairman of the Presidium) were often held by rivals or figureheads. Mar 1990: party's 'leading role' abolished and an executive Presidency created (Gorbachev, elected by the Congress of People's Deputies). Aug 1991 coup attempt (State Committee on the State of Emergency) failed; the USSR was dissolved 25-26 Dec 1991. Game: the player is the General Secretary. No no-confidence or impeachment; removal by Politburo/Central Committee vote (party_congress), coup, or death. Head of state and head of government are advisors/rivals, not the player's office (except when the GS also held them: Stalin as premier 1941-53, Khrushchev 1958-64, Brezhnev/Andropov/Chernenko/Gorbachev as head of state).
- **Russian Federation (transitional, 1978 RSFSR constitution as amended) (1991-12–1993-12)**: Directly elected president (Yeltsin, Jun 1991) in conflict with the Congress of People's Deputies/Supreme Soviet. The Sep-Oct 1993 constitutional crisis ended with Yeltsin dissolving parliament and shelling the White House; parliament's 'acting president' Rutskoy (22 Sep - 4 Oct 1993) was arrested.
- **Russian Federation (1993 constitution) (1993-12–present)**: President directly elected (4-year terms to 2012, 6-year since; two consecutive terms, 2020 amendments reset Putin's count, allowing him to serve to 2036). Impeachment requires Duma (2/3) + Supreme Court + Constitutional Court + Federation Council (2/3); attempted 1999, failed. The PM is nominated by the president and confirmed by the Duma (three rejections -> dissolution) and can be dismissed by the president at will. The Duma may pass no confidence, but the president may ignore the first vote and dissolve the Duma after a second. If the president dies or resigns, the PM becomes acting president (Putin, 31 Dec 1999). Game: in practice a dominant-president system; model the president as the player's office. Removal mainly via election defeat, resignation, death, or elite coup.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: 1917-03 to 1917-11 there was no head of state; the Provisional Government's minister-chairman acted for one. Soviet heads of state (VTsIK/CEC/Presidium chairmen) were largely ceremonial; the General Secretary held power.
- **Head of government**: Before 1810 the emperor presided over the Committee of Ministers himself; chairmen 1810-1864 had little power (dates approximate). Real head of government only from Oct 1905 (Witte).
- **Paramount leader (party)**: Use this as the player's office for 1917-1991. General Secretary formally from Apr 1922; Stalin not undisputed until c.1929. Mar-Sep 1953 collective leadership (Malenkov premier, Khrushchev party).
- **Foreign affairs**: Before Sep 1802 foreign affairs were run by the College of Foreign Affairs under a (vice-)chancellor; dates for 1789-1802 are approximate.
- **Defence / war**: Before Sep 1802: War College. 1917-18 collegial commissariat. The navy had a separate ministry 1802-1917 (see navy_minister) and a separate People's Commissariat of the Navy 1937-46 and 1950-53 (not listed).
- **Finance / treasury**: No finance minister before Sep 1802: state finances were overseen by the Procurator-General of the Senate (see interior) and the State Treasurer.
- **Interior / home**: Before 1802 the Procurator-General of the Senate acted as chief of internal administration. 1930-34 no all-union interior commissariat (OGPU handled policing). 1960-66 interior affairs handled by republican ministries only.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No dedicated political-police chief 1789-1810 (Secret Expedition of the Senate to 1801); Ministry of Police 1810-19; Third Section 1826-80; 1880-1917 Okhrana under the MVD Department of Police (game: use the Interior Minister). 1934-41 and 1941-43 state security was part of the NKVD, so the NKVD chief is listed. Post-1991 both FSB (domestic) and SVR (foreign) directors are listed; the GRU (military intelligence) chief is not.
- **Military chief**: 1789-1815 and 1832-1865 there was no separate general-staff chief: model the War Minister/field commander (e.g. Kutuzov 1812) as military chief. In WWI and 1917 the operational chief was the Supreme Commander/Stavka chief of staff rather than the GUGSh chief (who handled the rear). 1918-24 the Red Army's Commander-in-Chief (Glavkom) outranked the staff chiefs.

## Spain (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Kingdom of Spain - Bourbon absolute monarchy (Carlos IV) (1789-01–1808-05)**: Hereditary. The First Secretary of State (Primer Secretario de Estado y del Despacho) was the leading minister and also the foreign minister. Manuel Godoy dominated policy 1792-1808 (as First Secretary to 1798, then as royal favourite and Generalísimo). The Mutiny of Aranjuez (17-19 Mar 1808) toppled Godoy and forced Carlos IV to abdicate in favour of Fernando VII; both then renounced the crown to Napoleon at Bayonne (May 1808).
- **Bonapartist Kingdom of Spain (King Joseph I; Bayonne Statute) (1808-07–1813-12)**: King appointed by Napoleon; ministers answer to the king. Parallel to Patriot Spain. Joseph left Madrid several times and quit Spain after Vitoria (Jun 1813).
- **Patriot Spain - Junta Suprema Central (1808-10) and Council of Regency (1810-14), Cortes of Cádiz (Constitution of 1812) (1808-09–1814-05)**: Collective juntas/regencies acting for the captive Fernando VII; the Cortes appointed and replaced regencies. Parallel claimant. Game: playable as a resistance government; regencies could be replaced by the Cortes.
- **Absolutist restoration of Fernando VII (1814-05–1820-03)**: Hereditary; Fernando VII annulled the 1812 Constitution (4 May 1814). Riego's pronunciamiento (1 Jan 1820) forced the king to swear the Constitution (Mar 1820).
- **Liberal Triennium (Constitution of 1812 restored) (1820-03–1823-10)**: Hereditary monarch; ministers appointed by the king but answerable to the Cortes. Ended by French intervention (the 'Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis'), Apr-Oct 1823; a royalist regency in Madrid formed a rival government from May 1823.
- **Ominous Decade (second absolutist period) (1823-10–1833-09)**: Hereditary. Pragmatic Sanction (1830) allowed Isabel II to succeed, provoking the Carlist challenge.
- **Reign of Isabel II (Royal Statute 1834; Constitutions of 1837 and 1845) (1833-09–1868-09)**: Hereditary; regencies of María Cristina (1833-40) and Espartero (1840-43). The crown appointed and dismissed the President of the Council; governments then 'made' elections. Military pronunciamientos (1836, 1840, 1843, 1854, 1866, 1868) were the main way governments changed against the crown's will. First Carlist War 1833-1840 (rival claimant Carlos María Isidro). Isabel II deposed by the Glorious Revolution (Sep 1868).
- **Revolutionary Sexenio - Provisional Government and Regency of Serrano (Constitution of 1869) (1868-09–1871-01)**: Provisional government (Serrano, Prim); the Constituent Cortes elected Serrano regent (Jun 1869) and Amadeo of Savoy king (Nov 1870). Prim was assassinated Dec 1870.
- **Reign of Amadeo I (1871-01–1873-02)**: Elected king; cabinets responsible to the Cortes. Amadeo abdicated 11 Feb 1873.
- **First Spanish Republic (1873-02–1874-01)**: President of the Executive Power elected by the Cortes; four presidents in eleven months. Cantonal rebellion (1873) and Third Carlist War. General Pavía's coup dissolved the Cortes (3 Jan 1874).
- **Serrano's republican dictatorship (1874-01–1874-12)**: Serrano as President of the Executive Power without a Cortes. Martínez Campos's pronunciamiento at Sagunto (29 Dec 1874) restored the Bourbons.
- **Bourbon Restoration (Constitution of 1876) (1874-12–1923-09)**: Hereditary (Alfonso XII; regency of María Cristina 1885-1902; Alfonso XIII). Turno pacífico: the king alternated Conservative and Liberal leaders in office, and the incoming government then manufactured an electoral majority (caciquismo). Governments fell when the crown withdrew confidence or the ruling party split. Prime ministers Cánovas (1897), Canalejas (1912) and Dato (1921) were assassinated.
- **Dictatorship of Primo de Rivera (Military Directory 1923-25, Civil Directory 1925-30) (1923-09–1930-01)**: Primo de Rivera ruled by royal consent after his pronunciamiento (13 Sep 1923); Cortes suspended. Resigned Jan 1930 after losing the confidence of the army and the king.
- **Dictablanda (Berenguer and Aznar governments) (1930-01–1931-04)**: Royal appointment. Republican victory in the municipal elections of 12 Apr 1931 led Alfonso XIII to leave Spain (14 Apr 1931).
- **Second Spanish Republic (1931-04–1936-07)**: President elected for six years by the Cortes plus compromisarios; could be removed by the Cortes (Alcalá-Zamora was removed Apr 1936). The President appointed the head of government, who needed Cortes confidence. Military uprising 17-18 Jul 1936 began the Civil War.
- **Civil War - Republican government (1936-07–1939-03)**: Republican institutions continued; Casado's coup (5 Mar 1939) set up the National Defence Council in Madrid. Parallel to the Nationalist zone.
- **Civil War - Nationalist zone (1936-07–1939-04)**: National Defence Junta (Cabanellas) from 24 Jul 1936; Franco named Head of the Government of the State and Generalísimo, 1 Oct 1936; first regular cabinet 30 Jan 1938. Parallel claimant until victory (1 Apr 1939).
- **Francoist State (1939-04–1975-11)**: Franco Head of State for life (Caudillo); also President of the Government until Jun 1973. Law of Succession (1947) made Spain a kingdom with Franco as regent; Juan Carlos designated successor (1969). The Cortes (from 1942) were appointed/corporatist and could not dismiss the government. Carrero Blanco (PM) assassinated by ETA Dec 1973.
- **Transition to democracy (1975-11–1978-12)**: Juan Carlos I appointed the President of the Government (Arias, then Suárez Jul 1976); Law for Political Reform (Dec 1976); first free election Jun 1977.
- **Parliamentary monarchy (Constitution of 1978) (1978-12–present)**: Hereditary monarch with no executive power. The President of the Government is invested by the Congress of Deputies and can be removed only by a constructive motion of censure naming a successor (Art. 113; succeeded once: Rajoy replaced by Sánchez, 1 Jun 2018) or by losing a confidence vote. Failed military coup 23 Feb 1981 (23-F).

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Parallel claimants: Joseph I (1808-13) vs the Patriot Junta/Regency; Republic vs Nationalist zone (1936-39). Regents are listed as separate entries because they exercised the crown's powers. Carlist pretenders (1833-76) are not listed.
- **Head of government**: Before 1834 the First Secretary of State (Primer Secretario de Estado y del Despacho) was the leading minister, but under the absolute monarchy the king (and, 1792-1808, the favourite Godoy) held real power; game should treat the king as player and the First Secretary as chief advisor. During the First Republic (Feb 1873 - Jan 1874) the President of the Executive Power combined both roles. The Patriot governments of 1808-1813 had secretaries of state who are not listed here (gap). Franco combined head of state and government 1938-1973.
- **Foreign affairs**: 1789-1834: First Secretaries of State (same persons as head_of_government). 1808-1813: rulers.org lists only Joseph I's foreign ministers (Bonapartist); the Patriot foreign secretaries are not covered. 1834-1931: year-level dates only (rulers.org foreign-minister list); month precision would need the official Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores list. 1931-2026: full dates (rulers.org); Civil War entries split Republican vs Nationalist (Burgos) governments.
- **Defence / war**: Secretary of State / Minister of War 1807-1931 from es.wikipedia (cross-check grade; holders with overlapping dates are flagged uncertain). GAP 1789-1807: Carlos IV's war secretaries (e.g. conde de Campo Alange, Azanza, Álvarez, Cornel) are not included because dates could not be verified. 1931-39 War/National Defence; 1939-1977 there was no defence ministry - the Minister of the Army (Ejército) is listed; separate Navy (Marina) and Air (Aire) ministers are not. Ministry of Defence from Jul 1977.
- **Finance / treasury**: Hacienda: 1785-1931 from es.wikipedia annex list (cross-check grade; overlaps flagged; a few obvious year typos corrected and noted); 1931-2026 from rulers.org. Some pre-1931 entries in the source duplicate two names for one cabinet - both kept and flagged.
- **Interior / home**: Gobernación (Interior): GAP before Oct 1833 - the Secretaría de la Gobernación existed only 1812-1814 and 1820-1823 (not covered); Fomento/Interior 1832-1836, Gobernación 1836-1977, Interior since 1977. 1833-1931 from es.wikipedia (cross-check grade, incomplete in places, overlaps flagged), 1931-2026 from rulers.org.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No public national intelligence chief before 1977. Franco-era services (SIPM in the Civil War; SECED 1972-77 under Carrero Blanco) had chiefs who were not officially public. CESID directors 1977-2002 (year-level dates), CNI directors 2002-2026 (month-level).
- **Military chief**: No permanent chief of staff before 1904; the king was nominal commander-in-chief and the War Minister the senior military authority (game: use War Minister). Estado Mayor Central 1904-1931 chiefs are NOT covered (gap). Republic: Franco (1935-36), Martínez Cabrera, Rojo (approximate months, flagged). Nationalist/Francoist: Franco as Generalísimo, then Jefes del Alto Estado Mayor (1939-1980), Presidents of the Junta de Jefes de Estado Mayor (1977-1984), JEMAD (1984-).

### Head of state

- 1788-12 → 1808-03: **Carlos IV**, King of Spain — *Rey de España* — Abdicated after the Mutiny of Aranjuez (19 Mar 1808)
- 1808-03 → 1808-05: **Fernando VII**, King of Spain — *Rey de España* — Renounced the crown at Bayonne (6 May 1808); held captive in France until Dec 1813
- 1808-07 → 1813-12: **Joseph I (José Bonaparte)**, King of Spain (Bonapartist) — *Rey de España y de las Indias* — Imposed by Napoleon; parallel to the Patriot governments
- 1808-09 → 1810-01: **Junta Suprema Central (collective)**, Supreme Central Governing Junta (Patriot government) — *Junta Suprema Central Gubernativa del Reino* — Presided by the conde de Floridablanca until his death (Dec 1808)
- 1810-01 → 1814-05: **Council of Regency (collective)**, Regency (Patriot government, Cádiz) — *Consejo de Regencia de España e Indias* — Successive regencies appointed by the Junta and the Cortes of Cádiz
- 1813-12 → 1833-09: **Fernando VII**, King of Spain — *Rey de España* — Restored by the Treaty of Valençay (Dec 1813), returned Mar 1814; constitutional king 1820-23 (held by the liberals in Seville/Cádiz Jun-Oct 1823)
- 1833-09 → 1868-09: **Isabel II**, Queen of Spain — *Reina de España* — Minor until declared of age Nov 1843; deposed by the Glorious Revolution, went into exile 30 Sep 1868
- 1833-09 → 1840-10: **María Cristina de Borbón-Dos Sicilias**, Queen Regent (for Isabel II) — *Reina gobernadora / Regente*
- 1840-10 → 1843-07: **Baldomero Espartero**, Regent (for Isabel II) — *Regente del Reino* — President of the Provisional Regency to 10 May 1841, then sole regent; overthrown 1843
- 1868-10 → 1871-01: **Francisco Serrano**, President of the Provisional Government, then Regent (from 18 Jun 1869) — *Presidente del Gobierno Provisional / Regente del Reino*
- 1871-01 → 1873-02: **Amadeo I**, King of Spain — *Rey de España* — Elected by the Cortes; abdicated 11 Feb 1873
- 1873-02 → 1873-06: **Estanislao Figueras**, President of the Executive Power — *Presidente del Poder Ejecutivo*
- 1873-06 → 1873-07: **Francisco Pi y Margall**, President of the Executive Power — *Presidente del Poder Ejecutivo*
- 1873-07 → 1873-09: **Nicolás Salmerón**, President of the Executive Power — *Presidente del Poder Ejecutivo*
- 1873-09 → 1874-01: **Emilio Castelar**, President of the Executive Power — *Presidente del Poder Ejecutivo* — Fell when Pavía dissolved the Cortes, 3 Jan 1874
- 1874-01 → 1874-12: **Francisco Serrano**, President of the Executive Power — *Presidente del Poder Ejecutivo de la República*
- 1874-12 → 1885-11: **Alfonso XII**, King of Spain — *Rey de España* — Proclaimed after the Sagunto pronunciamiento (29 Dec 1874); died 25 Nov 1885
- 1885-11 → 1902-05: **María Cristina de Habsburgo-Lorena**, Queen Regent (for Alfonso XIII) — *Reina Regente*
- 1886-05 → 1931-04: **Alfonso XIII**, King of Spain — *Rey de España* — King from birth (17 May 1886); personal rule from 17 May 1902; left Spain 14 Apr 1931
- 1931-04 → 1931-10: **Niceto Alcalá-Zamora**, President of the Provisional Government (head of state) — *Presidente del Gobierno Provisional de la República*
- 1931-10 → 1931-12: **Manuel Azaña** (acting), President of the Provisional Government (acting head of state) — *Presidente del Gobierno Provisional*
- 1931-12 → 1936-04: **Niceto Alcalá-Zamora**, President of the Republic — *Presidente de la República* — Removed by the Cortes 7 Apr 1936
- 1936-04 → 1936-05: **Diego Martínez Barrio** (acting), Acting President of the Republic — *Presidente interino de la República*
- 1936-05 → 1939-03: **Manuel Azaña**, President of the Republic — *Presidente de la República* — Republican zone from Jul 1936; went into exile Feb 1939, resigned 27 Feb/3 Mar 1939
- 1936-07 → 1936-10: **Miguel Cabanellas**, President of the National Defence Junta (Nationalist zone) — *Presidente de la Junta de Defensa Nacional*
- 1936-10 → 1975-11: **Francisco Franco**, Head of State; Generalísimo; 'Caudillo' — *Jefe del Estado* — Nationalist zone only until Apr 1939. Prince Juan Carlos acted for him 19 Jul - 2 Sep 1974 and 30 Oct - 20 Nov 1975. Died 20 Nov 1975
- 1939-03 → 1939-03: **José Miaja**, President of the National Defence Council (Republican zone, after Casado's coup) — *Presidente del Consejo Nacional de Defensa*
- 1975-11 → 1975-11: **Alejandro Rodríguez de Valcárcel**, President of the Council of Regency — *Presidente del Consejo de Regencia* — 20-22 Nov 1975
- 1975-11 → 2014-06: **Juan Carlos I**, King of Spain — *Rey de España* — Abdicated 19 Jun 2014
- 2014-06 → present: **Felipe VI**, King of Spain — *Rey de España*

## United Kingdom (tier 1)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789-01 | 1800-12 | Kingdom of Great Britain | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | London | royal_dismissal, no_confidence, general_election |
| 1801-01 | 1834-12 | United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (pre-reform) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | London | royal_dismissal, no_confidence, general_election, assassination |
| 1835-01 | 1922-12 | United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | London | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |
| 1922-12 | present | United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | London | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |

- **Kingdom of Great Britain (1789-01–1800-12)**: Hereditary monarchy (male-preference primogeniture, Protestant under the Act of Settlement 1701). The King chooses the PM, who must also command the Commons; ministers serve at royal pleasure. Monarch retains real political power: George III effectively dismissed the Fox-North coalition (1783) and the Talents ministry (1807). Electorate tiny; elections managed by patronage. Game: player as PM can be removed by royal dismissal or loss of Commons confidence.
- **United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (pre-reform) (1801-01–1834-12)**: Act of Union 1800 merged the Irish Parliament into Westminster. Great Reform Act 1832 widened the franchise. William IV's dismissal of Melbourne (Nov 1834) was the last royal dismissal of a PM. Spencer Perceval assassinated 1812. Regency 1811-1820.
- **United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland (1835-01–1922-12)**: Monarch appoints whoever can command a Commons majority (by convention the majority party leader). Governments fall by losing a confidence vote, losing an election, or party revolt (e.g. Asquith replaced by Lloyd George Dec 1916, Lloyd George ousted by the Carlton Club meeting Oct 1922). Parliament Act 1911 curbed the Lords. Franchise widened 1867, 1884, 1918 (women over 30), 1928 (equal franchise).
- **United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (1922-12–present)**: Irish Free State left Dec 1922 (name formally changed 1927). PM is the leader of the majority party; a party leadership change installs a new PM without a general election (Eden 1955, Home 1963, Callaghan 1976, Major 1990, Brown 2007, May 2016, Johnson 2019, Truss and Sunak 2022, Burnham 2026). Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 repealed 2022. Game: no impeachment. Remove a UK player via (a) Commons no-confidence vote (last successful 1979), (b) defeat at a general election (max 5-year term), (c) a party leadership challenge / cabinet revolt (Thatcher 1990, Johnson 2022, Truss 2022). Monarch is ceremonial; never a coup.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: Before 1905 'Prime Minister' was not an official title; the holder was First Lord of the Treasury (Salisbury was Lord Privy Seal/Foreign Secretary instead in some ministries).
- **Defence / war**: 1789-1794: no cabinet war minister; the Secretary at War was an administrative office and war policy ran through the PM and Home Secretary. 1794-1801 Secretary of State for War; 1801-1854 War and the Colonies; 1854-1964 Secretary of State for War (army). 1940-46 the PM held the separate post of Minister of Defence; 1946-64 Minister of Defence coordinated the service ministries; from Apr 1964 a unified Secretary of State for Defence. During 1940-45 the War Secretaries (Eden, Margesson, Grigg) are not listed separately - Churchill is the defence advisor. The Royal Navy's political chief is in navy_minister (First Lord of the Admiralty, 1789-1964).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No intelligence service before Oct 1909 (Secret Service Bureau): the game should use the Foreign Secretary's secret-service fund / Home Office for 1789-1909. This list combines MI5 (domestic, title 'Director General of the Security Service') and SIS/MI6 (foreign, title 'Chief of the Secret Intelligence Service'). Names were officially secret until 1992 (MI5) / 1994 (SIS avowed by the Intelligence Services Act); the game may treat pre-1992 chiefs as 'unknown to the public'.
- **Military chief**: 1789-1904 Commander-in-Chief of the Forces (vacant 1789-92 and Apr-Aug 1827); 1904-1959 Chief of the (Imperial) General Staff - an army post that was de facto senior military advisor; from 1959 the Chief of the Defence Staff. The 1958-59 interval is covered by the Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee (Dickson).
- **Finance / treasury**: Before 1830s the Chancellor of the Exchequer was often the PM himself (First Lord of the Treasury).

### Uncertainties

- 2026 changes (Starmer -> Burnham 20 Jul 2026; Healey resignation 11 Jun 2026; Jarvis, Streeting, Healey, Miliband appointments) post-date the model's knowledge and were verified against news reports and worldstatesmen.org only; re-check before shipping.
- SIS chiefs 1968-1999: start/end months are approximate (SIS has published years only); flagged individually.
- First Lords of the Admiralty: Lord Auckland's 1834 and 1835 tenures - months approximate.
- Wellington's 1827-28 tenure as C-in-C was interrupted (Apr-Aug 1827 vacancy); simplified to one entry.
- Secretary of State for War 1794: Henry Dundas listed from Jul 1794; Sir George Yonge's Secretary at War tenure (from 1782) included as context, not a true cabinet war minister.

## Argentina (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1810-05 | Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (Spanish) | colonial_or_occupied | Buenos Aires | royal_dismissal, revolution |
| 1810-05 | 1862-10 | United Provinces / Argentine Confederation (revolution, civil wars) | revolutionary_government | Buenos Aires (Paraná 1853-61 for the Confederation) | coup, revolution |
| 1862-10 | 1930-09 | Republic (Conservative order, then Radical governments) | presidential_republic | Buenos Aires | term_limit, general_election, revolution |
| 1930-09 | 1932-02 | Uriburu provisional military government | military_junta | Buenos Aires | coup, general_election |
| 1932-02 | 1943-06 | 'Infamous Decade' (Concordancia) | presidential_republic | Buenos Aires | general_election, term_limit, coup |
| 1943-06 | 1946-06 | GOU military government | military_junta | Buenos Aires | coup |
| 1946-06 | 1955-09 | Perón presidency | presidential_republic | Buenos Aires | coup, general_election |
| 1955-09 | 1958-05 | Revolución Libertadora (military) | military_junta | Buenos Aires | coup, general_election |
| 1958-05 | 1966-06 | Semi-democracy with Peronism proscribed | presidential_republic | Buenos Aires | coup, general_election |
| 1966-06 | 1973-05 | 'Revolución Argentina' (military) | military_junta | Buenos Aires | coup |
| 1973-05 | 1976-03 | Return of Peronism | presidential_republic | Buenos Aires | coup, death_in_office, general_election |
| 1976-03 | 1983-12 | National Reorganization Process (military junta) | military_junta | Buenos Aires | coup, junta_decision |
| 1983-12 | present | Democracy (1853 Constitution, reformed 1994) | presidential_republic | Buenos Aires | general_election, term_limit, impeachment, revolution |

- **Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (Spanish) (1789–1810-05)**: Spanish viceroys. British invasions 1806-07 repelled by local militia. Not covered by named holders (tier 2).
- **United Provinces / Argentine Confederation (revolution, civil wars) (1810-05–1862-10)**: Juntas, Supreme Directors (1814-20), Rosas' Buenos Aires dictatorship (1829-32, 1835-52), Confederation under the 1853 Constitution (Urquiza, Derqui); Buenos Aires seceded 1852-61. May Revolution 25 May 1810; independence 9 Jul 1816. Not covered by named holders (tier 2).
- **Republic (Conservative order, then Radical governments) (1862-10–1930-09)**: President chosen by an electoral college for 6 years, no immediate re-election (1853 Constitution). Sáenz Peña Law (1912) introduced universal, secret, compulsory male suffrage; UCR won 1916. Failed Radical revolutions 1890, 1893, 1905. Paraguayan War 1865-70. Mass immigration.
- **Uriburu provisional military government (1930-09–1932-02)**: Coup of 6 Sep 1930 against Yrigoyen. First of six successful 20th-century coups.
- **'Infamous Decade' (Concordancia) (1932-02–1943-06)**: Fraudulent elections returned Concordancia presidents. Roca-Runciman Pact 1933; Argentina neutral in WWII until Mar 1945.
- **GOU military government (1943-06–1946-06)**: Coup of 4 Jun 1943; presidents Rawson, Ramírez, Farrell; Perón rose as labour secretary, war minister and vice-president. Perón arrested and freed by mass mobilisation 17 Oct 1945.
- **Perón presidency (1946-06–1955-09)**: Elected 1946; 1949 Constitution allowed re-election (1951). Increasingly authoritarian. Overthrown by the 'Revolución Libertadora' (16-21 Sep 1955).
- **Revolución Libertadora (military) (1955-09–1958-05)**: Lonardi, then Aramburu (palace coup 13 Nov 1955). Peronism banned.
- **Semi-democracy with Peronism proscribed (1958-05–1966-06)**: Frondizi (1958) deposed by the military 29 Mar 1962; Senate president Guido sworn in under military tutelage; Illia elected 1963, deposed 28 Jun 1966.
- **'Revolución Argentina' (military) (1966-06–1973-05)**: Junta of the three commanders appointed presidents (Onganía, Levingston, Lanusse) and removed them by internal coups (1970, 1971). Cordobazo 1969; Montoneros and ERP guerrillas.
- **Return of Peronism (1973-05–1976-03)**: Cámpora elected and resigned to allow new elections; Perón elected Sep 1973, died 1 Jul 1974; succeeded by Vice-President Isabel Perón.
- **National Reorganization Process (military junta) (1976-03–1983-12)**: The Junta of the Army, Navy and Air Force commanders was the supreme organ; it appointed and replaced the President (Videla, Viola, Galtieri, Bignone). Game: 'junta_decision' = removal by the junta. 'Dirty War' (est. 9,000-30,000 disappeared). Falklands/Malvinas War Apr-Jun 1982; defeat forced Galtieri out and a return to democracy.
- **Democracy (1853 Constitution, reformed 1994) (1983-12–present)**: Since 1994: direct two-round election, 4-year term, one consecutive re-election. Vice-president, then Senate provisional president, then the Legislative Assembly chooses a successor. The Chief of Cabinet (since 1994) is politically answerable to Congress and can be removed by an absolute-majority censure vote of either chamber (Art. 101). Alfonsín handed over early (Jul 1989) amid hyperinflation. Dec 2001 crisis: De la Rúa resigned after riots (game: 'revolution'), followed by five presidents in two weeks. Juicio político (impeachment) has never removed a president.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Presidential system: the President is head of state and of government. Holders are listed from 1862 (national reunification); tier-2 minimum is 1900. Military juntas appear as collective entries.
- **Head of government**: The President is head of government. Listed here is the Chief of the Cabinet of Ministers (Jefe de Gabinete de Ministros, created by the 1994 reform), a coordinating minister who answers to Congress and can be removed by a censure (moción de censura) vote - the closest Argentine analogue to a no-confidence target.
- **Foreign affairs**: Ministro de Relaciones Exteriores y Culto (title varied: '... Comercio Internacional y Culto' 1992-2023). Brief acting stand-ins during a minister's absence (<45 days) are omitted.
- **Defence / war**: Minister of War (Ministro de Guerra) to 1949, Minister of National Defence (Ministro de Defensa Nacional / de Defensa) from 1949; a separate Navy Ministry (Marina) existed 1898-1958. Sep 1955 - Jun 1958 no Defence minister: the Army, Navy and Air Force ministers (members of the governing junta) reported directly to the president.
- **Finance / treasury**: Ministro de Hacienda to 1950s; Economía (various combined names) thereafter; Hacienda y Finanzas Públicas / Hacienda Dec 2015 - Dec 2019 (Macri abolished the Economy ministry; Finanzas split off Jan 2017 - Jun 2018 under Luis Caputo, not listed).
- **Interior / home**: Ministro del Interior (from 2012 'del Interior y Transporte', 2015-19 'del Interior, Obras Públicas y Vivienda'). Security was split off to a separate Ministerio de Seguridad from Dec 2010 (Nilda Garré, Patricia Bullrich, ...). rulers.org shows the Interior portfolio ending 3 Jul 2026 when Diego Santilli moved to Chief of Cabinet - status after that not verified.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: SIDE (Secretaría de Informaciones del Estado / de Inteligencia del Estado) 1946-2015; Agencia Federal de Inteligencia (AFI) 2015-2024 (mostly run by 'interventores' 2019-24); SIDE re-created Jul 2024. Heads report directly to the president.
- **Military chief**: Chief of the Joint Staff of the Armed Forces (Jefe del Estado Mayor Conjunto, created 1948/49; minor role under the juntas). During military regimes real power lay with the Army, Navy and Air Force commanders-in-chief who formed the junta. No joint chief before 1949.

## Australia (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1901-01 | 1927-05 | Commonwealth of Australia (Melbourne seat of government) | dominion | Melbourne (temporary seat of government) | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, royal_dismissal |
| 1927-05 | present | Commonwealth of Australia (Canberra) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Canberra | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, royal_dismissal, death_in_office |

- **Commonwealth of Australia (Melbourne seat of government) (1901-01–1927-05)**: Westminster system: Governor-General commissions the leader able to command the House of Representatives. Unstable three-party parliaments 1901-1910 saw governments fall on the floor of the House (Deakin 1904, Watson 1904, Reid 1905, Deakin 1908, Fisher 1909). Hughes expelled from Labor over conscription (1916) and formed the Nationalist Party. Foreign policy formally under London until the 1926 Balfour Declaration; Australia adopted the Statute of Westminster only in 1942 (backdated to 1939).
- **Commonwealth of Australia (Canberra) (1927-05–present)**: PM is the leader of the majority party/coalition in the House. Party-room 'leadership spills' are the most common removal: Menzies 1941 (lost party support), Gorton 1971 (tied party vote), Hawke 1991, Rudd 2010, Gillard 2013, Abbott 2015, Turnbull 2018. Unique reserve-power removal: Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissed Whitlam on 11 Nov 1975 after the Senate blocked supply. Lyons (1939), Curtin (1945) and Holt (1967) died in office. Parliament moved to Canberra 9 May 1927. Australia Acts 1986 ended residual UK legal links. 1999 republic referendum failed - the monarch remains head of state, represented by the Governor-General.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: The monarch is represented by the Governor-General, who holds reserve powers (used once: dismissal of Whitlam, 1975). Game: the G-G is the actor for 'royal_dismissal'.
- **Foreign affairs**: External Affairs department abolished 14 Nov 1916 - 21 Dec 1921 (functions in the PM's Department); renamed Foreign Affairs 1970, Foreign Affairs and Trade 1987.
- **Defence / war**: 1939-1942 a Minister for Defence Co-ordination sat above separate Army/Navy/Air ministers. Defence portfolio gap Feb-Aug 1946 (Beasley/Forde) approximate.
- **Interior / home**: Home Affairs 1901-1932, Interior 1932-1972, no equivalent 1973-2007 (Home Affairs 1977-84/1987-88 was an arts/heritage portfolio - omitted); security functions lay with the Attorney-General (responsible for ASIO). Home Affairs revived 2007 (junior justice post) and as a security super-ministry from Dec 2017.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: ASIO founded Mar 1949. ASIS (foreign intelligence, 1952) and the Office of National Assessments/Intelligence (1977/2018) are separate; ASIO DG used as the game's intelligence chief.
- **Military chief**: No single defence chief before 1958: the Army's Chief of the General Staff is used (Navy and RAAF chiefs were coequal). 1958-76 Chairman, Chiefs of Staff Committee; 1976-84 Chief of the Defence Force Staff; Chief of the Defence Force since 1984.

## Cuba (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1899-01 | Spanish colony (Captaincy General of Cuba) | colonial_or_occupied | Havana | royal_dismissal, revolution |
| 1899-01 | 1902-05 | First U.S. military occupation | colonial_or_occupied | Havana | foreign_occupation |
| 1902-05 | 1906-09 | Republic of Cuba (Platt Amendment protectorate) | presidential_republic | Havana | general_election, foreign_occupation, revolution |
| 1906-09 | 1909-01 | Second U.S. occupation (Provisional Government) | colonial_or_occupied | Havana | foreign_occupation |
| 1909-01 | 1933-08 | Republic (Liberal/Conservative alternation; Machado dictatorship) | presidential_republic | Havana | general_election, term_limit, revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1933-08 | 1940-10 | Revolution of 1933 and Batista-dominated governments | military_junta | Havana | coup, revolution |
| 1940-10 | 1952-03 | Constitutional Republic (1940 Constitution) | semi_presidential_republic | Havana | general_election, term_limit, no_confidence, coup |
| 1952-03 | 1959-01 | Batista dictatorship | personalist_dictatorship | Havana | revolution, coup |
| 1959-01 | 1976-12 | Revolutionary Government | revolutionary_government | Havana | party_congress, death_in_office |
| 1976-12 | present | Socialist Republic (one-party communist state) | one_party_communist_state | Havana | party_congress, death_in_office, term_limit |

- **Spanish colony (Captaincy General of Cuba) (1789–1899-01)**: Captains-general appointed by the Spanish Crown. Independence wars: Ten Years' War 1868-78, Little War 1879-80, War of Independence 1895-98 (insurgent 'Republic in Arms' governments). Spanish-American War 1898. Not covered by named holders (tier 2).
- **First U.S. military occupation (1899-01–1902-05)**: U.S. military governors (Brooke, Wood). Platt Amendment (1901) incorporated in the Cuban constitution: U.S. right of intervention and Guantánamo lease (1903).
- **Republic of Cuba (Platt Amendment protectorate) (1902-05–1906-09)**: 1901 Constitution: president elected indirectly for 4 years. Estrada Palma's disputed re-election triggered the 1906 'August Revolution' and U.S. intervention.
- **Second U.S. occupation (Provisional Government) (1906-09–1909-01)**: U.S. provisional governors (Taft, Magoon).
- **Republic (Liberal/Conservative alternation; Machado dictatorship) (1909-01–1933-08)**: Indirect election, 4-year terms; Machado extended his term to 1935 via the 1928 'prórroga de poderes'. U.S. landings 1912 (Race War) and 1917 (Chambelona revolt). Machado (1925-33) became dictatorial; overthrown by a general strike, army defection and U.S. mediation, Aug 1933.
- **Revolution of 1933 and Batista-dominated governments (1933-08–1940-10)**: Sergeants' Revolt (4 Sep 1933) made Fulgencio Batista army chief; he made and unmade seven civilian presidents 1933-40. Game: the real power-holder is the Army Chief of Staff (Colonel Batista) - treat as the military advisor with coup power. Platt Amendment abrogated 1934.
- **Constitutional Republic (1940 Constitution) (1940-10–1952-03)**: Directly elected president, 4-year term, no immediate re-election. A Prime Minister and cabinet responsible to Congress (interpellation and censure votes). Ended by Batista's coup of 10 Mar 1952.
- **Batista dictatorship (1952-03–1959-01)**: Batista ruled under 'Constitutional Statutes'; staged elections 1954 and 1958. 26th of July Movement (Moncada 1953, Granma 1956, Sierra Maestra). Batista fled 1 Jan 1959.
- **Revolutionary Government (1959-01–1976-12)**: Council of Ministers held legislative power; Fidel Castro Prime Minister from Feb 1959; President Urrutia forced out Jul 1959. Party structures: ORI (1961), PURSC (1962/63), Communist Party of Cuba (Oct 1965). Bay of Pigs Apr 1961; Missile Crisis Oct 1962. Game: no elections; removal only by party/leadership decision, death or (hypothetical) revolution or invasion.
- **Socialist Republic (one-party communist state) (1976-12–present)**: 1976 Constitution: National Assembly of People's Power elects the Council of State, whose President is head of state and government. PCC First Secretary is paramount leader. 2019 Constitution: President of the Republic (max two 5-year terms, elected by the Assembly) and a separate Prime Minister. Fidel Castro handed power to Raúl (provisionally 31 Jul 2006, formally 2008/2011). Díaz-Canel President 2018/2019 and First Secretary 2021.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: U.S. military/provisional governors are listed for 1899-1902 and 1906-09. 1976-2019 the President of the Council of State was head of state and government; from Oct 2019 the President of the Republic.
- **Head of government**: Premiers 1940-1952 (1940 Constitution), Batista's appointed premiers 1955-59, Prime Ministers 1959-1976 (Fidel Castro from Feb 1959), Presidents of the Council of Ministers 1976-2019 (same person as head of state), Prime Minister again from Dec 2019 (Manuel Marrero). 1902-1940 and Mar 1952 - Feb 1955 the president headed the government directly.
- **Paramount leader (party)**: First Secretary of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Cuba (from Oct 1965) - the player's office in a one-party game model. Fidel Castro led the ruling organisations (ORI 1961, PURSC 1963) before the PCC was founded.
- **Foreign affairs**: Secretary of State (Secretario de Estado) 1902-1940, Minister of State 1940-1959, Minister of Foreign Relations (MINREX) from 1959. 1906-1932 holders are incomplete and year-only (flagged).
- **Defence / war**: Before 1959 the armed forces were run by the Secretary of War and Navy / Ministry of National Defence and, in practice, the Army chief of staff; those holders are not listed (gap). From Oct 1959 the MINFAR minister (Raúl Castro for 48 years) commands the armed forces.
- **Finance / treasury**: Pre-1959 Secretaries/Ministers of the Treasury (Hacienda) are not listed (gap).
- **Interior / home**: Pre-1959 Secretaries of Government (Gobernación) not listed (gap). MININT also controls state security and intelligence.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Intelligence (DGI, renamed DI) sits within MININT; its chiefs are rarely announced publicly. Brig. Gen. Eduardo Delgado Rodríguez is named as DI head in recent sources (dates not public, not listed). Game: map the intelligence advisor to the Interior minister when no chief is known.
- **Military chief**: Chief of the General Staff of the FAR (first vice-minister of MINFAR). Holders before 2001 are not reliably public; game should fall back to the MINFAR minister.

## Egypt (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1882-09 | 1914-12 | Khedivate of Egypt (Ottoman suzerainty, British occupation) | colonial_or_occupied | Cairo | royal_dismissal, foreign_occupation, assassination |
| 1914-12 | 1922-03 | Sultanate of Egypt (British protectorate) | colonial_or_occupied | Cairo | royal_dismissal, foreign_occupation, revolution |
| 1922-03 | 1952-07 | Kingdom of Egypt | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Cairo | royal_dismissal, no_confidence, general_election, assassination, foreign_occupation |
| 1952-07 | 1953-06 | Kingdom under the Free Officers (regency for Fuad II) | military_junta | Cairo | coup |
| 1953-06 | 1971-09 | Republic of Egypt / United Arab Republic (1958-61 union with Syria; name kept to 1971) | one_party_state | Cairo | coup, party_congress, death_in_office |
| 1971-09 | 2011-02 | Arab Republic of Egypt (1971 constitution) | presidential_republic | Cairo | assassination, revolution, coup, death_in_office |
| 2011-02 | 2012-06 | Supreme Council of the Armed Forces (transition) | military_junta | Cairo | coup, revolution |
| 2012-06 | 2013-07 | Arab Republic of Egypt (Morsi presidency) | presidential_republic | Cairo | coup, revolution, impeachment, general_election |
| 2013-07 | present | Arab Republic of Egypt (2014 constitution; Sisi era) | presidential_republic | Cairo (government relocating to the New Administrative Capital from 2023) | coup, revolution, impeachment, general_election |

- **Khedivate of Egypt (Ottoman suzerainty, British occupation) (1882-09–1914-12)**: Khedivate hereditary in the Muhammad Ali dynasty (primogeniture since 1866 firman). Real power lay with the British Agent and Consul-General (Cromer 1883-1907, Gorst 1907-11, Kitchener 1911-14). Ministers were appointed by the khedive with British approval; PM Boutros Ghali assassinated 1910. Game: semi-playable client state - foreign and military policy dictated by Britain.
- **Sultanate of Egypt (British protectorate) (1914-12–1922-03)**: Britain deposed Khedive Abbas II (19 Dec 1914) and installed his uncle Hussein Kamel as Sultan. British High Commissioner held real power. 1919 Revolution led by the Wafd; protectorate ended by unilateral British declaration of 28 Feb 1922.
- **Kingdom of Egypt (1922-03–1952-07)**: Hereditary monarchy (Fuad I, Farouk). 1923 constitution: PM responsible to parliament, but the king could dismiss governments and dissolve parliament, and repeatedly did so against Wafd majorities. Britain intervened directly (Abdeen Palace incident, 4 Feb 1942, tanks forced Farouk to appoint Nahhas). Britain retained reserved points (defence, Suez, Sudan, foreigners) until the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty; troops in the Canal Zone until 1956. Two PMs assassinated (Ahmad Maher 1945, Nokrashy 1948).
- **Kingdom under the Free Officers (regency for Fuad II) (1952-07–1953-06)**: Free Officers coup of 23 Jul 1952 forced Farouk to abdicate (26 Jul) for infant Fuad II; Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) ruled. Monarchy abolished 18 Jun 1953.
- **Republic of Egypt / United Arab Republic (1958-61 union with Syria; name kept to 1971) (1953-06–1971-09)**: RCC power struggle: Nasser ousted Naguib (Feb-Nov 1954). President nominated by the National Assembly and confirmed by plebiscite (1956 constitution). Single party: Liberation Rally -> National Union -> Arab Socialist Union. Military-backed presidential authoritarianism. Defeat in 1967 led to Nasser's (rejected) resignation offer and the purge of Field Marshal Amer.
- **Arab Republic of Egypt (1971 constitution) (1971-09–2011-02)**: People's Assembly nominates, referendum confirms (multi-candidate election from 2005). Vice-president succeeded (Sadat 1970, Mubarak 1981). Sadat assassinated 6 Oct 1981. Mubarak forced out by the 25 January Revolution (11 Feb 2011), with SCAF taking power. Dominant-party system (NDP from 1978). PM appointed and dismissed by the president; parliament never toppled a government.
- **Supreme Council of the Armed Forces (transition) (2011-02–2012-06)**: SCAF chairman Tantawi exercised presidential powers until the elected president took office.
- **Arab Republic of Egypt (Morsi presidency) (2012-06–2013-07)**: Direct presidential election (Jun 2012). Morsi removed by the military on 3 Jul 2013 after mass protests - the canonical 'coup' removal.
- **Arab Republic of Egypt (2014 constitution; Sisi era) (2013-07–present)**: Interim president Adly Mansour 2013-14; direct presidential elections 2014, 2018, 2023. 2019 amendments extended terms to six years and allow Sisi to serve to 2030. Military-dominated presidential system. PM appointed by the president with parliamentary approval; House can withdraw confidence but has never done so.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Pre-1914 the Ottoman Sultan was nominal suzerain and the British Consul-General (Cromer, Gorst, Kitchener) the real power; 1914-1936 British High Commissioners (McMahon, Wingate, Allenby, Lloyd, Loraine, Lampson) wielded a veto. Game: model a 'foreign overseer' advisor who can force dismissal.
- **Foreign affairs**: No Egyptian foreign minister before 1922 (foreign relations handled by Ottoman Porte/Britain; a nominal portfolio held by Adly Yakan and Rushdi 1914-17). Many PMs 1923-52 also held Foreign Affairs.
- **Defence / war**: Before 1952 the War Ministry was subordinate to the British-officered army (Sirdar until 1924; British Military Mission to 1947); ministers changed with every cabinet and are not listed here. Game: use the PM/king as defence authority pre-1952. After 1952 the War/Defence minister is always a senior officer and the key coup-maker.
- **Finance / treasury**: Pre-1952 finance ministers rotated with cabinets (Makram Ebeid for most Wafd governments, 1928-44); not listed due to incomplete dates.
- **Interior / home**: Pre-1952 the Interior portfolio was usually held by the Prime Minister himself (e.g. Nahhas, Sidqi, Nokrashy). Game: PM doubles as interior minister before 1952. 1962-65 holder(s) not confirmed.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: General Intelligence Service (al-Mukhabarat al-Amma) founded 1954. Military Intelligence and State Security Investigations (Interior Ministry; renamed National Security Agency 2011) are separate.
- **Military chief**: Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces from 1952. Under the monarchy the British Sirdar (to 1924) then Egyptian Chiefs of Staff (e.g. Ibrahim Atallah in 1948) - not listed.
