## Netherlands (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1795-01-19 | Dutch Republic (United Provinces) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | The Hague (seat); Amsterdam | revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1795-01-19 | 1813-11-30 | Batavian Republic / Kingdom of Holland / French annexation | colonial_or_occupied | The Hague / Amsterdam | foreign_occupation, coup |
| 1813-11-30 | 1848-11-03 | Kingdom of the Netherlands (royal government) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Amsterdam (constitutional capital); government at The Hague | royal_dismissal, abdication |
| 1848-11-03 | 1940-05-15 | Kingdom of the Netherlands (parliamentary monarchy) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Amsterdam (constitutional capital); government at The Hague | no_confidence, general_election, royal_dismissal |
| 1940-05-15 | 1945-05-05 | German occupation; government-in-exile in London | colonial_or_occupied | London (government-in-exile); occupied territory under Reichskommissar Arthur Seyss-Inquart | royal_dismissal, foreign_occupation |
| 1945-05-05 | present | Kingdom of the Netherlands (parliamentary democracy) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Amsterdam (constitutional capital); government, parliament and monarch at The Hague | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |

- **Dutch Republic (United Provinces) (1789–1795-01-19)**: Stadtholder William V (hereditary) with the States General. Outside required coverage (tier 2).
- **Batavian Republic / Kingdom of Holland / French annexation (1795-01-19–1813-11-30)**: French client states (Louis Bonaparte King of Holland 1806-1810); annexed to France 1810-1813. Outside required coverage.
- **Kingdom of the Netherlands (royal government) (1813-11-30–1848-11-03)**: King William I (abdicated 1840) and William II governed personally; ministers answered to the King. Belgium seceded 1830-1839.
- **Kingdom of the Netherlands (parliamentary monarchy) (1848-11-03–1940-05-15)**: Thorbecke's 1848 constitution made ministers responsible to the States General; ministerial responsibility to parliament settled by 1868. Hereditary House of Orange-Nassau (female succession from 1890). Proportional representation from 1917/1918. The prime ministership was a rotating chairmanship of the Council of Ministers until 1901 and a permanent post only from 1937/1945.
- **German occupation; government-in-exile in London (1940-05-15–1945-05-05)**: Queen Wilhelmina and the cabinet governed from London; the Queen dismissed PM De Geer in Sep 1940. Occupied Netherlands ruled by Reichskommissar Seyss-Inquart. Game: the exile government remains the playable Dutch government, without control of the homeland.
- **Kingdom of the Netherlands (parliamentary democracy) (1945-05-05–present)**: Multi-party coalition governments formed after negotiation (formateur/informateur). A cabinet or minister that loses the confidence of the Tweede Kamer (motion of no confidence or censure) resigns and stays on as caretaker (demissionair) until a successor cabinet is sworn in - hence long caretaker periods (e.g. Rutte IV 2023-24, Schoof 2025-26). Decolonisation: Indonesia 1949, Suriname 1975. Founding member of NATO and the EEC.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: Holders' end dates are the swearing-in of the successor cabinet; outgoing cabinets serve as caretakers (demissionair) in between.
- **Defence / war**: Minister of War (army) and a separate Minister of the Navy (not listed) until 1928, and again 1941-1959 (often held by one person, e.g. Staf 1951-59); Minister of Defence 1928-1941 and from 1959. Pre-1928 War ministers are year-level within cabinets (flagged).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No public national security chief before 1945 (the interwar Centrale Inlichtingendienst was secret). BVD (domestic security) 1949-2002, AIVD from 2002; the military service MIVD (not listed) is separate. Foreign intelligence IDB existed 1946-1994 (not listed).
- **Military chief**: No permanent supreme commander in peacetime before 1949: the Opperbevelhebber was appointed for mobilisations (1914-1919, 1939-1940). 1949-1976 Chairman of the Combined Chiefs of Staff; 1976-2005 Chief of the Defence Staff; from 2005 Commandant der Strijdkrachten (CDS). Inter-war army chiefs of the General Staff not listed.

- **Soviet Civil Administration / Provisional People's Committee for North Korea (1945-08–1948-09)**:  Soviet occupation north of the 38th parallel; Kim Il Sung chairman of the Provisional People's Committee from 1946-02.
- **DPRK under Kim Il Sung (1948-09–1994-07)**: Kim Il Sung as party chairman/General Secretary and (from 1972) President; rival factions purged (1956 August Faction Incident). Kim Jong Il designated successor from 1974/1980. Korean War 1950-53. Juche ideology.
- **DPRK under Kim Jong Il ('military-first' Songun) (1994-07–2011-12)**: Hereditary succession within the Kim family, ratified by party and SPA organs. Power exercised via the National Defence Commission; famine 1994-98; nuclear tests from 2006.
- **DPRK under Kim Jong Un (2011-12–present)**: Hereditary (Kim family 'Paektu bloodline'); offices conferred by WPK congresses/plenums and SPA sessions. Game: no elections or no-confidence; the player (Kim) can only be removed by death, coup or revolution. Ministers and generals are removed at will (purges).

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: Formal head of state changed several times: SPA Standing Committee chairman (1948-72), President (1972-94), SPA Presidium chairman as nominal head of state (1998-2019), SAC President since 2019. The SPA chairman is listed separately after 2019 as ceremonial.
- **Paramount leader (party)**: The game should make the Supreme Leader the player's office.
- **Head of government**: The Premier manages the economy only; no foreign or security authority.
- **Finance / treasury**: Ministers of Finance are obscure and not listed; the game should use the Premier/economic vice-premiers as the finance advisor.
- **Interior / home**: Ministry of Social Security (formerly People's Security) runs police; ministers not listed (gap; frequently changed and poorly documented).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Ministry of State Security (secret police) and the Reconnaissance General Bureau (military intelligence, from 2009). Heads are often unannounced; all entries uncertain. 1982-2012 the post was often nominally held or vacant with first vice-directors in charge.
- **Defence / war**: The Minister of National Defence is subordinate to the General Political Bureau and the Central Military Commission of the WPK.

## Pakistan (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1947-08 | 1956-03 | Dominion of Pakistan | dominion | Karachi | no_confidence, royal_dismissal, assassination |
| 1956-03 | 1958-10 | Islamic Republic of Pakistan (1956 constitution) | parliamentary_republic | Karachi | no_confidence, presidential_dismissal, coup |
| 1958-10 | 1971-12 | Military rule (Ayub Khan, then Yahya Khan) | military_junta | Karachi (to 1959); Rawalpindi interim capital 1959-67; Islamabad (from 1967) | coup, revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1971-12 | 1977-07 | Bhutto civilian government | parliamentary_republic | Islamabad | no_confidence, general_election, coup |
| 1977-07 | 1988-08 | Zia-ul-Haq military rule | military_junta | Islamabad | coup, assassination, death_in_office |
| 1988-08 | 1999-10 | Restored parliamentary democracy | parliamentary_republic | Islamabad | no_confidence, general_election, presidential_dismissal, coup |
| 1999-10 | 2008-08 | Musharraf military-led government | military_junta | Islamabad | coup, revolution, impeachment |
| 2008-08 | present | Islamic Republic of Pakistan (18th Amendment parliamentary system) | parliamentary_republic | Islamabad | no_confidence, general_election, impeachment, coup |

- **Dominion of Pakistan (1947-08–1956-03)**: Governor-General (representing the British monarch) held strong reserve powers and actually dismissed PM Nazimuddin (1953) and the Constituent Assembly (1954). PM chosen from the Muslim League majority. Use 'royal_dismissal' for Governor-General dismissal of the PM. Includes East Bengal (East Pakistan).
- **Islamic Republic of Pakistan (1956 constitution) (1956-03–1958-10)**: President Iskander Mirza appointed and removed four PMs in two years; ended by Mirza's martial law (7 Oct 1958) and Ayub Khan's coup against Mirza (27 Oct 1958).
- **Military rule (Ayub Khan, then Yahya Khan) (1958-10–1971-12)**: Ayub ruled under martial law then the 1962 presidential constitution (indirect 'Basic Democracies' election 1965); forced out by mass protests and handed power to army chief Yahya Khan (Mar 1969). Yahya resigned after the loss of East Pakistan (Bangladesh) in the Dec 1971 war. Model 1962-69 as presidential under military tutelage. No-confidence not available.
- **Bhutto civilian government (1971-12–1977-07)**: Bhutto was civilian Chief Martial Law Administrator and President, then PM under the 1973 constitution (parliamentary, ceremonial president). Overthrown by army chief Zia-ul-Haq (Operation Fair Play, 5 Jul 1977); executed 1979. Presidential system to Aug 1973.
- **Zia-ul-Haq military rule (1977-07–1988-08)**: Martial law until Dec 1985; Zia President from 1978 and remained COAS. 8th Amendment (1985) gave the President Art. 58(2)(b) power to dismiss the PM and dissolve the National Assembly. Ended with Zia's death in an air crash (17 Aug 1988). Non-party elections 1985 produced PM Junejo, whom Zia dismissed in May 1988.
- **Restored parliamentary democracy (1988-08–1999-10)**: President used 58(2)(b) to dismiss Benazir Bhutto (1990, 1996) and Nawaz Sharif (1993; restored by Supreme Court, then both he and the president resigned under army pressure). Caretaker PMs govern during elections. 13th Amendment (1997) removed 58(2)(b). Ended by Musharraf's coup (12 Oct 1999). Army chief is the decisive veto player ('troika' of President, PM, COAS).
- **Musharraf military-led government (1999-10–2008-08)**: Musharraf 'Chief Executive' then President (2001, referendum 2002), retaining COAS until Nov 2007. 17th Amendment restored 58(2)(b). Civilian PMs from Nov 2002 under his supervision. Resigned Aug 2008 facing impeachment by the new parliament. 2007 emergency rule and lawyers' movement.
- **Islamic Republic of Pakistan (18th Amendment parliamentary system) (2008-08–present)**: President elected by Parliament and provincial assemblies; 18th Amendment (2010) abolished the president's power to dismiss the PM. PMs removed by Supreme Court disqualification (Gilani 2012, Nawaz Sharif 2017) and by the first successful no-confidence vote (Imran Khan, 10 Apr 2022). Caretaker governments run elections. Game: add 'judicial disqualification' as a removal event (map to impeachment). Army remains the dominant power: 27th Amendment (Nov 2025) created Chief of Defence Forces (held by Field Marshal Asim Munir), lifetime field-marshal rank immunity, and a Federal Constitutional Court.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: No PM existed Oct 1958-Dec 1971 (except Ayub 3 days, Nurul Amin 13 days) and Jul 1977-Mar 1985 (Zia as CMLA/President); Oct 1999-Nov 2002 Musharraf ruled as Chief Executive. Game: in junta periods the COAS/CMLA is the player's office.
- **Military chief**: The Army Chief is the most powerful office in Pakistan: three successful coups (1958, 1977, 1999) were led by the serving army chief. Chairman Joint Chiefs of Staff Committee (1976-Nov 2025) was largely ceremonial and was abolished by the 27th Amendment; the COAS is now ex officio Chief of Defence Forces. Game: a COAS with low loyalty should be able to trigger a coup event.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence) DG is a serving lieutenant-general appointed by the PM from army nominees. Intelligence Bureau (civilian, under the PM) also exists. DG ISI months before 1987 are approximate.
- **Foreign affairs**: PMs Nawaz Sharif (1990-93, 2013-17) and Benazir Bhutto (1988-90) formally kept the foreign portfolio with a Minister of State/Adviser doing the work; these de facto FMs are listed.
- **Finance / treasury**: Several finance chiefs were unelected 'Advisers on Finance' with ministerial status.

## Poland (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1795-10 | Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Warsaw | foreign_occupation, abdication, revolution |
| 1795-10 | 1918-11 | Partitioned (Russia, Prussia, Austria); Duchy of Warsaw 1807-15; Congress Kingdom under Russia 1815-1915 | colonial_or_occupied | (Warsaw, under foreign rule) | revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1918-11 | 1926-05 | Second Polish Republic (parliamentary) | parliamentary_republic | Warsaw | no_confidence, general_election, coup, assassination |
| 1926-05 | 1935-04 | Second Republic under Sanacja (Piłsudski regime) | personalist_dictatorship | Warsaw | coup, death_in_office, royal_dismissal |
| 1935-04 | 1939-09 | Second Republic (April Constitution, authoritarian presidential) | presidential_republic | Warsaw | presidential_dismissal, foreign_occupation, coup |
| 1939-09 | 1990-12 | Government-in-exile (Angers, then London from 1940) | colonial_or_occupied | Angers (1939-40), London (1940-90) | foreign_occupation |
| 1944-07 | 1989-08 | Polish People's Republic (from 1952; Committee of National Liberation / Provisional Government 1944-47) | one_party_communist_state | Lublin (Jul 1944 - Jan 1945); Warsaw | party_congress, revolution, coup |
| 1989-08 | present | Third Polish Republic | parliamentary_republic | Warsaw | constructive_no_confidence, no_confidence, general_election, impeachment, term_limit |

- **Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (1789–1795-10)**: Elective monarchy (king chosen by the nobility); Constitution of 3 May 1791 sought a hereditary constitutional monarchy. Destroyed by the Second (1793) and Third (1795) Partitions; Stanisław August abdicated Nov 1795. Kościuszko Uprising 1794.
- **Partitioned (Russia, Prussia, Austria); Duchy of Warsaw 1807-15; Congress Kingdom under Russia 1815-1915 (1795-10–1918-11)**: No sovereign Polish state. Duchy of Warsaw (1807-15) was a Napoleonic client ruled by the King of Saxony; the Congress Kingdom (1815-) had the Russian emperor as king and lost its autonomy after the uprisings of 1830-31 and 1863-64. German/Austrian-sponsored Kingdom of Poland 1916-18 under a Regency Council. Not playable before Nov 1918.
- **Second Polish Republic (parliamentary) (1918-11–1926-05)**: Piłsudski Chief of State to Dec 1922, then presidents elected by the National Assembly (Sejm + Senate) for 7 years; President Narutowicz assassinated Dec 1922. Weak, short-lived coalition cabinets dependent on the Sejm (March Constitution 1921). Ended by Piłsudski's May Coup (12-15 May 1926).
- **Second Republic under Sanacja (Piłsudski regime) (1926-05–1935-04)**: Constitutional forms kept but real power with Marshal Piłsudski (minister of military affairs throughout, PM 1926-28 and 1930); PMs were his appointees, replaced at his will (model as 'royal_dismissal' by the strongman). Opposition persecuted (Brest trials 1930-32).
- **Second Republic (April Constitution, authoritarian presidential) (1935-04–1939-09)**: April 1935 constitution concentrated power in the president (Mościcki), who appointed and dismissed the PM. After Piłsudski's death (May 1935) power was shared by Mościcki, Marshal Rydz-Śmigły and PM Składkowski. Ended by the German and Soviet invasions (Sep 1939).
- **Government-in-exile (Angers, then London from 1940) (1939-09–1990-12)**: Constitutional continuity under the April Constitution: the president in exile designated his successor. Recognized by the Western Allies until 5 Jul 1945; afterwards largely symbolic until it handed the presidential insignia to Wałęsa in Dec 1990. Poland itself was occupied by Germany (General Government, annexed areas) and the USSR (1939-41). Game: 1939-44/45 the playable Polish government is the London exile government (armed forces in exile, Home Army).
- **Polish People's Republic (from 1952; Committee of National Liberation / Provisional Government 1944-47) (1944-07–1989-08)**: Soviet-backed regime (PKWN, Lublin, Jul 1944); rigged elections Jan 1947. Power with the First Secretary of the PPR/PZPR (paramount_leader) and Politburo, subject to Moscow. Leaders were replaced by Central Committee plenums after crises (Oct 1956 Gomułka's return; Dec 1970 Gierek after Baltic coast riots; Sep 1980 Kania after the Solidarity strikes; Oct 1981 Jaruzelski). Martial law 13 Dec 1981 - Jul 1983 under the Military Council of National Salvation (WRON, a military junta in all but name). Round Table talks and semi-free elections (Jun 1989) ended the regime.
- **Third Polish Republic (1989-08–present)**: President directly elected since 1990 (5-year term, max two), with a legislative veto (3/5 Sejm override) and influence over defence/foreign policy. Government headed by the Prime Minister (President of the Council of Ministers, Prezes Rady Ministrów), responsible to the Sejm; since the 1997 constitution only a constructive vote of no confidence can remove the cabinet. President may be tried by the State Tribunal (impeachment) on indictment by 2/3 of the National Assembly. Semi-presidential features (cohabitation e.g. Duda vs Tusk 2023-25; Nawrocki vs Tusk 2025-). Game: player = PM; president is a veto player.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: 1795-1918 no Polish head of state (partition; Duchy of Warsaw ruled by Frederick Augustus I of Saxony 1807-15; Russian emperors as kings of Congress Poland). 1939-45 two rival claims: London exile presidents (internationally recognized to Jul 1945) and the communist KRN (from 1944). 1952-89 collective Council of State.
- **Paramount leader (party)**: Use the PZPR First Secretary as the player's office 1944/47-1989. Dec 1981 - Jul 1983 Jaruzelski also chaired the WRON military council (martial law).
- **Head of government**: London exile PMs (1939-90) and Lublin/Warsaw communist PMs (1944-) overlap; select by the player's chosen government. Sanacja-era PMs (1926-35) were subordinate to Piłsudski.
- **Defence / war**: 1926-35 Piłsudski personally held the military affairs ministry; the Inspector General of the Armed Forces was the wartime commander-designate.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: 1918-39 no civilian intelligence chief; military intelligence was Section II (Oddział II) of the General Staff (chiefs not listed). 1956-90 the SB was part of the Interior Ministry (use interior). Since 2002 ABW = domestic security; Foreign Intelligence Agency (AW) chiefs not listed.
- **Military chief**: Second Republic: Chief of the General Staff (Main Staff from 1928) served under the Inspector General of the Armed Forces (Piłsudski 1926-35, Rydz-Śmigły 1935-39), who is arguably the real military chief in war.

- Polish chiefs of staff dates from Wikipedia only (cross-check source).
- Intelligence / security chief: Władysław Dworakowski (1954-12–1956-11) — from Nov 1956 the Security Service (SB) was part of the Interior Ministry: use the interior minister to 1990

## Republic of China (Taiwan) (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1895-04 | 1945-10 | Japanese Taiwan | colonial_or_occupied | Taihoku (Taipei) | revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1945-10 | 1949-12 | Taiwan Province of the Republic of China | colonial_or_occupied | Taipei (national capital Nanjing) | revolution |
| 1949-12 | 1987-07 | ROC on Taiwan: KMT one-party martial-law state | one_party_state | Taipei | death_in_office, party_congress, coup |
| 1987-07 | 1996-03 | ROC: democratic transition | semi_presidential_republic | Taipei | general_election, party_congress, presidential_dismissal |
| 1996-03 | present | ROC (Taiwan): democratic semi-presidential republic | semi_presidential_republic | Taipei | general_election, term_limit, impeachment, no_confidence, presidential_dismissal |

- **Japanese Taiwan (1895-04–1945-10)**:  Ceded to Japan by the Treaty of Shimonoseki; Japanese Governor-General. Not playable as a sovereign actor.
- **Taiwan Province of the Republic of China (1945-10–1949-12)**:  Province of mainland-ruled ROC (see CHN). February 28 Incident 1947.
- **ROC on Taiwan: KMT one-party martial-law state (1949-12–1987-07)**: President elected by the National Assembly (members frozen since 1947-48); Chiang Kai-shek re-elected until death; Temporary Provisions suspended term limits. Martial law 1949-05 to 1987-07. Claimed to be the government of all China; UN seat until 1971-10.
- **ROC: democratic transition (1987-07–1996-03)**:  Opposition DPP legalized; National Assembly and Legislative Yuan fully re-elected 1991-92.
- **ROC (Taiwan): democratic semi-presidential republic (1996-03–present)**: President directly elected for 4 years (max two terms); appoints the Premier without legislative consent since 1997. Legislative Yuan can pass no-confidence against the Premier (president may then dissolve the legislature). Presidential recall/impeachment requires supermajorities. Game: president removable by election/recall/impeachment; premier by presidential dismissal or no-confidence.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: The Premier (President of the Executive Yuan) heads the cabinet, but the President directs foreign, defence and cross-strait policy.
- **Defence / war**: 1949-1954 holders cross-checked only against Wikipedia's list (Yu Ta-wei's 1950-51 tenure was nominal).
- **Finance / treasury**: Not covered (tier 2 minimum: heads, foreign, defence).
- **Interior / home**: Not covered. Under martial law the Taiwan Garrison Command handled internal security.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: National Security Bureau (from 1955); directors not listed.
- **Military chief**: Chief of the General Staff not listed (gap).

## Saudi Arabia (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1902-01 | 1921-08 | Emirate of Riyadh / Nejd (Third Saudi State) | absolute_monarchy | Riyadh | death_in_office, family_council, coup, foreign_occupation |
| 1921-08 | 1932-09 | Sultanate of Nejd; Kingdom of Hejaz (1926) and Nejd (1927) | absolute_monarchy | Riyadh (Mecca for the Hejaz administration) | death_in_office, family_council, coup |
| 1932-09 | 1953-10 | Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (pre-Council of Ministers) | absolute_monarchy | Riyadh | death_in_office, family_council, coup |
| 1953-10 | 1992-03 | Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (Council of Ministers era) | absolute_monarchy | Riyadh | death_in_office, family_council, abdication, assassination, royal_dismissal |
| 1992-03 | present | Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (Basic Law) | absolute_monarchy | Riyadh | death_in_office, family_council, royal_dismissal |

- **Emirate of Riyadh / Nejd (Third Saudi State) (1902-01–1921-08)**: Abdulaziz ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh (15 Jan 1902) from the Rashidis; his father Abdul Rahman kept the honorific of Imam. Rule by conquest and tribal allegiance (bay'ah). Under British protection treaty (Darin, Dec 1915). No ministries: the ruler governs through family, ulema and tribal shaykhs.
- **Sultanate of Nejd; Kingdom of Hejaz (1926) and Nejd (1927) (1921-08–1932-09)**: Hereditary by royal designation; conquest of Hejaz 1924-25. Prince Faisal served as Viceroy of the Hejaz from 1926 and presided over its Council of Deputies. Treaty of Jeddah (May 1927) - British recognition of full independence. A Ministry of Foreign Affairs was created in Dec 1930 under Faisal.
- **Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (pre-Council of Ministers) (1932-09–1953-10)**: Agnatic seniority among sons of Abdulaziz; crown prince named by the king (Saud named 1933). Only a handful of ministries existed (Foreign Affairs 1930, Finance 1932, Defence 1944, Interior 1951). The king was his own head of government; worldstatesmen lists Faisal as head of the Hejaz council 1932-53 but there was no national prime minister.
- **Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (Council of Ministers era) (1953-10–1992-03)**: Council of Ministers founded 9 Oct 1953. Succession by agnatic seniority among Abdulaziz's sons, ratified by senior princes and the ulema (bay'ah). Saud was deposed in Nov 1964 by a family council backed by an ulema fatwa - the canonical 'family_council' removal. King Faisal was assassinated by a nephew in Mar 1975. The king is normally also President of the Council of Ministers (prime minister).
- **Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (Basic Law) (1992-03–present)**: Basic Law of Governance (Mar 1992) opens succession to grandsons of Abdulaziz; Allegiance Council created 2006. Crown princes have been replaced by royal order (Muqrin, Apr 2015; Muhammad bin Nayef, Jun 2017) - the game should model crown-prince removal as royal_dismissal rather than a vote. No legislature with confidence powers (the Consultative/Shura Council, 1993, is appointed and advisory). In Sep 2022 King Salman appointed Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Prime Minister, the first time since 1953-54/1960-62 that the king did not personally chair the cabinet.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of government**: No prime minister before 9 Oct 1953: the king ruled personally (game: king fills both offices). Since 1953 the king has normally chaired the Council of Ministers himself (game: one person, two offices), except Faisal 1954-60/1962-64 and MBS since Sep 2022.
- **Foreign affairs**: Faisal ran foreign affairs from 1926 (Hejaz) and formally from Dec 1930; before that Abdulaziz conducted diplomacy personally, largely with British agents.
- **Defence / war**: No ministry before 1943/44; Abdulaziz commanded the Ikhwan and tribal levies himself. The game should treat the king as defence minister pre-1944.
- **Finance / treasury**: Before 1932 the royal treasury (Bayt al-Mal) was run by Abdullah al-Sulaiman as the king's agent.
- **Interior / home**: No interior ministry before 1951 (a short-lived Hejaz interior function under Faisal 1931-34 is sometimes cited). Regional emirs governed provinces.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: General Intelligence Presidency (al-Ri'asa al-Amma lil-Istikhbarat) founded 1955. Before then: no public intelligence chief.
- **Military chief**: Chiefs of the General Staff before ~2014 are poorly documented in open sources; the defence minister (a senior prince) was the effective military chief. Game: use the defence minister as military chief pre-2014. Separate Saudi Arabian National Guard (commanded by Abdullah 1962-2010, Mutaib bin Abdullah 2010-17, Abdullah bin Bandar 2017-) answers directly to the king.

## South Africa (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1900-01 | 1910-05 | Boer republics (to 1902) and British colonies (Cape, Natal, Transvaal, Orange River Colony) | colonial_or_occupied | Pretoria / Bloemfontein / Cape Town / Pietermaritzburg | foreign_occupation |
| 1910-05 | 1961-05 | Union of South Africa | dominion | Pretoria (executive); Cape Town (legislature); Bloemfontein (judiciary) | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, death_in_office |
| 1961-05 | 1984-09 | Republic of South Africa (Westminster-style) | parliamentary_republic | Pretoria (executive); Cape Town (legislature); Bloemfontein (judiciary) | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership, assassination, death_in_office |
| 1984-09 | 1994-05 | Republic of South Africa (Tricameral constitution, executive State President) | presidential_republic | Pretoria (executive); Cape Town (legislature); Bloemfontein (judiciary) | loss_of_party_leadership, general_election, no_confidence |
| 1994-05 | present | Republic of South Africa (democratic, 1996 constitution) | parliamentary_republic | Pretoria (executive); Cape Town (legislature); Bloemfontein (judiciary) | no_confidence, impeachment, loss_of_party_leadership, general_election, term_limit |

- **Boer republics (to 1902) and British colonies (Cape, Natal, Transvaal, Orange River Colony) (1900-01–1910-05)**: Second Boer War: the South African Republic (Transvaal, President Paul Kruger) and Orange Free State (President M.T. Steyn) annexed by Britain in 1900; Treaty of Vereeniging 31 May 1902. Colonies under British governors; responsible government restored to Transvaal (1906, PM Louis Botha) and ORC (1907). Not a unified playable state before 31 May 1910. Game: treat as British colonial territory.
- **Union of South Africa (1910-05–1961-05)**: British monarch represented by a Governor-General; PM is leader of the majority in the House of Assembly (white electorate; limited Coloured/Black franchise in the Cape, removed 1936/1956). Sovereign independence confirmed by the Statute of Westminster (1931) and Status of the Union Act (1934). Smuts' government lost a parliamentary vote on entering WWII (Sep 1939), Hertzog resigned - Smuts became PM. National Party in power from 1948 (apartheid).
- **Republic of South Africa (Westminster-style) (1961-05–1984-09)**: Ceremonial State President elected by Parliament (7-year term). PM = leader of the National Party caucus. Verwoerd assassinated in Parliament (6 Sep 1966); Vorster resigned in the Information Scandal (1978). Left the Commonwealth on becoming a republic. Apartheid one-party dominance with white-only elections.
- **Republic of South Africa (Tricameral constitution, executive State President) (1984-09–1994-05)**: 1983 constitution merged PM and State President into an executive State President elected by an electoral college of the tricameral Parliament. P.W. Botha was forced to resign by his cabinet (Aug 1989) after losing the NP leadership to F.W. de Klerk. Negotiated transition 1990-94 (CODESA); Mandela released Feb 1990.
- **Republic of South Africa (democratic, 1996 constitution) (1994-05–present)**: Executive President elected by the National Assembly after each general election; max two terms. Removal: s.102 no-confidence vote (simple majority) or s.89 removal (two-thirds). In practice the ANC 'recalls' presidents: Mbeki resigned Sep 2008 after the ANC NEC recall; Zuma resigned Feb 2018 under threat of a no-confidence vote after losing the ANC presidency to Ramaphosa. ANC lost its majority in May 2024; Government of National Unity (ANC, DA, IFP and others) formed June 2024. Head of state and government are the same person.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: 1910-61 the British monarch was represented by a Governor-General (Gladstone, Buxton, Prince Arthur of Connaught, Athlone, Clarendon, Duncan, de Wet (acting), van Zyl, Jansen, Steyn (acting), Swart). Since 1984 head of state and government are one office.
- **Foreign affairs**: 1910-1927 foreign relations were conducted by the British Foreign Office/Colonial Office through the PM's office. 1927-1955 the PM was also Minister of External Affairs.
- **Interior / home**: Interior (to 1984), Internal Affairs (1984-85), Home Affairs (from 1985). Police/security was a separate Justice / Law and Order (Police) portfolio - for repression events the game may prefer the Minister of Justice/Police (e.g. B.J. Vorster 1961-66, Louis le Grange 1982-86, Adriaan Vlok 1986-91).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No civilian foreign intelligence service before BOSS (1969); the Security Branch of the police handled internal security. Post-2009 ministers responsible: Intelligence/State Security ministers (Ronnie Kasrils 2004-08, Siyabonga Cwele 2009-14, David Mahlobo 2014-17), then the Minister in the Presidency from 2021.
- **Military chief**: Union Defence Force (1912-57) -> South African Defence Force (1957-94) -> SANDF (1994-). Before 1920 the UDF had no single professional chief (Citizen Force Commandant-General C.F. Beyers resigned 1914 to lead the Maritz rebellion).

### Head of state

- 1910-05-31 → 1936-01-20: **George V**, King — Represented by Governor-General
- 1936-01-20 → 1936-12-11: **Edward VIII**, King
- 1936-12-11 → 1952-02-06: **George VI**, King (King of South Africa)

## South Korea (Republic of Korea) (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1897-10 | Joseon Kingdom | absolute_monarchy | Hanseong (Seoul) | death_in_office, coup, revolution, abdication |
| 1897-10 | 1910-08 | Korean Empire | absolute_monarchy | Hanseong (Seoul) | abdication, foreign_occupation |
| 1910-08 | 1945-08 | Japanese Korea (Chōsen) | colonial_or_occupied | Keijō (Seoul) | revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1945-09 | 1948-08 | United States Army Military Government in Korea | colonial_or_occupied | Seoul | foreign_occupation |
| 1948-08 | 1960-04 | First Republic | presidential_republic | Seoul (wartime Busan 1950-53) | general_election, revolution, impeachment |
| 1960-06 | 1961-05 | Second Republic | parliamentary_republic | Seoul | no_confidence, general_election, coup |
| 1961-05 | 1963-12 | Military junta (Supreme Council for National Reconstruction) | military_junta | Seoul | coup |
| 1963-12 | 1972-10 | Third Republic | presidential_republic | Seoul | general_election, term_limit, coup, assassination |
| 1972-10 | 1981-03 | Fourth Republic (Yushin) and 1979-80 transition | personalist_dictatorship | Seoul | assassination, coup, revolution |
| 1981-03 | 1988-02 | Fifth Republic | personalist_dictatorship | Seoul | revolution, coup, term_limit |
| 1988-02 | present | Sixth Republic | presidential_republic | Seoul | general_election, term_limit, impeachment |

- **Joseon Kingdom (1789–1897-10)**:  Qing tributary state; 'Hermit Kingdom'. Opened by the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1876. Ministers not modeled (tier 2).
- **Korean Empire (1897-10–1910-08)**: Emperor Gojong (1897-1907, forced to abdicate by Japan), Emperor Sunjong (1907-1910). Japanese protectorate from 1905 (Eulsa Treaty); annexed 1910-08-29. Cabinet (Uijeongbu) not modeled.
- **Japanese Korea (Chōsen) (1910-08–1945-08)**:  Japanese Governor-General. Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea in exile (Shanghai/Chongqing) 1919-45: not playable.
- **United States Army Military Government in Korea (1945-09–1948-08)**:  South of the 38th parallel.
- **First Republic (1948-08–1960-04)**: President elected by the National Assembly (1948), then directly (1952 amendment). Rhee removed term limits for himself (1954). Korean War 1950-53. Ended by the April Revolution after rigged 1960 election.
- **Second Republic (1960-06–1961-05)**: Prime Minister (Chang Myon) responsible to the bicameral National Assembly; ceremonial president. Overthrown by Park Chung-hee's 16 May 1961 coup.
- **Military junta (Supreme Council for National Reconstruction) (1961-05–1963-12)**: SCNR Chairman (Chang Do-yong, then Park Chung-hee from 1961-07).
- **Third Republic (1963-12–1972-10)**:  Park elected 1963, 1967, 1971 (third term after 1969 amendment).
- **Fourth Republic (Yushin) and 1979-80 transition (1972-10–1981-03)**: President chosen by the rubber-stamp National Conference for Unification; unlimited terms. Park assassinated 1979-10-26; Chun Doo-hwan's 12.12 coup (1979) and the Gwangju massacre (1980-05).
- **Fifth Republic (1981-03–1988-02)**: President elected indirectly by an electoral college for a single 7-year term. June 1987 Democratic Struggle forced direct elections.
- **Sixth Republic (1988-02–present)**: President directly elected for a single 5-year term. Impeachment by 2/3 of the National Assembly suspends the president; the Constitutional Court decides removal (Roh 2004 reinstated; Park 2017 and Yoon 2025 removed). PM appointed by the president with Assembly consent; acting president in a vacancy; new election within 60 days. Game: no no-confidence; removal by impeachment + court ruling or end of the single term. A failed self-coup (martial law) is a modeled path (2024).

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: The president is both head of state and real head of government (except the 1960-61 Second Republic).
- **Head of government**: The Prime Minister is an appointed deputy to the president (first in line to act as president) except in the Second Republic (Chang Myon), when the PM held executive power. 1954-1960 the post did not exist. 1961-63 'Chief Cabinet Minister' under the junta.
- **Finance / treasury**: Before 1998 economic policy was led by the Deputy PM/Minister of the Economic Planning Board (1961-94) and separate Ministers of Finance; those holders are a known gap. Listed from 1998 (Ministry of Finance and Economy; Ministry of Strategy and Finance 2008; English name Economy and Finance from 2018).
- **Interior / home**: Only Ministers of the Interior and Safety (2017-) are listed; earlier Home Affairs / Government Administration ministers are a known gap. 2024-12 to 2025-07 handled by vice-minister/acting.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: KCIA (1961) -> Agency for National Security Planning (1981) -> NIS (1999). 2023-11 to 2024-01 vacancy (acting first deputy director).
- **Military chief**: Operational wartime control of ROK forces rests with the U.S.-led Combined Forces Command (since 1978); peacetime control returned 1994.

## South Vietnam (State of Vietnam / Republic of Vietnam) (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1949-06 | 1955-10 | State of Vietnam (associated state of the French Union) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Saigon | royal_dismissal, foreign_occupation, coup |
| 1955-10 | 1963-11 | First Republic of Vietnam (Ngo Dinh Diem) | personalist_dictatorship | Saigon | coup, assassination |
| 1963-11 | 1967-10 | Military juntas | military_junta | Saigon | coup |
| 1967-10 | 1975-04 | Second Republic of Vietnam (Nguyen Van Thieu) | presidential_republic | Saigon | general_election, coup, foreign_occupation |

- **State of Vietnam (associated state of the French Union) (1949-06–1955-10)**: Former emperor Bao Dai as Chief of State (Quoc truong) under the Elysee Accords (Mar 1949); prime ministers appointed and dismissed by Bao Dai. Limited sovereignty under France until 1954. After Geneva (Jul 1954) confined to south of the 17th parallel. Bao Dai deposed by Diem's rigged referendum of 23 Oct 1955.
- **First Republic of Vietnam (Ngo Dinh Diem) (1955-10–1963-11)**: Presidential republic (1956 constitution) dominated by the Ngo family and the Can Lao party; no prime minister. Ended by the ARVN generals' coup of 1-2 Nov 1963 (Diem and Nhu killed) with US acquiescence.
- **Military juntas (1963-11–1967-10)**: Military Revolutionary Council (Duong Van Minh); Nguyen Khanh coup Jan 1964; repeated coups and a civilian interlude (Phan Khac Suu / Tran Van Huong / Phan Huy Quat); National Leadership Committee (Thieu chairman, Ky PM) from Jun 1965. Game: extreme instability - frequent coup checks.
- **Second Republic of Vietnam (Nguyen Van Thieu) (1967-10–1975-04)**: 1967 constitution: directly elected president (Thieu 1967, unopposed 1971). PM appointed by the president. Fell to North Vietnam on 30 Apr 1975; Provisional Revolutionary Government nominally ruled the South until reunification (2 Jul 1976).

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Foreign affairs**: Coverage partial: 1963-65 and 1967-69 foreign ministers changed with each junta reshuffle and are not listed.
- **Defence / war**: Under Diem the president held defence himself. Coverage partial and uncertain.
- **Finance / treasury**: Not covered - finance ministers rotated rapidly; game should use generic 'Minister of Finance'.
- **Interior / home**: Not covered. Under Diem the real security apparatus was run by his brother Ngo Dinh Nhu (Political Adviser) - the game may treat Nhu (1955-63) as the de facto interior/security chief.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Tran Kim Tuyen headed Diem's Office of Political and Social Studies (secret police) c.1956-62; later the Central Intelligence Organization (CIO, 1961-75). Heads not listed due to unverified dates.
- **Military chief**: Before Cao Van Vien the JGS chiefs changed with each coup (e.g. Le Van Ty 1955-63, Tran Van Don 1963, Tran Thien Khiem 1964). Military figures dominated government 1963-75.

## Sweden (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1809-06-06 | Kingdom of Sweden (Gustavian absolutism) | absolute_monarchy | Stockholm | coup, assassination, abdication, royal_dismissal |
| 1809-06-06 | 1917-10-19 | Kingdom of Sweden (1809 Instrument of Government, royal government) | constitutional_monarchy_executive | Stockholm | royal_dismissal, general_election |
| 1917-10-19 | present | Kingdom of Sweden (parliamentary democracy) | constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary | Stockholm | no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership |

- **Kingdom of Sweden (Gustavian absolutism) (1789–1809-06-06)**: Gustav III (assassinated 1792), Gustav IV Adolf (deposed by officers' coup 1809). Not covered in detail (tier 2). Outside required coverage; generic absolute-monarchy titles apply.
- **Kingdom of Sweden (1809 Instrument of Government, royal government) (1809-06-06–1917-10-19)**: Hereditary Bernadotte dynasty (from 1818). Ministers appointed by and responsible to the King; the Riksdag controlled taxation. Union with Norway 1814-1905. Office of Prime Minister (statsminister) from 1876. Courtyard Crisis 1914: Gustaf V's intervention forced Staaff out - royal dismissal was still possible.
- **Kingdom of Sweden (parliamentary democracy) (1917-10-19–present)**: Parliamentarism accepted from Edén's government (1917). Under the 1974 Instrument of Government the Speaker nominates the PM and the Riksdag tolerates him unless an absolute majority (175 of 349) votes against (negative parliamentarism); a declaration of no confidence (misstroendeförklaring) by an absolute majority forces the PM or a minister out (Löfven lost one in Jun 2021). Neutral/non-aligned through both World Wars and the Cold War; joined the EU 1995 and NATO 7 Mar 2024.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Defence / war**: Minister of War (Lantförsvarsdepartementet) and Minister for the Navy (Sjöförsvarsdepartementet, listed separately as navy_minister) until 1 Jul 1920, then a single Minister for Defence.
- **Finance / treasury**: 1976-1982 the ministry was split: the Minister for Economic Affairs (listed) held the senior role while a Budget Minister handled the budget.
- **Interior / home**: Sweden has had no stable interior ministry (Civil ministry to 1920; Inrikesdepartementet only 1947-1973 and 1996-1998). The Minister for Justice, responsible for the police and the Security Service, is listed as the game's interior advisor.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: Before 1964 security policing lay with the State Police / General Security Service (not public). Säpo heads listed from 1964 (year-level dates). The military service MUST (from 1994) is led by a general under the Supreme Commander - not listed.
- **Military chief**: No unified commander before Dec 1939: the King was nominal commander-in-chief and the Chief of the General Staff (army) is listed 1885-1937 (year-level). 1937-1939 gap (Defence Staff established 1937). Supreme Commander (ÖB) from 8 Dec 1939.

## Ukraine (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1789 | 1917-11 | Part of the Russian Empire (Galicia under Austria) | colonial_or_occupied | (Kiev was a Russian governorate seat; Lemberg/Lviv in Austrian Galicia) | revolution |
| 1917-11 | 1921-03 | Ukrainian People's Republic / Ukrainian State (Hetmanate) / Directory | revolutionary_government | Kyiv (frequently lost; government moved to Vinnytsia, Kamianets-Podilskyi) | coup, revolution, foreign_occupation |
| 1919-03 | 1991-08 | Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic | one_party_communist_state | Kharkiv to 1934; Kyiv from 1934 | party_congress, coup |
| 1991-08 | 1996-06 | Ukraine (independence; amended Soviet-era constitution) | semi_presidential_republic | Kyiv | general_election, impeachment, no_confidence, presidential_dismissal |
| 1996-06 | 2006-01 | Ukraine (1996 constitution, presidential-parliamentary) | semi_presidential_republic | Kyiv | general_election, impeachment, presidential_dismissal, no_confidence, revolution |
| 2006-01 | 2010-10 | Ukraine (2004 amendments, parliamentary-presidential) | semi_presidential_republic | Kyiv | general_election, impeachment, no_confidence, revolution |
| 2010-10 | 2014-02 | Ukraine (1996 constitution restored) | semi_presidential_republic | Kyiv | general_election, impeachment, presidential_dismissal, no_confidence, revolution |
| 2014-02 | present | Ukraine (2004 amendments restored) | semi_presidential_republic | Kyiv | general_election, impeachment, no_confidence, revolution |

- **Part of the Russian Empire (Galicia under Austria) (1789–1917-11)**: No Ukrainian state; the Cossack Hetmanate was abolished by 1764 and fully incorporated in 1780s. Not playable; use RUS (and AUT for Galicia).
- **Ukrainian People's Republic / Ukrainian State (Hetmanate) / Directory (1917-11–1921-03)**: Central Rada (1917-Apr 1918) overthrown by the German-backed coup of Hetman Pavlo Skoropadsky (Apr-Dec 1918), who was in turn overthrown by the Directory (Dec 1918). Contested by the Bolsheviks, Whites and Poland; the Treaty of Riga (Mar 1921) divided Ukraine between Soviet Russia and Poland. Government-in-exile continued to 1992. Civil-war state: game should treat as unstable, removal by coup/foreign occupation.
- **Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic (1919-03–1991-08)**: Constituent republic of the USSR from Dec 1922 (founding UN member 1945) but not sovereign: party leaders appointed by Moscow. Not playable separately; use RUS. 1941-44 under German occupation (Reichskommissariat Ukraine).
- **Ukraine (independence; amended Soviet-era constitution) (1991-08–1996-06)**: Independence declared 24 Aug 1991, confirmed by referendum 1 Dec 1991 (Kravchuk elected president the same day). Early presidential and parliamentary elections in 1994 after a Donbas miners' strike crisis.
- **Ukraine (1996 constitution, presidential-parliamentary) (1996-06–2006-01)**: President directly elected for 5 years (max two consecutive terms) and could dismiss the PM; the Rada could pass no confidence in the cabinet (e.g. Yushchenko cabinet, Apr 2001). The 2004 Orange Revolution forced a re-run of the presidential run-off (Yushchenko defeated Yanukovych).
- **Ukraine (2004 amendments, parliamentary-presidential) (2006-01–2010-10)**: PM nominated by the parliamentary majority coalition and appointed by the Rada; president nominates only the foreign and defence ministers. The Constitutional Court restored the 1996 text in Oct 2010.
- **Ukraine (1996 constitution restored) (2010-10–2014-02)**: Yanukovych fled during the Revolution of Dignity (Euromaidan); on 22 Feb 2014 the Rada voted him 'self-removed' from office (not a constitutional impeachment) and named Turchynov acting president.
- **Ukraine (2004 amendments restored) (2014-02–present)**: President directly elected for 5 years; impeachment needs 2/3 then 3/4 of the Rada plus court opinions (never used). The PM and cabinet are appointed by and responsible to the Rada (no-confidence possible, not within a year of approving the programme); the president nominates the PM (on the coalition's proposal) and the foreign and defence ministers, and appoints/dismisses the SBU head with Rada consent. Under martial law since 24 Feb 2022 elections are suspended, so Zelensky's 2019-24 term continues until elections can be held. Russia annexed Crimea (2014) and has occupied parts of the east and south since 2014/2022; full-scale war since Feb 2022.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Head of state**: 1921-91 no sovereign Ukrainian head of state (Ukrainian SSR leaders answer to Moscow; government-in-exile presidents are not modelled).
- **Military chief**: Until Mar 2020 the Chief of the General Staff was also the Commander-in-Chief; since 2020 the posts are separate and the Commander-in-Chief is listed (Chiefs of the General Staff since 2020: Korniychuk 2020-21, Shaptala 2021-24, Barhylevych 2024-25, Hnatov 2025-26, Skybiuk from Jul 2026 per Wikipedia).
- **Intelligence / security chief**: SBU = domestic security/counter-intelligence chief. Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) and Defence Intelligence (HUR, e.g. Kyrylo Budanov 2020-2026) not listed.
- **Defence / war**: Defence and foreign ministers are nominated by the president (since 2006/2014).

## Vietnam (tier 2)

### Periods

| From | To | Regime | Government type | Capital | Removal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1883-08 | 1945-03 | Nguyen dynasty under French protectorate (Annam, Tonkin) / French Indochina | colonial_or_occupied | Hue (imperial court); Hanoi (seat of the Governor-General of Indochina from 1902); Saigon (Cochinchina colony) | foreign_occupation, royal_dismissal, abdication |
| 1945-03 | 1945-08 | Empire of Vietnam (Japanese client state) | colonial_or_occupied | Hue | foreign_occupation, revolution, abdication |
| 1945-09 | 1976-07 | Democratic Republic of Vietnam (North Vietnam from 1954) | one_party_communist_state | Hanoi (government in the Viet Bac jungle base Dec 1946 - Oct 1954) | party_congress, death_in_office, foreign_occupation |
| 1976-07 | present | Socialist Republic of Vietnam | one_party_communist_state | Hanoi | party_congress, death_in_office |

- **Nguyen dynasty under French protectorate (Annam, Tonkin) / French Indochina (1883-08–1945-03)**: Emperors chosen/approved by the French Resident-Superior; Thanh Thai (1907) and Duy Tan (1916) were deposed and exiled by France. Not sovereign: the French Governor-General of Indochina held real power. The court's Co Mat (Privy Council) ministers were figureheads. Japanese occupation from Sep 1940 (Vichy French administration left in place).
- **Empire of Vietnam (Japanese client state) (1945-03–1945-08)**: After the Japanese coup against the French (9 Mar 1945) Bao Dai proclaimed independence; Tran Trong Kim cabinet. Ended by the Viet Minh August Revolution; Bao Dai abdicated 25/30 Aug 1945.
- **Democratic Republic of Vietnam (North Vietnam from 1954) (1945-09–1976-07)**: Proclaimed by Ho Chi Minh 2 Sep 1945. Real power with the Indochinese Communist Party / Vietnam Workers' Party (1951) Politburo. Leadership changes by Central Committee plenum or party congress (e.g. Truong Chinh demoted after the 1956 land-reform errors; Le Duan First Secretary from the 3rd Congress, 1960). First Indochina War 1946-54 (Geneva Accords split the country at the 17th parallel); Vietnam War 1955-75; reunification after the fall of Saigon (30 Apr 1975).
- **Socialist Republic of Vietnam (1976-07–present)**: Communist Party of Vietnam congress every five years elects the Central Committee, which elects the Politburo and General Secretary. The National Assembly then 'elects' the State President, Prime Minister and NA Chairman as nominated by the party ('four pillars'). Since 2023-24 anti-corruption campaign, office-holders are frequently removed by forced resignation (Phuc 2023, Thuong 2024, Hue 2024) - model as party_congress. Doi Moi reforms from the 6th Congress (Dec 1986). 14th Congress (Jan 2026) re-elected To Lam as General Secretary; in Apr 2026 he was also elected State President, combining the top two posts.

### Role notes (game handling)

- **Paramount leader (party)**: The party General Secretary is the real ruler and the game's player office for the DRV/SRV; State President and PM are senior advisors ('four pillars' collective leadership with the NA Chairman). Removal only via Central Committee/Politburo (party_congress) or death.
- **Head of state**: 1883-1945 the French Governor-General of Indochina (e.g. Paul Doumer 1897-1902, Albert Sarraut 1911-14/1917-19, Jean Decoux 1940-45) held real power; emperors were figureheads. Game: not playable before Sep 1945 (or treat France as owner).
- **Head of government**: No responsible cabinet under the protectorate; the emperor's Co Mat (Privy Council) had no autonomy.
- **Interior / home**: DRV Interior Ministry (civil) 1945-; Ministry of Public Security (police and intelligence) from 1953, renamed Ministry of the Interior 1975-1998, then Public Security again. For the game the Public Security minister is the interior/security advisor.
- **Intelligence / security chief**: No separate public intelligence chief: domestic and foreign intelligence (General Department of Security / General Department V) sit within the Ministry of Public Security; military intelligence (General Department II) is under Defence and its chiefs are not public. Game: use the interior (Public Security) holder as intelligence chief.
- **Military chief**: Vo Nguyen Giap was Commander-in-Chief of the VPA throughout 1945-1980 and outranked the Chief of the General Staff; for 1946-1975 the game may prefer Giap as military chief.

## Generic role titles (tier 3)

### absolute_monarchy

- Head of state: King / Emperor / Sultan / Shah / Emir
- Head of government: Chief Minister / Grand Vizier / Chancellor (appointed by and serving at the pleasure of the monarch)
- Foreign affairs: Minister / Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of War
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance / Treasurer
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior / Royal Household
- Intelligence / security chief: — (role does not exist; see notes)
- Military chief: Commander-in-Chief (often the monarch or a royal prince)
- Removal: royal_dismissal, death_in_office, abdication, coup, revolution, assassination, foreign_occupation
- Notes: Monarch may act as own foreign minister and commander. Ministers removed by royal dismissal; ruler removed only by death, abdication, palace coup, revolution or foreign conquest. Before c.1900 there is usually no standing intelligence chief: model as a court/police function.

### constitutional_monarchy_parliamentary

- Head of state: King / Queen / Emperor (ceremonial)
- Head of government: Prime Minister
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence (Minister of War / of the Navy before c.1945)
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior / Home Affairs
- Intelligence / security chief: Director of the Intelligence/Security Service
- Military chief: Chief of the Defence Staff / Chief of the General Staff
- Removal: no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership
- Notes: Monarch reigns but does not rule; PM depends on parliamentary majority.

### constitutional_monarchy_executive

- Head of state: King / Emperor (holds executive power)
- Head of government: Minister-President / Chancellor / Prime Minister (answerable to the crown)
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of War
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior
- Intelligence / security chief: — (role does not exist; see notes)
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff
- Removal: royal_dismissal, abdication, revolution, coup
- Notes: Parliament controls budgets but cannot directly dismiss ministers; removal is by the monarch.

### parliamentary_republic

- Head of state: President (largely ceremonial, elected by parliament or people)
- Head of government: Prime Minister / Chancellor / Premier
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior
- Intelligence / security chief: Director of the National Intelligence Service
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff / Chief of Defence
- Removal: no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership

### presidential_republic

- Head of state: President
- Head of government: President (head of state and government)
- Foreign affairs: Secretary / Minister of Foreign Affairs (Foreign Relations)
- Defence / war: Minister / Secretary of Defence (National Defence)
- Finance / treasury: Minister / Secretary of Finance (Treasury)
- Interior / home: Minister / Secretary of the Interior (Government)
- Intelligence / security chief: Director of National Intelligence
- Military chief: Chief of the Armed Forces Joint Staff
- Removal: impeachment, term_limit, general_election, coup
- Notes: Fixed terms; legislature cannot dismiss president except by impeachment.

### semi_presidential_republic

- Head of state: President
- Head of government: Prime Minister (appointed by the president, responsible to parliament)
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance / Economy
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior
- Intelligence / security chief: Director of the State Security / Intelligence Service
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff / Chief of Defence Staff
- Removal: general_election, impeachment, no_confidence, presidential_dismissal
- Notes: President removed by election/impeachment; PM by no-confidence or presidential dismissal.

### one_party_communist_state

- Head of state: Chairman of the Presidium / President of the State
- Head of government: Premier / Chairman of the Council of Ministers
- Paramount leader (party): General Secretary (First Secretary) of the Central Committee
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of National Defence
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior / Public Security
- Intelligence / security chief: Chairman of State Security (secret police)
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff
- Removal: party_congress, death_in_office, coup, revolution
- Notes: Real power sits with the party General Secretary and Politburo; the game should treat the GS as the player's office and state posts as advisors. No-confidence does not exist; removal is by Politburo/Central Committee vote, death, or revolution.

### one_party_state

- Head of state: President / Leader
- Head of government: Prime Minister / Leader of the ruling party
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence / War
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior
- Intelligence / security chief: Chief of the Secret Police / State Security
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff
- Removal: coup, revolution, party_congress, foreign_occupation, death_in_office
- Notes: Legislature is a rubber stamp; removal by coup, party intrigue, revolution or defeat in war.

### military_junta

- Head of state: Chairman of the Junta / President of the Revolutionary Command Council
- Head of government: Chairman of the Junta (or appointed Prime Minister)
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs (often a civilian technocrat)
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence (a junta member)
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance (often a civilian technocrat)
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior (usually a general)
- Intelligence / security chief: Director of Military Intelligence / State Security
- Military chief: Commanders of the Army, Navy and Air Force (collectively the junta)
- Removal: junta_decision, coup, revolution
- Notes: No elections or no-confidence; leader removed by counter-coup within the junta, popular revolution, or negotiated return to civilian rule.

### personalist_dictatorship

- Head of state: President / Leader (for life in practice)
- Head of government: President / Prime Minister (figurehead)
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior
- Intelligence / security chief: Head of the Presidential Guard / Secret Police
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff
- Removal: coup, revolution, assassination, death_in_office
- Notes: Ministers are courtiers removed at will. Ruler removed by death, coup, assassination or revolution.

### theocratic_republic

- Head of state: Supreme Leader
- Head of government: President (elected; government head under the Supreme Leader)
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Economy and Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior
- Intelligence / security chief: Minister of Intelligence
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff of the Armed Forces
- Removal: religious_council, general_election, impeachment, revolution
- Notes: Supreme Leader removable only by the clerical Assembly of Experts (never used); president by election, parliamentary impeachment or Supreme Leader dismissal.

### revolutionary_government

- Head of state: President of the Provisional Government / Chairman of the Revolutionary Council
- Head of government: Chairman of the Provisional Government
- Foreign affairs: Commissioner / Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Commissioner / Minister of War
- Finance / treasury: Commissioner / Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Commissioner / Minister of the Interior
- Intelligence / security chief: Head of the Revolutionary Security Committee
- Military chief: Commander-in-Chief of the Revolutionary Army
- Removal: coup, revolution, party_congress
- Notes: Short-lived and unstable; removal by factional purge, coup or counter-revolution.

### colonial_or_occupied

- Head of state: Foreign sovereign (represented by a Governor-General / High Commissioner / Military Governor)
- Head of government: Governor-General / Military Governor (or a collaborating Prime Minister)
- Foreign affairs: — (role does not exist; see notes)
- Defence / war: — (role does not exist; see notes)
- Finance / treasury: Colonial Treasurer
- Interior / home: Colonial Secretary / Chief Secretary
- Intelligence / security chief: — (role does not exist; see notes)
- Military chief: Garrison Commander (foreign)
- Removal: revolution, foreign_occupation
- Notes: Not playable as a sovereign actor; foreign and defence policy are controlled by the metropole/occupier. Ends by independence, revolution or the occupier's withdrawal.

### dominion

- Head of state: British Monarch (represented by a Governor-General)
- Head of government: Prime Minister
- Foreign affairs: Secretary of State for External Affairs (handled by London before the 1920s-1931)
- Defence / war: Minister of Defence / Militia and Defence
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance / Treasurer
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior / Home Affairs
- Intelligence / security chief: — (role does not exist; see notes)
- Military chief: Chief of the General Staff
- Removal: no_confidence, general_election, loss_of_party_leadership
- Notes: Parliamentary (Westminster) system; foreign policy autonomy grew after the 1926 Balfour Declaration and 1931 Statute of Westminster.

### empire_napoleonic

- Head of state: Emperor
- Head of government: Emperor (no prime minister; ministers report individually)
- Foreign affairs: Minister of Foreign Affairs
- Defence / war: Minister of War
- Finance / treasury: Minister of Finance
- Interior / home: Minister of the Interior / Minister of Police
- Intelligence / security chief: Minister of General Police
- Military chief: Major-General (Chief of Staff) of the Grande Armée
- Removal: abdication, foreign_occupation, revolution, coup
- Notes: Authoritarian empire with plebiscitary legitimacy; ends by military defeat, abdication or revolution.
